chunks: ANATOMY OF ANS DR TAHIR HUSSAIN MBBS, DLO, MPhil, CHPE, (FCPS) DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 2 OBJECTIVES JSMU-2026 Describe the anatomical components of ANS Differentiate between sympathetic and parasympathetic systems based on gross structure and distribution DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 3 INTRODUCTION TO THE ANS Part of the Peripheral Nervous System (PNS). Controls involuntary functions (heart rate, digestion, respiration). Maintains homeostasis automatically. DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 4 DIFFERENCE BETWEEN SOMATIC AND AUTONOMIC NS Somatic NS Autonomic NS Effector Skeletal muscles Cardiac muscle, smooth muscles and glands Control of motor neuron Voluntary Involuntary Motor neuron Direct connection between CNS and effector Autonomic ganglion inserted between CNS and effector DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 5 DIVISIONS OF THE ANS Sympathetic Nervous System: "Fight or Flight" Parasympathetic Nervous System: "Rest and Digest" DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 7 SYMPATHETIC VS PARASYMPATHETIC NS Feature Sympathetic Parasympathetic Origin Thoracolumbar Craniosacral Ganglia Near spinal cord Near target organs Fiber Length Short pre-, long post- ganglionic Long pre-, short post- ganglionic Main NT Norepinephrine Acetylcholine DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 9 SYMPATH

ETIC NERVOUS SYSTEM DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 10 SYMPATHETIC GANGLIA TYPES Paravertebral Ganglia (sympathetic trunk) Prevertebral Ganglia (celiac, superior mesenteric, inferior mesenteric) DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 11 PARAVERTEBRAL GANGLIA They are interconnected to form 2 sympathetic chains, one on each side of vertebral column. Number of ganglia: 3 in cervical part of chain 11 to 12 in thoracic part 4 in lumbar & sacral parts each. The chains end into a common ‘ganglion impar’ in front of coccyx DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 12 PREGANGLIONIC FIBERS Run in the ventral roots of the spinal nerve. Travel through the spinal nerve, and then join the sympathetic chain via the white rami communicants. (WRC) DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 13 PREGANGLIONIC FIBERS Cont. Within the sympathetic chain, these fibers may: Ascend, descend or remain at the same level to synapse with neurons (postganglionic) of paravertebral ganglia located in sympathetic chain. Leave the sympathetic chain (without synapse) to reach coeliac & mesenteric ganglia (around branches of abdominal aorta) to synapse with their neurons (postganglionic). DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 15 POSTGANGLIONIC FIBERS From the sympathetic chain ganglia enter again into the spinal nerve throu

gh grey rami communicants (GRC) to supply structures in head & thorax + blood vessels & sweat glands. From the cells of coeliac & mesenteric ganglia supply abdominal & pelvic viscera. DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 17 PARASYMPATHETIC NERVOUS SYSTEM Origin: Brainstem (cranial nerves III, VII, IX, X) and S2-S4. Long preganglionic fibers; short postganglionic fibers. Ganglia located near or inside target organs. DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 19 PARASYMPATHETIC DIVISION Cont. Preganglionic fibers from cranial outflow are carried by 3rd, 7th, 9th & 10th cranial nerves and terminate in Ciliary, Pterygopalatine, Submandibular & Otic ganglia Postganglionic fibers innervate organs of the head, neck. DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 20 PARASYMPATHETIC DIVISION Cont. Preganglionic fibers from sacral outflow are carried by pelvic splanchnic nerves to peripheral ganglia in pelvis where they synapse. Postganglionic fibers innervate organs of the pelvis and lower abdomen. DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 21 POST-ASSESSMENT Briefly describe the difference in neuron length between the sympathetic and parasympathetic pathways. DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 22 SUMMARY ANS controls involuntary actions. Sympathetic = Emergency, Parasympathetic = Calm. Structure: Different
origins, fiber lengths, ganglia locations. Critical for survival and homeostasis.

chunks: MUSCULAR AND FASCICULAR ARCHITECTURE Dr. Faizan Ahmed MUSCLES: “Muscle is a contractile tissue which brings about movements. Muscles can be regarded as motors of the body.” Derivation of Name: Muscles (L. Mus = mouse) are so named because, many of them resemble a mouse, with their tendons representing the tail. A. Contractile tissue: • Each muscle is composed of numerous muscle fibres. • Each muscle fibre is a multinucleated, cross-striated cylindrical cell (myocyte) • It is made up of sarcolemma (cell membrane) enclosing sarcoplasm (cytoplasm). • Embedded in the sarcoplasm there are several hundred of nuclei arranged at the periphery beneath the sarcolemma and a number of evenly distributed longitudinal threads called myofibrils. • Each myofibril shows alternate dark and light bands. Dark bands are known as A bands (anistropic) and the light bands as I bands (isotropic). • The bands of adjacent fibrils are aligned transversely so that the muscle fibre appears cross-striated. • In the middle of dark band there is a (light) H band with M band (dark), in its middle. In the middle of I band there is a dark Z disc or Krause's membrane, the segment of myofibril between two Z discs is ca

lled sarcomere. B. Supporting tissue: • It helps in organization of the muscle. • Endomysium: surrounds each muscle fibre separately. • Perimysium: surrounds bundles (fasciculi or myonemes) of muscle fibres of various sizes. • Epimysium: surrounds the entire muscle. The connective tissue of the muscle becomes continuous with the tendon (Fig. 4.6). Slow and Fast Muscle Fibres (Dubowitz, 1969; Gauthier and Schaeffer, 1974): 1. Type I (slow) fibres: 2. Type II (fast) fibres: 3. Intermediate fibres: • Show a slow 'tonic' contraction characteristic of postural muscles. • These are red in colour because of large amounts of myoglobin. • The fibres are rich in mitochondria and oxidative enzymes, but poor in phosphorylases. • Because of a well-developed aerobic metabolism, slow fibres are highly resistant to fatigue. • Show a fast 'phasic' contraction required for large-scale movements of body segments. • These are paler (white) in colour because of small amounts of myoglobin. • The fibres are rich in glycogen and phosphorylases, but poor in mitochondria and oxidative enzymes. • Because of a glycolytic respiration, the fast fibres are quite easily fatigued. • Represent a variant of type II

(fast) fibres which are relatively resistant to fatigue, although less than type I (slow) fibres (Burkeetal, 1973). Fascicular Architecture of Muscles: • The arrangement of muscle fibres varies according to the direction, force and range of habitual movement at a particular joint. • The force of movement is directly proportional to the number and size of muscle fibres. • The range of movement is directly proportional to the length of fibres. • The muscles can be classified according to the arrangement of their fasciculi into the following groups (Fig. 4.7). A. Parallel Fasciculi: When the fasciculi are parallel to the line of pull, the muscle may be : 1. Quadrilateral (thyrohyoid), 2. Strap-like (sternohyoid and sartorius). 3. Strap-like with tendinous intersections (rectus abdominis). 4. Fusiform (biceps brachii, digastric, etc.). The range of movement in such muscles is maximum (Fig. 4.7). B. Oblique Fasciculi: When the fasciculi are oblique to the line of pull, the muscle may be triangular, or pennate (feather-like) in the construction. This arrangement makes the muscle more powerful, although the range of movement is reduced. Oblique arrangements are of the following types: 1.

Triangular, e.g. temporalis, adductor longus. 2. Unipennate, e.g. flexor pollicis longus, extensor digitorum longus, peroneus tertius, palmar interossei (Fig. 4.8). 3. Bipennate, e.g. rectus femoris, dorsal interossei (Fig. 4.7), peroneus longus, flexor hallucis longus. 4. Multipennate, e.g. subscapularis, deltoid (acromial fibres) (Fig. 4.8). 5. Circumpennate, e.g. tibialis anterior (Fig. 4.7). C. Spiral or Twisted Fasciculi: • Spiral or twisted fibres are found in trapezius, pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi, supinator, etc. (Fig. 4.9). • In certain muscles the fasciculi are crossed. These are called cruciate muscles, e.g.sternocleido-mastoid, masseter, and adductor magnus.

chunks: Definition Joint is a junction between two or more bones or cartilages. It is a device to permit movements. Components of joints Cartilage: covers the surface of a bone at a joint. Cartilage helps reduce the friction of movement within a joint. Synovial membrane: lines the joint and seals it into a joint capsule. The synovial membrane secretes a clear, sticky fluid (synovial fluid) around the joint to lubricate it. Ligaments: Strong ligaments (tough, elastic bands of connective tissue) surround the joint to give support and limit the joint's movement. Ligaments connect bones together. Tendons: Tendons (another type of tough connective tissue) on each side of a joint attach to muscles that control movement of the joint. Tendons connect muscles to bones. Bursas: Fluid-filled sacs, called bursas, between bones, ligaments, or other nearby structures. They help cushion the friction in a joint. Synovial fluid: A clear, thick fluid secreted by the synovial membrane. Meniscus: This is a curved part of cartilage in the knees and other joints. Functional Classification(according to the degree of mobility) 1. Synarthrosis (immovable), like fibrous joints 2. Amphiarthrosis (slightly m

ovable), like cartilaginous joints 3. Diarthrosis (freely movable), like synovial joints Regional Classification 1. Skull type: immovable. 2. Vertebral type: slightly movable. 3. Limb type: freely movable. According to number of articulating bones 1. Simple joint: When two bones articulate, e.g. interphalangeal joints 2. Compound joint: More than two bones articulate within one capsule, e.g. elbow joint, wrist joint  3. Complex joint: When joint cavity is divided by an intra-articular disc, e.g., temporomandibular FIBROUS JOINTS In fibrous joints the bones are joined by fibrous tissue. These joints are either immovable or permit a slight degree of movement.  These can be grouped in the following three subtypes 1. Sutures(skull bones) 2. Syndesmosis(Interosseous ligament) 3. Gomphosis(tooth in socket) CARTILAGINOUS JOINTS 1. Primary cartilaginous joints (synchondrosis, or hyaline cartilage joints) 2. Secondary cartilaginous joints (symphyses or fibrocartilaginous joints) SYNOVIAL JOINTS Synovial joints are most evolved, and, therefore, most mobile type of joints Characters 1. The articular surfaces are covered with hyaline (articular) cartilage. 2. Between the articular

surfaces there is a joint cavity filled with synovial fluid. 3. The joint is surrounded by an articular capsule which is made up of a fibrous capsule lined by synovial membrane. 4. Varying degrees of movements are always permitted by the synovial joints. Classification of Synovial Joints and their Movements Type of Joint  A. Plane or gliding type  B. Uniaxial joints  1. Hinge joint  2. Pivot joint  C. Biaxial joints  1. Condylar joint  2. Ellipsoid joint  D. Multiaxial joints  1. Saddle joint  2. Ball-and-socket (spheroidal) joint Movement  Gliding movement  Flexion and extension  Rotation only  Flexion and extension, and limited rotation  Flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, and circumduction  Flexion and extension, abduction, adduction, and conjunct rotation  Flexion and extension ,abduction, adduction, circumduction, and medial and lateral rotation Classification of Synovial Joints 1. Plane Synovial Joints Articular surfaces are more or less flat (plane). They permit gliding movements (translations) in various directions. 2. Hinge Joints (Ginglymi) Articular surfaces are pulley-shaped. There are strong collateral ligaments. Movements are permitted in one

plane around a transverse axis. 3. Pivot (Trochoid) Joints Articular surfaces comprise a central bony pivot (peg) surrounded by an osteoligamentous ring. Movements are permitted in one plane around a vertical axis. 4. Condylar (Bicondylar) Joints Articular surfaces include two distinct condyles (convex male surfaces) fitting into reciprocally concave female surfaces. 5. Ellipsoid Joints Articular surfaces include an oval, convex, male surface fitting into an elliptical, concave female surface. 6. Saddle (Sellar) Joints Articular surfaces are reciprocally concavoconvex. Movements are similar to those permitted by an ellipsoid joint, with addition of some rotation (conjunct rotation) 7. Ball-and-Socket (Spheroidal) Joints Articular surfaces include a globular head (male surface) fitting into a cup-shaped socket (female surface). MECHANISM OF LUBRICATION OF A SYNOVIAL JOINT 1. Synovial fluid, secreted by synovial membrane, It serves the main function of lubrication of the joint, but also nourishes the articular cartilage. 2. Hyaline cartilage covering the articular surfaces possesses inherent slipperiness, like that of the ice. 3. Intra-articular fibrocartilages, articular dis

cs or menisci,complete or incomplete, help in spreading the synovial fluid throughout the joint cavity.  4. Haversian fatty pads (Haversian glands) occupy extra spaces in the joint cavity between the incongruous bony surfaces. All of them are covered with synovial membrane, and perhaps function as swabs to spread the synovial fluid. 5. Bursa is a synovial fluid filled bag in relation to joints and bones,to prevent friction. The inflammation of bursa is called bursitis. BLOOD SUPPLY OF SYNOVIAL JOINTS The articular and epiphysial branches given off by the neighbouring arteries form a arterial plexus. This plexus pierce the fibrous capsule and form a rich vascular plexus in the deeper parts of synovial membrane. The blood vessels of the synovial membrane terminate around the articular margins in a fringe of looped anastomoses termed the circulus vasculosus (circulus articularis vasculosus).  It supplies capsule, synovial membrane, and the epiphysis. The articular cartilage is avascular. After epiphysial fusion, communications between circulus vasculosus and the end arteries of metaphysis are established, thus minimizing the chances of osteomyelitis in the metaphysis. NERVE SUP

PLY OF SYNOVIAL JOINTS The capsule and ligaments possess a rich nerve supply, which makes them acutely sensitive to pain. The principles of distribution of nerves to joints were first described by Hilton (1891). Hilton's law states that a motor nerve to the muscle acting on joint tends to give a branch to that joint (capsule) and another branch to the skin covering the joint. The concept of innervation of a joint was further elucidated by Gardner (1948) who observed that each nerve innervates a specific region of the capsule, and that the part of the capsule which is rendered taut by a given muscle is innervated by the nerve supplying its antagonists. Thus the pattern of innervation is concerned with the maintenance of an efficient stability at the joint. LYMPHATIC DRAINAGE OF SYNOVIAL JOINTS Lymphatics form a plexus in the subintima of the synovial membrane, and drain along the blood vessels to the regional deep nodes. STABILITY OF SYNOVIAL JOINTS The various factors maintaining stability at a joint are described here in order of their importance. 1. Muscles: The tone of different groups of muscles acting on the joint is the most important and indispensable factor in maintaining

the stability. 2. Ligaments: Are important in preventing any over-movement, and in guarding against sudden accidental stresses. However, they do not help against a continuous strain, because once stretched, they tend to remain elongated. 3. Bones: Help in maintaining stability only in firm type of joints, like the hip and ankle. CLINICAL ANATOMY If disc prolapse occurs in lumbar or sacral nerves, there is radiating pain in the lower limb, then the condition is called Sciatica Inflammatory systemic disease resulting in thickened synovial membrane of small joints Rheumatoid arthritis Degenerative condition of the large weight- bearing joints. The articular cartilage wears out, degenerates and there is formation of peripheral osteophytes Osteoarthritis

chunks: Skeleton system Prof Dr Imran Ishaque HOD Anatomy UNDC OBJECTIVES • By the end of the lecture, the student will be able to: 1. Define skeleton system. 2. List the function of skeleton system. 3. Define bone 4. Composition of bone 5. Classification of bone • According to shape • Developmental classification • Regional • According to structure 1. Describes the structure of long bone 2. Describes the structure of periostem and endosteum 3. Parts of long bone 4. Types of epiphysis 5. Blood supply of long bone 6. Applied anatomy of bone • The skeleton composed of bones, cartilages and ligaments joins tightly to form strong flexible frame work of the body. The Adult Human Skeleton Is Made Up of 206 Bones Bones Are Grouped into the Axial Skeleton and the Appendicular Skeleton 1. Axial skeleton: bones forming the trunk (longitudinal axis) of body 2. Appendicular skeleton: bones forming the girdles & limbs Bones • Definition: The dense, semirigid, porous, calcified connective tissue forming the major portion of the skeleton. • It consists of a dense organic matrix and an inorganic, mineral component. GENERAL FEATURES • Bone is rigid and hard because the matrix is infiltrated with inorganic

salts. • Bone gives attachment to muscles and serves as a lever for muscular action. • It bears body weight. • It protects vital organs like brain, heart and lungs. • Bone stores calcium, phosphate and other ions. • It contains bone marrow, which is a haemopoietic tissue. (d) Flat Bones Flat bones have thin, parallel surfaces. Flat bones form the roof of the skull, the sternum (breastbone), the ribs, and scapulae (shoulder blades). They provide protection for underlying soft tissues and offer an extensive surface area for the attachment of skeletal muscles. Parietal bone Sectional view (e) Long Bones Humerus Long bones are relatively long and slender. They are located in the arm and forearm, thigh and leg, palms, soles, fingers, and toes. The femur, the long bone of the thigh, is the largest and heaviest bone In the body. (f) Sesamoid Bones Patella Sesamoid bones are usually small, round, and flat. They develop inside tendons and are most often encountered near joints at the knee, the hands, and the feet. Few individuals have sesamoid bones at every possible location, but everyone has sesamoid patellae (pa-TEL-e; singular, patella, a small shallow dish), or kneecaps. – (a) Sutural

Bones Sutural bones, or Wormian bones, are small, flat, oddly shaped bones found between the flat bones of the skull. They range in size from a grain of sand to a quarter. Their borders are like pieces of a jigsaw puzzle. Sutures Sutural bone (b) Irregular Bones Irregular bones have complex shapes with short, flat, notched, or ridged surfaces. The vertebrae that form the spinal column, the bones of the pelvis, and several bones in the skull are examples of irregular bones. Vertebra Carpal bones (c) Short Bones Short bones are boxlike in appearance. Examples of short bones include the carpal bones (wrists) and tarsal bones (ankles). Pneumatic Bones 1. These bones contain air filled spaces 2. Lined by mucous membrane. 3. They are present around the nasal cavity. 4. They help in adding resonance to the voice. 5. They make the skull light in weight 6. Act as air conditioning chambers for the inspired air. 7. Examples: Maxilla, sphenoid, ethmoid, frontal • Sinusitis is an inflammation of the mucous membranes that line the sinuses. • Resulting in symptoms that may include production of thick nasal mucus, nasal congestion, facial congestion, facial pain, facial pressure, loss of smell, or

fever • Sesamoid bones are the bones that are embedded in the tendons e.g. patella in the tendon of quadriceps femoris and pisiform in the tendon of flexor carpi ulnaris. Characteristic features • They develop in the tendons and ossify after birth. • They are found where the tendons cross the end of long bones of limbs. • They are not covered by periosteum. • They don’t have Haversian system. • Their surface that comes in contact with the bone is covered by hyaline cartilage. Functions 1. To minimize friction 2. To alter the direction of pull of a muscle. 3. To maintain local circulation. • Short bones • Their shape is usually cuboid. • They have a central marrow cavity • They ossify in cartilage. • They ossify after birth • Examples – carpals and tarsals. Flat bones • Consist of two plates of compact bone with intervening spongy tissue (skull bones it is called diploe). • Examples: 1. Bones of vault of skull 2. Ribs 3. Sternum. Irregular bones • They are irregular in shape. • Examples Hip bone, vertebra, bones of base of skull (sphenoid, maxilla, ethmoid). Long Bones 1. Their length exceeds the breadth. 2. They are weight bearing. 3. A long bone presents a shaft and two ends. 4.

The shaft ossifies from primary center of ossification (appears before birth) and ends ossify from secondary centers of ossification (usually appear after birth. 5. The shaft consists of tube of compact bone which contains medullary cavity filled with bone marrow. 6. They ossify in cartilages. 7. Examples – humerus, femur, radius, ulna, tibia, fibula. • Miniature long bones have only one epiphysis 1. Metacarpals 2. Metatarsals 3. Phalanges • Modified long bones have no medullary cavity like clavicle Periostium • It is a dense connective tissue membrane covering the external surface of bone, except on articular surfaces, sesamoid bones and at the attachments of tendons and ligaments. • Periosteum sends perforating fibres perpendicular to the bone surface to nail or anchor it to the cortical bone. These fibres are called Sharpey’s fibres. • Periosteum also has two layers 1. Outer vascular fibrous layer 2. Inner cellular osteogenic layer • It has rich nerve supply and is very sensitive. • It is involved in bone growth and repair PRESSURE EPIPHYSIS • Pressure epiphyses assist in transmitting the weight of the human body and are the regions of the bone that are under pressure during mov

ement or locomotion. • Example of a pressure epiphysis is the head of the humerus which is part of the shoulder complex and head of the femur, part of the hip joint complex. TRACTION EPIPHYSIS • The regions of the long bone which are non-articular. Traction epiphyses ossify later than pressure epiphyses. • Tubercles of the humerus • Trochanters of the femur • Aberrant Epiphysis: • These epiphyses are deviations from the norm and are not always present. • For example, Epiphysis at the head of the first metacarpal bone • Atavistic Epiphysis: • These types of fused bones are called atavistic • e.g. the coracoid process of the scapula which has been fused in humans but is separate in four-legged animals Nutrient Artery • It enters the shaft through the nutrient foramen. • Runs obliquely through the cortex of shaft. • Reaches medullary cavity and divides into ascending and descending branches. • These branches reach the metaphysis and form ‘hair pin loops’ and anastomose with the metaphyseal and epiphyseal arteries. • Nutrient artery supplies the 1. Medullary cavity 2. Inner 2/3rd of cortical bone of diaphysis 3. Metaphysis Periosteal arteries • Periosteal arteries are the arteries of p

eriosteum being especially numerous beneath the muscular and ligamentous attachment. • Beneath the Periosteum they divide into branches and thereby entering the Volkmann’s canals supply 1. Outer one third (1/3) portion of the cortex. Epiphyseal & Metaphyseal Arteries • These are the arteries of epiphyses and are derived from the peri-articular vascular arcades found on the non-articular bony surfaces. • These arteries are derived from the neighboring systemic vessels. • Each metaphysis is the zone of active growth. chunks: Order of Enzyme Catalyzed Reaction In a first-order reaction of enzyme catalysis, the rate of product formation is directly proportional to the concentration of the substrate. This means that the reaction velocity increases linearly with increasing substrate concentration, without dependence on the enzyme concentration. In a zero-order reaction of enzyme catalysis, the reaction velocity remains constant regardless of changes in substrate concentration, indicating that the rate is independent of substrate concentration. This implies that the enzyme active sites are saturated, and further increases in substrate concentration do not enhance the reaction rate. Enzymes Kinetics Enzyme kinetics is the study of the rates at which enzymes catalyze chemical reactions and the factors that influence these rates. The most commonly studied enzyme kinetics involve enzyme-catalyzed reactions obeying Michaelis-Menten kinetics, which can be described by Michaelis-Menten equation: Where: V is the initial reaction velocity (rate of product formation), Vmax is the maximum reaction velocity, [S] is the substrate concentration Km is the Michaelis constant, which represents the substrate concentration at

which the reaction velocity is half of Vmax Enzymes Kinetics Key concepts in enzyme kinetics include: Michaelis-Menten Kinetics: Describes the relationship between substrate concentration and reaction velocity for enzyme-catalyzed reactions. V max : Represents the maximum velocity achievable by the enzyme when all enzyme active sites are saturated with substrate. Km: Reflects the affinity of the enzyme for its substrate, with lower Km values indicating higher substrate affinity. Enzymes Kinetics Lineweaverburk enzyme kinetics The Lineweaver-Burk plot, also known as the double reciprocal plot, is a graphical representation of enzyme kinetics data used to determine kinetic parameters such as Vmax(maximum velocity) and Km(Michaelis constant) from experimental data. The Lineweaver-Burk plot is created by taking the reciprocal of both sides of the Michaelis-Menten equation: Lineweaverburk enzyme kinetics • The Lineweaver-Burk derivation provides a significant advantage concerning substrate concentration by transforming the Michaelis-Menten equation into a linear form. • This transformation allows for the creation of a Lineweaver-Burk plot, where the reciprocal of the reaction velocity

(1/V) is plotted against the reciprocal of the substrate concentration (1/[S]). • In this linear plot, the slope represents Km/Vmax, and the y- intercept represents 1/Vmax. This linear representation simplifies the determination of kinetic parameters, such as Km and Vmax, facilitating the accurate analysis of enzyme kinetics across a range of substrate concentrations. • Additionally, it enables easy comparison of enzyme activities under different experimental conditions and aids in identifying inhibitors or activators of enzymatic reactions.

Proteins are classified on the basis of: 1. Physicochemical properties or Solubility. 2. Structure. 3. Nutritional value. 4. Functions Classification of Proteins Based on chemical composition or physico chemical properties or solubility. ❖Simple ❖Conjugated ❖Derived Protein Description SIMPLE PROTEINS •Upon hydrolysis they yield mixture of amino acids and nothing else. CONJUGATED PROTEINS •Composed of simple proteins combined with a non-protein substance •The non-prot

einous substance is called prosthetic group or cofactor. DERIVED PROTEINS •Not naturally occurring proteins •Obtained from simple proteins by the action of enzymes or chemical agents. OR •Results from hydrolysis of proteins Types of Simple Proteins ▫Albumin ▫Globin ▫Prolamine ▫Histone ▫Protamine Albumin is a protein of biological importance • Soluble in pure water. • Present in milk , eggs & leguminous plants have nutritional value. • Coagulated on heating. • Precipitated with full saturation of ammonium sulphate . • Synthesized in liver Biological importance of albumin: ▫Carrier function in the blood e.g Calcium, Bilirubin, Fatty acids, Hormones etc. ▫Exerts osmotic pressure in the plasma. ▫Like other proteins, acts as buffer. ▫Nutritive function. chunks: Structure of Proteins Prof. Akhtar H. Makhdoom Lecture Objectives At the end of lecture, students should be able to describe: • Primary & secondary Structure of Proteins • Tertiary & Quaternary Structure of Proteins • Unstructured proteins • Chaperones (Heat shock protein) • Protein misfolding (Amyloid disease) • Protein denaturation Protein Structure Every Protein has unique three dimensional structure which is referred as its native conformation. Protein conformation is complex and is best analyzed in terms of organizational levels ie Primary, Secondary, Tertiary and Quaternary. Primary Structure of Proteins • It is linear & refers to specific sequence of a.a in a polypeptide chain. • Thus polypeptide chain having different sequence of a.a are said to differ with respect to their primary structure. Structure of Insulin • In some proteins linear polypeptide chain is cross linked mostly by disulfide bonds formed by ordination of pair of cysteine residues. Extra cellular proteins have several disulfide bonds, as collagen fiber, fibrin blood clots, where as I/C proteins usually lack them Amino Acid sequence is important for: 1) Understanding mechanism of enzyme action. 2) Determining

the three dimensional structure of proteins & its link with genetic message in DNA for biological function of proteins. 3) Alteration in sequence causes abnormal functions & fatal diseases e.g sickle cell disease. Secondary Structure • It refers to local arrangement of polypeptide backbone. It includes mainly the regional bends and local folding, e.g. ▫∝-helix ▫β-pleated ∝-Helix • It is spiral structure consisting of polypeptide chain that is coiled around longitudinal axis in helical fashion. • The ∝-helix is stabilized by H-bond formed between the peptide bond, i.e. c=o group forms H-bond with N-H group of a.a situated four residues ahead in the helix. Each residue is related to the next one by a rise of 1.5 Aº along the ∝- helix axis & rotation of 100º degrees which give 3.6 amino acids per turn. ∝-Helix • The ∝-helix is generally right handed because a.a found in protein are L- variety. Right handed helices are energetically more favorable because there are less steric clash between side chains of the back bone. • ∝-helical content of proteins ranges from none to 100% e.g 75% of residues in ferritin that stores iron are alpha-helices. Hb & myoglobin have high contents of ∝ hel

ix, but carboxypeptidase & ribonuclease are low in ∝helices. • Single ∝- helix are usually less than 45 Aº long. Two or more ∝-helices can entwine to form very stable structure up to length of 1000 Aº (100nm or 0.1µm). • Such alpha-helices are found in: ▫Myosin, ▫tropomycin in muscle, ▫fibrin in blood clots and ▫keratin in hair. A.A not compatible with ∝-helix • Proline, when incorporated it cause chain to bend • valine, leucine isoleucine have bulky R- group to be accomodated • Aspartate, glutamate & Arginine interfere because of electrostatic attractions or repulsions between R- groups. β-pleated sheet • A polypeptide chain in β-pleated is almost fully extended rather than being coiled as in helix. The distance between adjacent a.a. along β-strand is 3.5 Aº, in contrast to 1.5 Aº in ∝-helix. • β-sheet is formed by layers of poly peptide chain held by linking H-bonds in neighboring poly peptide chain. All poly peptide chains run parallel or anti parallel. • β sheet is important structural element in many proteins e.g. F.A binding proteins are built almost entirely for β sheet. • β-sheet is formed by layers of poly peptide chain held by H-bonds in neighboring poly peptide chain. Al

l poly peptide chains run parallel when adjacent chain run in same direction or anti parallel. • β sheet structure is usually associated with structural proteins but also found in some parts of globular proteins. Silk fiber are rich in β pleated sheet which are already packed in extended form. This makes silk fibers mechanically strong but resistant to stretch. Tertiary Structure • It refers the over all folding pattern. The secondarily order polypeptide chain of protein tends to fold in to itself and assume a spherical or globular shape. Forces Stabilizing the Tertiary Structure • Five kinds of interactions, cooperate to stabilize the tertiary structure. 1) Hydrophobic interactions: These arise due to tendency of non-polar substances to minimize their contact with water. In water soluble globular proteins, the non-polar side chain aggregate in the interior hydrophobic core & hydrophilic side chains occupy surface. This provides much of the driving force for protein folding. 2) Hydrogen bonds: Formed by sharing of hydrogen atom between (donor) & another atom that has alone pair of electrons (acceptor). The donors are – NH of peptide, imadazole), -OH (serine), and –NH2 (lysine, argi

nine), and the accepting groups are COO- (aspartate, glutamate). 3) Ionic interactions: Between two ionic side chains of opposite charge (e.g. +ve lysine or arginine and –ve Glu or Asp) is known as an ion pair or salt bridge. These interactions contribute little to the stability of tertiary structure because of their relatively small number. 4) Vander Waals interactions and London dispersion forces: These are very short range interactions between atoms that occur between oscillating dipoles when atoms are packed very closely to each other. They serve to bring the atoms closer especially in the hydrophobic core in the interior. 5) Covalent cross linkages: Cysteine residues, when present on the adjacent loops of the polypeptide(s), form covalent cross links by disulphide bonds These linkages how ever do not establish the higher-ordered structure. They only stabilize the structure that has been formed by non-covalent interactions. Quaternary Structure Oligomeric proteins, e.g. Hemoglobin consists of four polypeptide chains of two different types ∝& β. Number, size and shape of component polypeptide chains and their spatial relationship with one another is called the quaternary structu

re of the protein. Quaternary Structure Noncovalent interactions, such as hydrophobic interactions, hydrogen bonds, electrostatic bonds, hold the subunits togather in some proteins. Intrinsically Unstructured Proteins (IUPs) • They do not have discrete 3-dimential structure under physiological conditions. • 50% of euokaryotic proteins have at least one unstructured region greater than 30 amino acids & these regions are rich in charged amino acids. • This molecular adaptability means that one protein can assume different structures & interact with different partners, yielding different biochemical functions. Chaperones • This is group of specialized proteins required for native folding of proteins. • They are called as polypeptide binding proteins or heat- shock proteins. • They bind to hydrophobic patches in peptide chain & aid in folding of protein during synthesis. • They keep polypeptide chain unfolded until its synthesis is completed & prevent faulty foldings. • They prevent aggregation of incompletely folded proteins by inhibiting adventitious contact between exposed hydrophobic regions. • Defective interaction of polypeptide chain with corresponding chaperone may cause diseas

e. Protein Misfolding (Amyloid disease) •It is host of many diseases including Alzheimer;s disease, some types of Parkinson’s disease, Huntingtons disease & Prio disease. All are associated with improperly folded proteins •Misfolding of protein occur spontaneously or by mutation. •It results in the formation of abnormally long fibrillar protein assemblies composed of beta- pleated sheet. • These protein aggregates are called amyloids & disease is called as amyloidosis •These amyloid fibers are seen in the brain of patients with age related non infectious neuro-degenerative disease like Alzheimer (Loss of memory, confusion, dementia & hallucinations) •It is due to accumulation of amyloids of 40-42 aa. Protein denaturation • The higher order structure of protein may be disrupted by a number of agents, which break physical bonds in protein, without splitting any peptide linkage. Thus neatly folded poly peptide chain is converted to a random coil. Only non- covalent interactions are disrupted. Denaturation is accompanied by loss of biologic functions • Enzymes are inactivated, antibodies fails to act with antigen & toxins lose their disease-producing effects. • Denaturation is generall

y irreversible. • Denaturation under ideal condition is reversible when denaturing agents are removed e.g ribonuclease is denatured by 8M urea, but when urea is removed by dialysis renaturation occurs & enzyme activity is restored. Changes in physical properties • Water soluble proteins become insoluble. • As proteins become less symetric, it exert resistance to various type of movements & in many cases it precipitates. • The sedimentation rate & diffusion rate falls & the intrinsic viscosity increases. Agents causing denaturation • Heat , detergents ,organic solvents, strong acids, bases, heavy metals & Physical agents : X-rays , uv rays , high pressure & vigorous shaking.

chunks: AP Biology Purines & Pyrimidines Humaira Sharif AP Biology Learning Objectives • Describe the chemical structures of purine and pyrimidines • Differentiate between de novo and salvage pathways of purine and pyrimidine synthesis • Discuss the degradation pathways of purines and pyrimidines • Identify the biochemical basis of common disorders: Gout, Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, Severe combined immunodeficiency (ADA deficiency), Orotic aciduria • Explain the mechanism of action of drugs targeting purine/pyrimidine metabolism AP Biology Structure of Purine Bases A purine is a fused heterocyclic ring: Pyrimidine ring (6-membered) fused to an imidazole ring (5-membered) Numbering: 1–9 Major purines: Adenine (6-amino group) Guanine (6-keto group + 2-amino group) Minor purines: Hypoxanthine, Xanthine, Uric acid (end product) AP Biology Structure of Pyrimidine Bases Single 6-membered heterocyclic ring with two nitrogen atoms at positions 1 and 3. Major pyrimidines: Cytosine 4-amino, 2-keto Thymine 5-methyl, 2,4-diketo Uracil 2,4-diketo (no methyl) Minor pyrimidines: 5-methylcytosine, dihydrouracil AP Biology Purine De Novo Synthesis • Occurs primarily in the liver (and cytoplasm of all cells

) • Requires PRPP (phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate) as the ribose donor • Builds the purine ring on top of the ribose-5-PO4 • Rate-limiting enzyme: Glutamine-PRPP amidotransferase • End product: IMP (inosine monophosphate) • Energy cost: ~6 ATP per IMP AP Biology Important enzymes and Regulation • PRPP synthetase: Inhibited by AMP, IMP, and GMP. • Glutamine PRPP amidinotransferase: Inhibited by AMP, IMP, and GMP. • IMP dehydrogenase: Inhibited by GMP. • Adenylosuccinate synthetase: Inhibited by AMP. AP Biology Pharmacological Inhibitors • Tetrahydrofolate is involved in two reactions of de novo purine synthesis. • Folic acid analogs, such as methotrexate, inhibit the formation of tetrahydrofolate and thus interfere with purine synthesis. AP Biology Inhibitory Mechanism via Methotrexate • Methotrexate is a folic acid analog that inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, preventing formation of tetrahydrofolate (THF). THF is required as a one-carbon donor in two reactions of de novo purine synthesis. • Without THF, purine synthesis is blocked →cells cannot replicate DNA →reduced cell proliferation. Clinical use: (1) Cancer chemotherapy (rapidly dividing cancer cells are most affected), (2) Auto

immune diseases (rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis) — suppresses rapidly proliferating immune cells. AP Biology Purine Salvage Pathway A salvage pathway is a pathway in which nucleotides are synthesized from intermediates in the degradative pathway for nucleotides. Purine synthesis via the salvage pathways occurs in all tissues. It is especially important in the brain and the bone marrow. Substrates: Hypoxanthine; PRPP; guanine; adenine. Products: GMP; AMP; IMP. AP Biology Important enzymes and Regulation • HGPRT: Inhibited by IMP and GMP. • Adenine phosphoribosyltransferase: Inhibited by AMP. Associated Disease • Deficiency of HGPRT leads to Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, which is characterized by self-mutilation and CNS deterioration. AP Biology De novo and salvage • Difference between de novo and salvage pathways of purine synthesis with respect to: (a) site of occurrence, (b) energy requirement, (c) substrates used. • De novo: Occurs primarily in the liver; high energy cost (~6 ATP per IMP); starts from simple molecules (PRPP, glutamine, CO2, etc.); builds the purine ring on ribose-5- phosphate. • Salvage pathway: Occurs in all tissues especially brain and bone marrow; requires less energ

y; substrates are free purine bases (hypoxanthine, guanine, adenine) + PRPP; accounts for ~90% of daily purine nucleotide biosynthesis. AP Biology Uric Acid-Clinical Significance • Gout = Inflammatory arthritis caused by deposition of urate crystals Treatment: • Acute: NSAIDs, colchicine • Chronic: Allopurinol, febuxostat (xanthine oxidase inhibitors) • Uricosurics: Probenecid (increase excretion) Primary Secondary Genetic defects in purine metabolism Chronic kidney disease HGPRT deficiency (Lesch-Nyhan) Diuretics (thiazides) Overactivity of PRPP synthetase • Myeloproliferative disorders • High purine diet (alcohol, meat) AP Biology Uric Acid-Clinical Significance • Uric acid is the final end product of purine catabolism in humans (via xanthine oxidase). Excess uric acid leads to gout. • Minor purines include hypoxanthine and xanthine (intermediates in the pathway), while uric acid is the excreted end product. AP Biology Lesch-Nyhan syndrome Deiciency of Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT) leads to Lesch-Nyhan syndrome (X-linked recessive). Without HGPRT, purines cannot be salvaged →they are degraded → excess uric acid. The brain (especially basal ganglia) is par

ticularly dependent on the salvage pathway, explaining the neurological features. • Symptoms: self-biting behavior, intellectual disability, choreoathetosis, and elevated serum uric acid levels. • Genetic testing reveals a near-total deficiency of an enzyme in the purine salvage pathway. Deficiency →accumulation of dATP (especially in lymphocytes) • dATP inhibits ribonucleotide reductase →depletes dNTP pools → prevents lymphocyte proliferation • Result: Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) – “bubble boy” disease Treatment: • PEG-ADA (enzyme replacement) • Bone marrow transplantation • Gene therapy AP Biology SCID Child in protective environment AP Biology Adenosine Deaminase Deficiency Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID) due to ADA deficiency ('Bubble Boy' disease). Mechanism: ADA normally converts adenosine→inosine and deoxyadenosine→deoxyinosine. ll immunity abolished. AP Biology Adenosine Deaminase Deficiency Why accumulation in Lymphocytes? Lymphocytes are particularly vulnerable because: (1) They have high levels of deoxynucleoside kinases that phosphorylate deoxyadenosine to dATP, (2) They have low levels of 5'-nucleotidase (which would dephosphorylate it back), and (3) They are rapidly dividing cells requiring continuous dNTP pools for DNA synthesis. Ligases ENZYME • An enzyme is a protein (or RNA) biocatalyst that accelerates the rate of a specific chemical reaction without being permanently altered or consumed in the process. CLASSIFICATION & NOMENCLATURE OF ENZYMES • In the beginning enzymes were given “unsystematic” names e.g trypsin, chymotrypsin, ptyalin etc. • In more recent times enzymes have been named by adding suffix “-ase,” to the substrate e.g sucrase, maltase, lactase • In order to have uniformity & un-ambiguity in identification of enzymes IUBMB adopted a nomenclature system, based on chemical reactions & reaction mechanisms. Activation Energy • Enzymes lower the activation energy of a chemical reaction by providing an alternative reaction pathway, allowing the reaction to proceed faster at physiological temperatures. Activation Energy • This reduction in activation energy increases the number of substrate mo

lecules that can overcome the energy barrier per unit time, thereby accelerating the reaction rate without being consumed. Catalytic activity • Enzymes accelerate biochemical reactions by specifically binding to substrates at their active site, forming an enzyme-substrate complex that lowers the activation energy. Catalytic activity • This catalytic activity is highly efficient, often increasing reaction rates by millions of times, and is essential for maintaining metabolic processes under mild physiological conditions. Specificity to Active Site The active site of an enzyme has a unique three-dimensional structure and chemical complementarity that allows it to bind only its specific substrate(s), much like a lock and key or an induced fit. Nomenclature committee of IUBMB • All the enzymes are classified into six major classes. • Each major class is divided into sub classes. • Each sub class is further divided into sub-sub classes. Enzymes are assigned a four- digit code number • Example EC 2.7.1.1 denotes: • Class 2 (a transferase), • Subclass 7 (transfer of phosphate), • Sub-subclass 1 (an alcohol is the phosphate acceptor). • The final digit 1 denotes ATP: D-hexose 6-phosphotran

Explain the properties and functions of polysaccharides 3. Describe the clinical importance of polysaccharides Polysaccharide (multi saccharides). A saccharide refers to the unit structure of carbohydrates. Thus, a polysaccharide is a carbohydrate comprised of many saccharides, particularly, more than 10 (mono)saccharide. The process of condensing many similar molecules to form a large molecule is called polymerization. Structural Classification Polysaccharides are mainly classified into: Polysaccharide Made up of only one type of monosaccharide, (homoglycans) e.g, Starch, Cellulose, Glycogen Homopolysaccharide Composed of different types of monosaccharides, (heteroglycans) e.g, Glycosaminoglycans Heteropolysaccharide Functional Classification Based on their function, polysaccharides may be classified : Polysaccharide Storage polysaccharides are those that are used for storage. For instance, • Plants store glucose in the form of starch. • Animals store simple sugars in the form of glycogen. Storage polysa

ccharid e Carbohydrates that have a structural role. • Plants have Cellulose, polymers of repeated glucose units that are joined by beta-linkages. • Certain animals produce chitin that serves as a structural component, i.e, of exoskeleton. Structural polysaccharide Many monosaccharide (Glucose) units are linked together to form polysaccharide by the process of polymerization that is done by condensation (releases water molecules) Starch Cellulose Glycogen Polymerization Starch • One of the most important sources of carbohydrates in our food. • Commonly present in vegetable foods i.e, cereals, potatoes, etc. • However, starch is not formed or stored by animals. • Made up of a very large number of glucose molecules condensed together to form chains of glucose units. • These chains are a mixture of straight and branched chains. • The glucose units are linked by “bridges” or chemical bonds. • A starch molecule may contain as many as 200 glucose units. Cemical Structure Amylose Amylopectin Composition 20-30% of starch 70-80% of starch Structure Linear, unbranched chains of glucose linked by α-(1→4) glycosidic bonds Highly branched polymer with both α- (1→4) and α-(1→6) glycosidic bonds

Solubility Insoluble in cold water; forms a gel when heated Soluble in both cold and hot water Color Produces a blue color with iodine Gives a purple color with iodine Functional Properties of Starch • Thickening Agent: Starch is commonly used in cooking and food processing to thicken sauces and soups. • Adhesive: In industrial applications, starch acts as an adhesive in papermaking and textiles. • Dietary Fiber: Certain types of starch, like resistant starch, are beneficial for digestive health and can improve insulin sensitivity. Clinical Importance of Starch • Primary Energy Source: Broken down by salivary and pancreatic amylase to maltose/glucose, providing systemic glucose. • Resistant Starch: A fraction that resists digestion, acting as a prebiotic fiber—fermented by colonic bacteria to produce short- chain fatty acids (SCFAs) beneficial for colon health. • Glycemic Index: The structure (amylose vs. amylopectin ratio) affects the rate of digestion and postprandial blood glucose response, crucial in diabetes management. Chemical Structure of Cellulose • Composition: Made up of linear chains of D-glucose units linked by β(1→4)-glycosidic bonds. • Chain Length: Varies from 300 t

o 10,000 glucose units, affecting its properties. • key structural component of plant cell walls, contributing to their rigidity and stability. Functional Properties of Cellulose Biological Role • Dietary Fiber: Acts as an insoluble fiber in human nutrition, aiding digestion. • Digestibility: Indigestible by humans but digestible by some animals (e.g., ruminants) with the help of microorganisms. Industrial Applications • Uses: Primarily used in the production of paper, cardboard, and textiles. Also utilized in food additives and biofuels. Cellulose Human can not digest cellulose but it forms a bulk of undigested matter usually consist of fiber. This fiber is important for the proper functioning of the large intestine Cellulose is the type of carbohydrate that makes up the cell wall of the plants, it contains glucose units linked together to form straight chains Clinical Association Conditions Improved by Cellulose Intake: • Constipation • Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS-C) • Diverticular Disease (Small pouches form in colon linings) Condition Caused by Deficiency: Inadequate cellulose/fiber intake is a major risk factor for chronic constipation and its complications e.g., hemorrhoids

(swollen veins in lower rectum).cc Glycogen • A highly branched polysaccharide. • Acts as the primary short-term energy storage in animals, fungi and bacteria. • Stored as cytoplasmic granules primarily in liver and muscle cells. • It is a polymer of 𝛼-glucose. • Linear 𝛼(1→4) bonds and frequent 𝛼(1→6) branches every 8- 12 units. • Allowing rapid, enzyme-driven energy release. Glycogen, also termed as animal starch, stored formed of carbohydrate in animals and in fungi. In Mammals it is stored mainly in liver and muscles. Due to the large size glycogen molecules are unable to diffuse the cell membrane and can easily be hydrolyzed when needed Clinical Importance of Glycogen Glucose Homeostasis: Liver glycogenolysis is the first-line defense against hypoglycemia between meals. Exercise Physiology: Muscle glycogen is the critical fuel for moderate-to-high intensity exercise. Metabolic Buffer: Rapidly stores excess dietary glucose postprandially. Glycogen Storage Diseases A group of inherited disorders caused by defects in glycogen synthesis or breakdown enzymes. GSD Type I (Von Gierke's Disease): Defect: Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency (primarily liver). Effect: Severely impaired gl

ucose release. Causes profound fasting hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, hepatomegaly, growth failure, and hyperlipidemia. Glycogen Storage Diseases GSD Type V (McArdle's Disease): Defect: Muscle glycogen phosphorylase deficiency. Pathology: Exercise intolerance, muscle cramps/pain with activity, and myoglobinuria (dark urine) due to muscle breakdown. Andersen Disease (Glycogen Storage Disease Type IV): Defect: Deficiency of glycogen branching enzyme (GBE1). Pathology:The body produces an abnormal, amylopectin-like glycogen with fewer branches (similar to starch). Heteropolysaccharides • Composed of two or more different monosaccharide derivatives. • Structural/functional diversity is far greater in heteropolysaccharides due to variations in sugar types, linkages, and modifications (e.g., sulfation). • Glycosaminoglycans (GAGs): Repeating units of an amino sugar and a uronic acid. • Hyaluronic Acid: Glucuronic acid + N-Acetylglucosamine. Lubricant in joints and tissues. • Chondroitin Sulfate: Glucuronic acid + N-Acetylgalactosamine (sulfated). Structural role in cartilage. Heteropolysaccharides • Heparin: Uronic acid + D-Glucosamine (Potent natural anticoagulant drug). • Bacterial Cap

sules: Complex heteropolymers. (Immune evasion, target for vaccines). chunks: CHEMICAL NATURE OF WATER DR.AQLEEMA AFTAB Molecular Structure & Geometry Water is a solvent that dissolves a variety of substances. It is considered the universal solvent because it can dissolve compounds (like polar molecules and ions) than the available solvents. Its physical and chemical attributes make it an excellent solvent. Composition: One Oxygen atom covalently bonded to two Hydrogen atoms.  consists of one oxygen atom covalently bonded to two hydrogen atoms in a bent or V-shape. Due to oxygen's high electronegativity and two lone electron pairs, the molecule is highly polar, with a partial negative charge on the oxygen and partial positive charges on the hydrogens. Molecular Structure & Geometry It gives a partial negative charge to an O-atom and a partial positive charge to the H-atoms. Water can dissolve any substance with charged particles or electronegative atoms. Compounds can be hydrophilic or hydrophobic based on their solubility in water. “Hydrophilic compounds” like polar molecules and ions can dissolve in water. In contrast, “Hydrophobic compounds” like fats and oils do not dissolve in water. Key Aspects of a Dipole: A dipole is a pair of equal and opposit

e electric charges or magnetic poles separated by a small distance.  It represents a system with a positive charge at one end and a negative charge at the other, creating a polarized entity.  Examples include polar molecules like water and magnets. Structure: Two opposite poles/charges separated by distance. Electric Dipole: Occurs when positive and negative charges do not coincide within a molecule, making it polar. Magnetic Dipole: A pair of North and South poles. Dipole Moment: A measure of the separation of charges, pointing from the negative to the positive charge. Hydration shell or Solvation shell A hydration shell (or solvation shell) is a structured, spherical layer of water molecules that surrounds dissolved ions, proteins, or other charged molecules in an aqueous solution.  These shells are held together by electrostatic interactions (hydrogen bonds) between the polar water molecules and the charged solute, crucial for maintaining dispersion, enabling dissolution, and influencing biological function. Ionization of salt in water When ionic compounds are added to water, individual ions interact with the polar regions of the water molecules during the dissociation

process, disrupting their ionic bonds. Dissociation occurs when atoms or groups of atoms break off from molecules and form ions. Consider table salt (NaCl, or sodium chloride): when NaCl crystals are added to water, the molecules of NaCl dissociate into Na+ and Cl–ions, and spheres of hydration form around the ions.  The positively-charged sodium ion is surrounded by the partially-negative charge of the water molecule’s oxygen; the negatively-charged chloride ion is surrounded by the partially-positive charge of the hydrogen in the water molecule. Ionization of water biochemical importance  pH Regulation: The balance between and determines the pH of cellular environments. Since most enzymes and proteins only function within a very narrow pH range, even slight shifts in ionization can denature proteins and halt metabolism.  Enzymatic Catalysis: Many enzymes use water's ability to donate or accept protons to break chemical bonds (hydrolysis) or form new ones. The ions produced by water ionization are often direct participants in these chemical reactions.  Molecular Structure: The ionization state of water influences the folding of DNA and proteins. It affects how hydrophilic (wa

ter-loving) and hydrophobic (water-fearing) parts of molecules interact, ensuring biological structures stay intact.  Proton Wire (Conductivity): In processes like photosynthesis and cellular respiration, water allows for "proton hopping." This enables the rapid movement of ions across membranes to create energy gradients, which the cell eventually turns into ATP.  Essentially, without the ionization of water, the complex "acid-base" chemistry required for life would be impossible.

Water aids the folding of biomolecules like proteins, nucleic acids etc. Water 5. Semi-fluid nature of body is due to water. 6. Water regulates body temperature. 7. Water accelerates biochemical reactions by providing ions. 8. Water content in the body alters in dehydration and edema. Total Body Water (TBW) Total Body Water (TBW) is the total amount of water present in the human body, expressed as a percentage of body weight. Normal TBW Percentages • Adult males: ~ 60% of body weight • Adult females: ~ 50–55% of body weight • Infants: ~ 70–75% of body weight Factors Affecting TBW 1. Age • Infants: highest TBW (more water content, less fat) • Elderly: ↓ TBW due to ↓ muscle mass and ↑ fat 2. Sex • Males: higher TBW due to more muscle mass • Females: lower TBW due to higher fat content 3. Body Composition (Fat vs Muscle) • Muscle tissue: contains more water → ↑ TBW • Adipose (fat) tissue: contains

less water → ↓ TBW Therefore: • Lean individuals → higher TBW • Obese individuals → lower TBW Distribution of Body Water Classification of Body Water Body Water Compartments Total Body Water (TBW) is divided into two main compartments: 1. Intracellular Fluid (ICF) • Fluid inside the cells • Accounts for 2/3 of TBW (~66%) 2. Extracellular Fluid (ECF) • Fluid outside the cells • Accounts for 1/3 of TBW (~33%) Subdivision of ECF ECF is further divided into: • Interstitial Fluid • Fluid between cells (tissue spaces) • Forms ~75% of ECF • Plasma • Fluid part of blood • Forms ~25% of ECF • Transcellular Fluid • Specialized fluids in body spaces: • Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) • Synovial fluid • Pleural, peritoneal fluids • Small portion of ECF Electrolyte Composition of Body Fluids ICF (Intracellular Fluid) • High: K⁺, Mg²⁺, Phosphate (PO₄³⁻), Proteins • Low: Na⁺, Cl⁻ ECF (Extracellular Fluid) • High: Na⁺, Cl⁻, HCO₃⁻ • Low: K⁺, Mg²⁺ Importance of Electrolyte Gradient • Maintains osmotic balance • Controls water movement across membranes • Prevents cell swelling/shrinkage • Essential for nerve & muscle function Osmosis in the human body is the passive movement of water molecules across semip

ermeable cell membranes from areas of low solute concentration to high solute concentration. This critical process maintains homeostasis by regulating water balance, absorbing nutrients in the intestines, producing sweat, filtering blood in the kidneys, and ensuring red blood cells maintain their shape and function. Key Examples of Osmosis in the Body: Red Blood Cell Maintenance: Red blood cells exist in an isotonic environment to prevent bursting (hypotonic) or shriveling (hypertonic). Intestinal Nutrient Absorption: Water moves into intestinal epithelial cells via osmosis, bringing nutrients with it. Kidney Function: The kidneys use osmosis to reabsorb water, regulating blood pressure and removing waste products (urea). Skin & Sweat Glands: Sweat gland cells use osmosis to move water from the body to the skin surface for temperature regulation Role of Na⁺ • Main determinant of ECF osmolality • Controls: • Blood volume • Water distribution • Cell hydration Osmolality (mOsm/kg): Measures solute particles per unit weight of solvent (water). It is generally preferred in laboratory settings as it remains constant despite temperature changes. Osmolarity (mOsm/L): Measures solute partic

les per unit volume of solution. It is easier to calculate in clinical settings when measuring fluid volumes. Membrane Transport Mechanisms Types of Transport 1. Simple Diffusion • Movement of molecules down concentration gradient • No energy required 2. Facilitated Diffusion • Uses carrier proteins • No ATP required • Example: glucose transport Types of Transport 3. Active Transport • Moves against gradient (requires ATP) • Example: Na⁺/K⁺ pump Cell Membrane Role • Lipid bilayer → selective barrier • Controls entry/exit of ions and water • Maintains fluid compartment separation Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase Pump Mechanism • Pumps: • 3 Na⁺ out • 2 K⁺ in • Uses ATP energy Functions • Maintains cell volume • Maintains resting membrane potential • Establishes electrochemical gradients • Prevents cell swelling Regulation of Body Water Hormonal Control • ADH (Vasopressin) • Released from posterior pituitary • Increases water reabsorption in kidneys • ↓ urine output Aldosterone • Acts on kidneys • Increases Na⁺ reabsorption → water follows Na⁺ • Renin-Angiotensin System • Activated in low blood pressure • Increases aldosterone + ADH + thirst Organs Involved • Kidneys: main regulator • Hypothalamus: thir

st center + osmoreceptors Functions of Body Water • Universal solvent for biochemical reactions • Medium for transport of nutrients & waste • Maintains body temperature (heat regulation) • Essential for acid–base balance (buffers) Clinical Correlation Dehydration • ↓ body water • Causes: diarrhea, vomiting • Effects: hypotension, dizziness Overhydration (Water Intoxication) • Excess water intake • Leads to hyponatremia Edema • Fluid accumulation in interstitial space • Causes: heart failure, kidney disease Electrolyte Imbalance Effects • Na⁺ imbalance → brain dysfunction • K⁺ imbalance → muscle/heart problems Clinical Correlation Laboratory Values Interpretation Normal Plasma Osmolality 275–295 mOsm/kg Serum Sodium • Normal: 135–145 mmol/L Clinical Interpretation • High Na⁺ (Hypernatremia): dehydration, water loss • Low Na⁺ (Hyponatremia): water excess, edema Fluid Shifts • High ECF osmolality → water leaves cells → cell shrinkage • Low ECF osmolality → water enters cells → cell swelling

Biochemical composition of cell membrane 2. Importance of lipids, carbohydrates and proteins in membrane 3. Functions of selectively permeable membrane Cell Membrane • Cell membrane is a biological membrane that separates the interior of all cells from extracellular space and protects the cell Cell Membrane • It consists of a lipid bilayer, it is fluid under various temperatures, in combination with membrane proteins Fluid mosaic model • According to fluid mosaic model of S. J. Singer and G. L. Nicolson (1972), cell membrane can be considered as a two-dimensional liquid in which lipid and protein molecules diffuse easily Fluid mosaic model • Lipids present in membrane are amphipathic with both hydrophilic and hydrophobic regions • Their polar ends face outwards and nonpolar ends face each other • Proteins are embedded in irregular distribution giving it a mosaic appearance Fluid mosaic model • The mosaic is not constant, it is fluid and changeable from moment to moment • Fluidity is due to weak, noncovale

nt interactions between lipid and protein molecules • Lipid and protein molecules can move laterally in the plane of membrane CELL MEMBRANE IS COMPOSED OF: • Lipids (60%) Phospholipids, Sterols • Proteins(40%) Integral, Peripheral • Carbohydrates(1to10%) Glycolipids, Glycoproteins Functions of cell membrane • It controls the movement of substances in and out of cells and organelles • It is selectively permeable to ions and organic molecules •Barrier to toxic molecules • It enables the molecular composition of a cell to differ from that of the cell’s environment •Cell membrane is the boundary •Separates cell from its environment IN Food, water, oxygen OUT Waste products, CO2 Functions of cell membrane • Helps accumulate nutrients • Mediates cell-cell interactions • Carries out energy transduction • Facilitates cell motion • Assists in reproduction Functions of cell membrane • It maintains concentration of electrolytes, nonelectrolytes and water between interior and exterior of the cell, by active and passive transport • It takes part in endocytosis and exocytosis Functions of cell membrane •It is involved in cell adhesion •It is implicated in ion conductivity •It has role in cell si

gnaling Functions of cell membrane •It serves as the attachment surface for extracellular structures like carbohydrate layer (glycocalyx) and intracellular network of protein fibers (cytoskeleton) •It helps in enzymatic activity as enzymes are embedded in it CELL MEMBRANE • In eukaryotic cells, enzymes that span the ER catalyze the formation of membrane lipids • Lipids are synthesized in the ER, and flippases move lipid molecules between leaflets of the bilayer MEMBRANE LIPIDS • Three types of lipid are found in biological membranes: 1. Phospholipids 2. Glycolipids 3. Sterols MEMBRANE LIPIDS • Phospholipids consist of two fatty acid chains linked to glycerol and a phosphate group • Phospholipids containing sphingosine are sphingophospholipids e.g. sphingomyelin MEMBRANE LIPIDS • Glycerophospholipids: Phospholipids containing glycerol e.g. Phosphatidylcholine: has a choline molecule attached to phosphate group If serine attached to phosphate group, it is phosphatidylserine If ethanolamine is attached, it is phosphatidylethanolamine MEMBRANE LIPIDS • Glycolipids containing either glycerol or sphingosine, and a sugar e.g. glucose • Sterols are an important component of cell membrane (

typically cholesterol) Glycolipids containing glycerol and a sugar MEMBRANE LIPIDS • Cholesterol has a quite different structure to that of the phospholipids and glycolipids • It consists of a hydroxyl group (which is the hydrophilic ‘head’ region), a four-ring steroid structure and a short hydrocarbon side chain MEMBRANE LIPIDS • Cholesterol makes membranes thicker and more rigid MEMBRANE LIPIDS Lipid Rafts • Membrane microdomains rich in cholesterol and sphingolipids • Involved in lateral compartmentalization of molecules at the cell surface • Ligands attached to receptors, enter the cell through these domains by a process called raft-dependent endocytosis MICELLE BILAYER • A spherical structure formed by aggregation of surfactants in monolayer, in an aqueous solution, with hydrophilic heads facing outwards and hydrophobic tails facing inwards, creating hydrophobic interior BILAYERS • Formed by self assembly of two amphiphilic lipids molecules in two concentric layers MEMBRANE PROTEINS • Membrane proteins consist of three main types: 1. Integral proteins 2. Peripheral proteins 3. Lipid-anchored proteins MEMBRANE PROTEINS Integral proteins : • Amphipathic transmembrane proteins e.

g. ion channels, proton pumps, and G-protein coupled receptors • They allow inorganic ions e.g. Na, K, Ca, or Cl to diffuse down their electrochemical gradient across lipid bilayer through hydrophilic pores • Electrical behavior of nerve cells is controlled by ion channels MEMBRANE PROTEINS Proton pumps : • Protein pumps embedded in lipid bilayer that allow protons to travel through membrane by transferring from one amino acid side chain to another e.g. electron transport chain uses proton pumps for generating ATP MEMBRANE PROTEINS G-protein coupled receptor: • A single polypeptide chain that crosses lipid bilayer 7 times • It responds to signal molecules like hormones and neurotransmitters, used in cell to cell signaling MEMBRANE PROTEINS • Their cell-surface portion has specialized integral membrane proteins and binds the ligand (the messenger molecule) on extracellular side of membrane, and on intra cellular side it binds a GTP- binding protein (G protein) MEMBRANE PROTEINS • Functions of membrane proteins also include cell– cell contact, surface recognition, cytoskeleton contact, signaling, enzymatic activity transporting substances across the membrane MEMBRANE PROTEINS • Membr

ane proteins are synthesized in cytosolic ribosomes • They can be made up of α-helices or β-barrels • β-barrel membrane proteins often function as pores • Non-spanning proteins which associate with bilayer, use a hydrophobic anchor MEMBRANE PROTEINS • Proteins serve as membrane transporters • Some proteins that are loosely attached to outer side of cell membrane act as enzymes and help in shaping the cell MEMBRANE PROTEINS • Membrane also contains a large quantity of proteins, which provide more structure • Examples of such structures are protein-protein complexes, pickets and fences formed by actin-based cytoskeleton, and lipid rafts MEMBRANE PROTEINS • Techniques used for studying membrane proteins are : • XRAY Crystallography • Nuclear Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy • Gel Electrophoresis MEMBRANE CARBOHYDRATES • Carbohydrates are covalently linked to proteins (glycoproteins) or lipids (glycolipids) and function as adhesion and address loci for cells GLYCOCALYX •It is important especially in epithelium with microvilli •It is a carbohydrate-enriched coating composed of strands of sugars and proteins bound together, forming a thick, sticky layer that helps cells survive in environ

ments with lots of physical stress • It is a factor used for recognition of cell •It participates in cell adhesion and lymphocyte homing MEMBRANE CARBOHYDRATES • Sugars attached to lipids and proteins in membrane can act as markers due to structural diversity of sugar chains e.g. antigens composed of sugar chains on surface of RBCs determine an individual’s blood group Antigens composed of sugar chains on surface of RBCs MEMBRANE CARBOHYDRATES • These antigens are recognized by antibodies to cause an immune response, which is why matching blood groups must be used in blood transfusions MEMBRANE CARBOHYDRATES • Other carbohydrate markers are also present in disease (e.g. specific carbohydrates on surface of cancer cells), and can be used to make a diagnosis and treatment CYTOSKELETON • Cytoskeleton is a network of microfilaments, intermediate filaments, and microtubules • It gives shape to cells , allows cell movement, enables movement of organelles within the cell, endocytosis, and cell division BIOMEDICAL IMPORTANCE OF CELL MEMBRANE • The "folding" of membrane into microvilli effectively increases surface area for absorption while minimally impacting the cytosolic volume • Such ce

lls are found lining the small intestine, which absorbs nutrients from digested food BIOMEDICAL IMPORTANCE OF CELL MEMBRANE • Membrane forms an outer boundary of cell and holds the cell together • Membrane moves and flexes in response to surrounding environment • Fluid nature of membrane allows the cell to survive in various environments BIOMEDICAL IMPORTANCE OF CELL MEMBRANE • Keeps toxic substances out of the cell • Contains receptors/channels that allow specific ions, nutrients, wastes, and metabolic products, that mediate cellular and extracellular activities while passing between organelles and between the cell and the outside environment BIOMEDICAL IMPORTANCE OF CELL MEMBRANE • Separates vital and incompatible metabolic processes conducted within organelles • Membranes maintain separation between inside and outside of a cell, controlling by means of their selective permeability which substances enter and leave the cell BIOMEDICAL IMPORTANCE OF CELL MEMBRANE • Membrane allows gradient of ions across them , this enables them to generate energy • They control flow of messages between cells by sending, receiving and processing information in the form of chemical and electrical si

chunks: Gestational age covers the entire pregnancy from the last menstrual period (40 weeks), while the embryonic period is a specific, early sub-stage (weeks 3–8/10) focused on organ development. Gestation starts before conception; the embryo phase begins at fertilization and ends when it becomes a fetus. SUMMARY • Week 3: Beginning development of the brain, heart, blood cells, circulatory system, spinal cord, and digestive system. • Week 4: Beginning development of bones, facial structures, and limbs (presence of arm and leg buds); continuing development of the heart (which begins to beat), brain, and nervous tissue. • Week 5: Beginning development of eyes, nose, kidneys, lungs; continuing development of the heart (formation of valves), brain, nervous tissue, and digestive tract. • Week 6: Beginning development of hands, feet, and digits; continuing development of brain, heart, and circulation system. • Week 7: Beginning development of hair follicles, nipples, eyelids, and sex organs (testes or ovaries); first formation of urine in the kidneys and first evidence of brain waves. • Week 8: Facial features more distinct, internal organs well developed, the brain can signal for muscles to m

ove, heart development ends, external sex organs begin to form. • Congenital malformations can occur due to exposure of the embryo to teratogens during this developmental period • ABOUT DAYS 22 TO 23 (3rd week): embryo is almost straight or slightly curved, and somites create conspicuous surface elevations. The neural tube is closed opposite the somites but is open at its caudal and rostral neuropores ABOUT DAY 24: the first (mandibular) and second (hyoid) branchial arches become distinct Most of the mandibular process of the first arch gives rise to the lower jaw and a rostral extension of it; the maxillary process helps form the upper jaw Head- and tail folds cause a slight curvature of the embryo The heart produces a large ventral prominence ABOUT DAY 28 (END OF WEEK 4): the fourth pair of branchial arches and the leg buds are seen The lens placodes (ectodermal thickenings) represent the future lenses on the side of the head HEAD GROWTH is accelerated as a result of rapid brain Development The face contacts the heart prominence The forelimbs show some regional differentiation as the hand plates develop • LIMB BUDS, especially the forelimbs, show regional differentiation. nd limbs develop later Elbow and wrist areas are identifiable • Paddle-shaped hand plates develop digital ridges, the finger rays, for future fingers • SOME SMALL SWELLINGS appear around the groove between the first branchial arches. Contributing to the development of fetal gastrointestinal tract • Formation: It develops during the second week of development from the hypoblast cells. • Hypoblast cells line the blastocyst cavity to form the primary yolk sac. • Later it is replaced by a secondary (definitive) yolk sac. • Structure • The primary yolk sac consists of: 1. Hypoblast-derived cells 2. Exocoelomic (Heuser’s) membrane 3. It surrounds the exocoelomic cavity. • Definition: The secondary yolk sac is the smaller yolk sac that forms after the degeneration of the primary yolk sac during the second week of development • Definition: The vitelline duct (also called the omphalomesenteric duct) is a narrow tube that connects the midgut of the developing embryo to the yolk sac. • Clinical Importance: Failure of the vitelline duct to disappear may cause congenital anomalies such as: 1. Meckel's dive

rticulum – most common anomaly. 2. Vitelline fistula – intestinal contents discharge through the umbilicus. 3. Vitelline cyst – cystic swelling along the duct. 4. Fibrous band between ileum and umbilicus. • Functions 1. Early nutrition of the embryo before placental circulation develops. 2. First site of blood cell formation (hematopoiesis). 3. Source of primordial germ cells. 4. Formation of the primitive gut during embryo folding. 5. Contributes to the vitelline duct and vitelline vessels. Amnion • Formation; During the second week of development, a small space appears within the Epiblast called the amniotic cavity. • Cells from the epiblast differentiate into amnioblasts. • These amnioblasts line the cavity and form the amnion membrane. Chorion • Formation: The chorion is formed by two layers: 1. Trophoblast 2. Extra-embryonic mesoderm • The trophoblast further differentiates into: 1. Cytotrophoblast 2. Syncytiotrophoblast • These layers together form the chorionic membrane.

chunks: Fetal Period By Professor Dr. Rais Ahmed Professor of anatomy United medical and dental college Gestational age covers the entire pregnancy from the last menstrual period (40 weeks), while the embryonic period is a specific, early sub-stage (weeks 3– 8/10) focused on organ development. Gestation starts before conception; the embryo phase begins at fertilization and ends when it becomes a fetus. Lanugo is fine, downy hair that covers a fetus and newborn baby, while vernix is a white, waxy, cheesy substance that coats the skin of the fetus in the womb. Lanugo helps vernix adhere to the skin, protecting the fetus's delicate skin from amniotic fluid and promoting warmth.

chunks: FOLDING OF EMBRYO & ENDODERM Prof Dr Imran Ishaque Objectives • After studying folding of the embryo, the student should be able to: 1. Define embryonic folding 2. Describe the causes of embryonic folding s 3. Identify the two main types of embryonic folding: Cephalocaudal folding Lateral folding 4. Explain the process of head fold and tail fold 5. Describe the process of lateral folding. 6. Explain the formation of the primitive gut tube (foregut, midgut, and hindgut). 7. Describe the changes in position of important structures such as: 8. List the results of embryonic folding. • Folding of the Embryo is an important process in week 4 of embryonic development. • During this stage, the flat trilaminar embryonic disc becomes a cylindrical embryo due to rapid growth of the neural tube, somites, and amniotic cavity. • Definition: Folding of the embryo is the process by which the flat trilaminar germ disc is transformed into a three-dimensional body form by cephalocaudal folding and lateral folding. • Causes of Embryonic Folding 1. Rapid growth of the neural tube 2. Rapid development of somites 3. Expansion of the amniotic cavity 4. Relatively slow growth of the yolk sac • Types of E

mbryonic Folding • There are two main types: 1. Cephalocaudal Folding (Head and Tail Folding) 2. Lateral Folding Folding in Median Plane • Occurs in the cranial and caudal ends • Causing head and tail folds • Moving ventrally as the embryo elongates cranially and caudally Head Fold • At the beginning of the 4th week • Neural folds in the cranial region thickened to form primordium of the brain • Initially the developing brain projects dorsally into the amniotic cavity • Later grows cranially beyond the oropharyngeal membrane • Overhangs the developing heart • Septum transversum, primordial heart, pericardial coelom & oropharyngeal membrane move onto the ventral surface • Endoderm of the yolk sac is incorporated into the embryo as a foregut • The foregut lies between the brain & heart • Oropharyngeal membrane separates the foregut from the stomodeum • Septum transversum lies caudal to heart after the folding and develops into central tendon of diaphragm Tail Fold • Results primarily from growth of the distal part of the neural tube • This is primordium of the spinal cord • As embryo grows, the caudal eminence projects over the cloacal membrane • During folding, part of endoderm is i

ncorporated into the embryo as a hindgut • Terminal part of the hindgut soon dilates to form the cloaca • Cloaca is the primordium of urinary bladder and rectum • Before folding primitive streak lies cranial to the cloacal membrane • After folding it lies caudal to it • The connecting stalk (primordium of umbilical cord) is attached to the ventral surface of the embryo • Allantois (a diverticulum of yolk sac) is partially incorporated into the embryo • Lateral Folding: Occurs due to growth of somites and lateral plate mesoderm. • Results 1. Right and left sides of the embryo move ventrally and fuse in the midline. 2. Part of the yolk sac is incorporated into the embryo forming the midgut. 3. The intraembryonic coelom begins to form body cavities. 4. Formation of the primitive gut tube.
