< 1g/100ml. • Level increases during pregnancy. • Clinically considered as tumor marker for the diagnosis of hepatocellular carcinoma or teratoblastomas. a1-Fetoprotein & Hepatocellular Carcinoma Hepatocellular Carcinoid cells secrete AFP; levels >400 ng/mL are highly suggestive, >1000 ng/mL diagnostic in cirrhotics. • Causes: Chronic hepatitis B/C, alcoholic/non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) cirrhosis, aflatoxin; mutations in certain genes like TERT, TP53, CTNNB1. • Symptoms: Right upper quadrant pain, weight loss, ascites, jaundice; paraneoplastic hypoglycemia or hypercalcemia. • Treatment: Resection/transplant/ablation for early; TACE, Case Scenerio • A 55-year-old man with hepatitis B-related cirrhosis undergoes routine ultrasound, which shows a new 3 cm liver nodule. n into the kidney. This conserves the valuable iron present in hemoglobin, which would otherwise be lost to the body. Clinical consequences of Heptoglobin • Concentration rises in inflammatory conditions and decreases in hemolytic anemias. • Half-life of haptoglobin is approximately 5 days. • The half-life of the Hb-hp complex is about 90 minutes, the complex being rapidly removed from plasma by hepatocytes. • Thus, when haptoglobin is bound to hemoglobin, it is cleared from the plasma about 80 times faster than normal. • The level of haptoglobin falls rapidly in hemolytic anemias. • Free Hp level or Hp binding capacity depicts the intravascular hemolysis. Each molecule of ceruloplasmin binds eight atoms of copper very tightly so, that the copper is not readily exchangeable. * Normal plasma concentration: approx 30 mg/dL Clinical Significance of Ceruloplasmin • Normal level:- 30 mg/dL. • Low levels of ceruloplasmin are found in Wilsons disease (hepatolenticular degeneration), a disease due to abnormal me

tabolism of copper. • The amount of ceruloplasmin in plasma is also decreased in liver diseases, malnutrition and nepnrotic synarome. Wilson's disease • In Wilson's disease, mutations in ATP7B impair copper incorporation into apoceruloplasmin, leading to low serum ceruloplasmin (<20 mg/dL) and free copper accumulation. • Causes: Autosomal recessive ATP7B gene mutations (chromosome 13) → defective biliary copper excretion → copper deposition in liver, brain (basal ganglia), cornea, and kidneys. • Symptoms: Hepatic (hepatitis, cirrhosis, acute liver failure), neurologic (tremors, dysarthria, dystonia), psychiatric (personality changes), and Kayser-Fleischer rings (copper in cornea). Wilson's disease • Treatment: Zinc acetate (maintenance, blocks copper absorption) or chelators (D-penicillamine, trientine) for symptomatic/decompensated disease; liver transplantation for fulminant failure. chunks: IMMUNOGLOBULINS Key Players in Immune Response HUMAIRA SHARIF Learning Objectives 01 04 Differentiate between immunoglobulins and antibodies Clinical significance of immune deficiency diseases 02 Classifications of immunoglobulins 03 Chemical structure & biochemical functions of immunoglobulins Immunoglobulins Immunoglobulins (Igs) are glycoproteins produced by plasma cells (activated B lymphocytes). They function as antibodies, which are critical components of the adaptive immune system. Each immunoglobulin is specific to a particular antigen (foreign molecule). Immunoglobulins KEY RULES: Recognize & bind to antigens Neutralize pathogens (viruses, bacteria, toxins) Facilitate phagocytosis and complement activation Difference b/w Immunoglobulins & Antibodies Immunoglobulins (Igs) are glycoprotein molecules produced by plasma cells. Antibodies are the functional form of immunoglobulins that bind specifically to antigens. All antibodies are immunoglobulins, but not all immunoglobulins are necessarily acting as antibodies at a given time. Immunoglobulins refer to the structural classification (IgG, IgA, IgM, IgE, IgD), whereas antibodies refer to their action in immune defense. The te

Structure–Function Relationship of RBCs • Biconcave shape increases surface area for gas exchange • Membrane proteins: spectrin, ankyrin, band 3 • Flexible cytoskeleton allows passage through capillaries • Absence of mitochondria prevents oxygen consumption • High hemoglobin concentration optimizes oxygen transport Major Metabolic Pathways in RBCs 1. ry ATP source in RBCs (Anaerobic Glycolysis) • Rapoport-Luebering Pathway: Generates 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG), which regulates hemoglobin's oxygen affinity. • Hexose Monophosphate Pathway (HMP): Detoxifies harmful reactive oxygen species (ROS) using NADPH. • Methemoglobin Reductase Pathway: Keeps Hb in its functional ferrous (Fe2+) state, essential for oxygen binding. HEPATIC JAUNDICE Glucose 6 Phosphate Dehydrogenase deficiency Hexosemonophosphate shunt ERYTHROBLASTOSIS FOETALIS • The mother produces IgG-type antibodies against red cell antigens on fetal red blood cells (RBC); these antibodies pass through the placenta into the fetal circulation. • Once in the fetal circulation, the offending antibodies attach to corresponding antigens on fetal RBC, marking them to be destroyed by haemolysis. • Mild cases may have only mild anaemia and jaundice at birth. • In severe cases, the bilirubin level may rise dramatically within 24 hours of birth, and enter the brain to cause kernicterus, a potentially fatal condition. PREVENTION OF ERYTHROBLASTOSIS FOETALIS • In all expectant mothers, blood type (ABO and Rh groups) should be determined and serum screened for atypical antibodies (that will recognise antigens on fetal RBC), in the first trimester and again at 28 weeks' gestation to identify at-risk pregnancies. • In Rh D-negative women with a negative antibody screen, the risk of sensitization is reduced by administering anti-Rh D immunoglobulin when sensitizing events occur and routinely in the third trimester (routine antenatal anti-D prophylaxis); th

is should be offered to all Rh D-negative women. • Anti-D immunoglobulin destroys the Rh D-positive RBC and prevents active immunization, thus preventing production of Rh D antibodies. Aedes Aegypti (spreads Malaria, Dengue, Chikungunya and Yellow fever)

chunks: LEARNING OBJECTIVES FOR ZINC METABOLISM • Define trace elements in the body. • Explain the biological importance of zinc in human metabolism. • Describe the dietary sources with recommended daily requirements of zinc. • Explain the mechanisms of absorption of zinc in the gastrointestinal tract. • Describe the transport proteins involved in Zinc metabolism (e.g., albumin, metallothionein) • Enlist the major biochemical functions of zinc • Explain how zinc is stored in the body. • Describe the routes of excretion of zinc • Identify causes, biochemical basis, and clinical features of zinc deficiency • Discuss zinc toxicity and its effects By the end of this lecture, students should be able to: LEARNING OBJECTIVES FOR COPPER METABOLISM • Explain the biological importance of copper in human metabolism. • Describe the dietary sources with recommended daily requirements of copper. • Explain the mechanisms of absorption of copper in the gastrointestinal tract. • Describe the transport proteins involved in Copper metabolism (e.g., ceruloplasmin, albumin) • Describe the functions of copper a) Role in redox reactions enzymes such as cytochrome oxidase, superoxide dismutase, tyrosinase • Expla

in how copper is stored in the body. • Describe the role of metallothionein in regulating copper levels. • Describe the routes of excretion of copper (e.g., feces, bile, urine). • Describe copper deficiency: Anemia, bone abnormalities, neurological manifestations • Explain copper toxicity and its consequences. • Describe the biochemical basis, clinical features, and laboratory findings of: Wilson disease, Menkes disease • Interpret basic laboratory tests related to copper metabolism. By the end of this lecture, students should be able to: INTRODUCTION • In the biological system ,Zinc is always found in divalent state (+2). • The adult human body contains 2–3 g of Zinc. • Zinc (Zn) is an essential trace mineral that is important for immune function, wound healing, normal taste and smell, and is needed for DNA synthesis. • Zinc also supports normal growth and development during pregnancy, childhood, and adolescence. • Zinc is present in all body tissues and fluids . ABSORPTION OF ZINC • Like iron, zinc need to be liberated from food prior to absorption. • During digestive process protease ,nucleases and hydrochloric acid release zinc bound to protein and nucleic acids. • Zinc is abso

rbed throughout the small intestine(duodenum and jejunum) ,with absorption being most efficient and varies depending on the content of the zinc in the meal and the composition of the diet. • Availability of zinc improves when the diet includes animal protein or milk or other protein sources or milk ABSORPTION OF ZINC Zinc is absorbed firstly in the enterocytes by Zrt- and Irt-like Protein (ZIP) Named after Zrt (Zinc-regulated transporter) and Irt (Iron-regulated transporter) which imports zinc into the cytoplasm. Also known as CRIP (Cysteine rich intestinal protein) However with increased zinc concentration metallothionein concentration rises because of the diet high in zinc appear to induce gene expression of metallothionein (MTI). Zinc bound to metallothionein stays in the cell. Zinc not bound to the metallothionein or stored within the cell is transported across the basolateral membrane with the help of zinc transporters (ZnTs) Many ZnTs have been identified in the different tissues The utilization of zinc depends on the overall composition of the diet FACTORS AFFECTING ZINC ABSORPTION INHIBITORS • Phytates (whole grains, seeds, nuts, and legumes, tea, coffee) • Fiber, • High le

vels of calcium (Casein in milk) • Iron supplements. PROMOTORS • Animal protein, (Fish, meat, poultry) • Amino acids (e.g., histidine), and • Organic acids (e.g., citrate). • The skeletal muscle(60%), • bone (30%), • Liver (5%) • Skin (5%) • Less than 1% of the total Zn is found in the serum; • Approximately 0.1% of the total Zn is supplemented by daily food intake (or for infants, breast milk). STORAGE TRANSPORT • 80% of the serum Zinc is bound to serum albumin, and 20% is strongly bound to α2-macroglobulin. • It is transported to the liver. • From there it is transported to different tissues and incorporated in different enzymes. • Since zinc is important component of various metallo-enzyme within the cells ,enzyme synthesis and zinc uptake are correlated EXCRETION OF ZINC • Gastrointestinal tract : Majority lost in feces (0.5 mg/day-3 mg/day) depending on zinc intake the higher the intake ,the greater the losses. • Kidney : Excreted in the urine (0.3-0.7 mg/day) • Starvation and muscle catabolism increases the zinc losses in the urine. • Body surface : Exfoliation of skin and sweating (0.7- 1.0 mg/day ) • Another route of zinc loss is hair contain 0.1-0.2 mg Zn/gram hair • Stren

uous exercise and elevated ambient temperature can lead to high losses through perspiration FUNCTIONS OF ZINC 1. Component of metalloenzymes: Zinc is a component of 300 metalloenzymes and therefore vital for fundamental life process for e.g. a) As a component of carbonic anhydrase it helps in rapid disposal of carbon dioxide. b) As part of alcohol- dehydrogenase it is involved in conversion of alcohol to aldehyde such as conversion of retinol to retinal. 2. Protein digestion: It is required for protein digestion since its component of carboxypeptidase A and aminopeptidase,the enzyme involved in the digestion of smaller peptides. 3. Component of Superoxide dismutase: Superoxide dismutase that catalyzes the removal of superoxide radical requires two atom of both zinc and copper. 4. DNA and RNA polymerase are involved in nucleic acid synthesis are zinc dependent. 5. Synthesis of retinol binding protein requires Zinc. 6. Helps in Insulin storage in pancreatic beta cells. FUNCTIONS OF ZINC RECOMMENDED DIETARY ALLOWANCE (RDA) • Adult males at 11mg /day • Adult females at 8 mg /day • Pregnancy 11 mg / day • Lactation 12mg / day • The US Food and nutrition board has derived a tolerable upp

er limit of 40 mg /day for adults ZINC DEFICENCY • Growth retardation (Hypogonadism) • Delayed sexual and bone maturation • Skin lesions • Diarrhea • Alopecia (loss of hair ) • Impaired appetite • Increased susceptibility to infection mediated via defect in immune system • Impaired taste and wound healing are result of low zinc intake Acrodermatitis Enteropathica Rare autosomal recessive genetic disorder causing severe zinc deficiency due to a defect in intestinal absorption, usually stemming from mutations in the SLC39A4 gene which causes deficient ZIP transporter. TOXICITY AND ITS EFFECTS The toxicity sign are: nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, lethargy are observed after ingestion of 4-8 grams of zinc. Adventitious zinc in water from contaminated wells and from galvanized cooking utensils lead to high zinc intakes. • Copper is an important and scarce element found in the human body, present in the structure of various metalloproteins. • Copper ions can exist in biological systems in two forms: Cuprous monovalent (Cu+) Cupric divalent (Cu2+ ). • The amount of Copper present in the human body is approximately 90 milligrams. • While about two-thirds of the body’s copper is found in the m

uscles and bones, the liver is a key organ in copper homeostasis. INTRODUCTION • Copper helps the body’s enzymes that are involved in making energy, managing iron levels, building connective tissue, and maintaining chemicals and signals in the brain. • It can also aid in the new growth of blood vessels, support the immune system, and help protect the body from molecules called free radicals. INTRODUCTION • Copper is absorbed from the gastrointestinal system in food. Small intestine. • 1.5 to 3 mg/day of dietary copper is safe and adequate for the body. • Ctr1 (Copper Transporter 1): The primary high-affinity plasma membrane protein responsible for importing dietary copper into cells. • Copper chaperones deliver copper to enzymes and organelles (e.g., Cox17 brings copper to the mitochondria for cytochrome c oxidase). • ATP7A and ATP7B (ATPase pumps) move copper out of the cytoplasm to either be secreted or incorporated into proteins like ceruloplasmin. • COPPER/ZINC RATIO: • Zinc and copper compete for absorption, so taking more zinc may interfere with absorption of copper. The ideal copper/zinc ratio is 1.1. ABSORPTION TRANSPORT • Copper is bound to Ceruloplasmin (α-2 globulin) wit

h ferroxidase activity. • Copper is also transported in plasma loosely bound to albumin. • A small fraction of the copper is complexed with amino acids. EXCRETION • Excretion of copper occurs mainly in the bile and a small fraction in the urine (<40 µg/day). • Plasma copper is not a reliable indicator of blood copper level. • Factors that will give a raised level of copper are: • Oral contraceptives. • Pregnancy. • Inflammation or infectious process. How the Body Uses Copper Ions • Instead of increasing general “conductivity,” absorbed copper ions are essential for specific biochemical reactions in the body. • Enzyme Cofactor: Copper acts as a vital cofactor for several enzymes (cuproenzymes). • Energy Production: Copper is essential for cytochrome c oxidase, an enzyme in the mitochondria that is crucial for cellular respiration and generating ATP (energy). • Neurotransmission: Copper-containing enzymes are involved in synthesizing neurotransmitters, which are vital for brain function and nerve communication. Iron Metabolism: • -A copper-containing protein, ceruloplasmin, is necessary to oxidize iron to the form needed for transport and red blood cell formation. COPPER and IRON: •

chunks: Definition and Classification • Fat soluble vitamins – Found in the fats and oils of food. – Absorbed into the lymph and carried in blood with protein transporters = chylomicrons. – *Stored in liver and body fat and can become toxic if large amounts are consumed. Vitamin E • Vitamin E – tocopherol, *alpha‐, beta ‐, gamma‐, and delta‐ – Roles: Alpha tocopherol is used by the human body Function: • Antioxidant (against reactive oxygen species) • Prevention of damage to lungs, RBCs, WBCs (immunity), heart • Necessary for normal nerve development Vitamin E • Vitamin E – Cause of Deficiencies (decreased absorption of fats‐ liver disease, low fat diets, Premature babies may also Vitamin E deficiency) • Loss of muscle coordination, vision problem, decreased immunity, nerve damage and loss of sensation in arms and legs due to it. Vitamin E • Vitamin E – DRI 15 mg/day (alpha‐tocopherol) – Sources – Wheat germ, mayonnaise, cannola oil, sunflower seeds, safflower oil – Toxicities (more than 1000 milligrams/day) • Increases the effects of anticoagulants (Coumadin, Warfarin) Absorption and Excretion Free tocopherols and their esters are readily absorbed in small intestine with the help of bile

acids Absorbed vitamin E is transported to the liver where it gets incorporated into lipoproteins and carried by the blood to muscle tissue and to adipose tissue for storage. Under normal conditions there is no significant excretion of tocopherols in urine or faeces as it rapidly and extensively undergoes destruction in the GI tract and in tissues. Placental transfer is limited whereas mammary transfer is much more in breast fed infants. Deficiency Muscular dystrophy: Deficiency of vitamin E leads to increase in peroxides which in turn causes increase in intracellular hydrolase activity by affecting lysosomal membrane. Those hydrolases may the catalyse such breakdowns in muscle and produce muscle dystrophy. Deficiency Hemolytic anemia: Low levels of tocopherols causes increase susceptibility to hemolysis due to peroxides. As RBC have increased susceptibility to hemolyse due to the effect of peroxides. This could be the reason for hemolytic anemia. Deficiency Dietary Hepatic Necrosis: Diets low in cystine and rich in polyunsaturated fatty acids can cause hepatic necrosis. Fall in acetate utilization and in respiration of necrotic liver is more effectively cured or prevented by t

ocopherols. Clinical and Therapeutic Uses Vitamin E can also be used in the following diseases: Nocturnal muscle cramp Intermittent claudication Fibrocystic Breast Disease Atherosclerosis Vitamin E and Coagulation There have been several different mechanisms of action of vitamin E on coagulation and platelet function. Vitamin K precursors need enzymes to convert into their active forms. It is thought that vitamin E may challenge these precursors for these enzymes. As a result, the circulation of vitamin-K induced coagulation factors is decreased. Vitamin K-dependent proteins such as factors II, VII, IX, and X,are involved in the clotting cascade. If vitamin K concentrations are reduced, then these factors are decreased as well, promoting bleeding. Vitamin E and Coagulation Glutamate is needed for factor IX production, and vitamin E reduces the production of glutamate. In patients who take warfarin and vitamin E, vitamin-K antagonism is increased, thus increasing their risk of bleeding. Platelet aggregation was found to be decreased in patients taking vitamin E supplementation. The exact mechanism is unknown but is thought to be related to protein kinase C inhibition, which is l

inked to the inhibition of platelet aggregation. Through these mechanisms, it is easy to see why vitamin E can be associated with higher risks for bleeding, especially in patients taking oral anticoagulants or antiplatelet medications. Vitamin K • Vitamin K – produced by bacteria in large intestine • Also consumed in diet – Roles • Promotes synthesis of blood clotting proteins • Bone formation • Role in oxidative phosphorylation( as a co‐factor) – Toxicities (>1000 mg/day): rupture of RBCs and jaundice 3 Forms of Vitamin K • Vitamin K1 or phylloquinone (usually consumed in diet.mostly plant based) • Vitamin K2 or menaquinone ( made by intestinal microbiota) • Vitamin K3 or menadione (synthetic) Vitamin K and Clotting Vitamin K helps to make protein (prothrombin)that are needed for blood clotting. Prothrombin is a vitamin K-dependent protein directly involved with blood clotting Vitamin K dependent Clotting factors: Vitamin K acts as a cofactor for a group of proteins known as the vitamin K-dependent clotting factors (II, VII, IX, and X ), which are involved in the activation of blood-clotting proteins Effect on bone Vitamin K is found to carboxylate specific glutamate residues of

calcium binding proteins of bones, spleen, placenta and kidneys. This enhances the capacity of these proteins to deposit calcium in the tissues concerned. Vitamin K also regulates the transcription of osteoblastic markers, the formation of osteoclasts, and bone resorption Deficiency Causes Deficiencies are rare but seen in Immediate Post-natal Infants: Relatively small amounts of vitamin K are obtained from mother through placenta and also because the intestinal microflora has not yet been established. May cause hypoprothrombinemia and bleeding in many tissues. Note: can be prevented by administering vitamin K before parturition or by giving infant small dose of vitamin K Deficiency Causes Malabsorption and Biliary tract obstruction: Coeliac disease, sprue and steatorrhea can lead to vitamin deficiency. Being fat soluble it is absorbed with the help of bile salts. Hence biliary obstruction can cause Vitamin K deficiency Prolonged use of antibiotic and sulfa drugs: This suppressed the growth of Vitamin K2 producing gut bacteria thus causing deficiency. Contd.. Short circuiting of the bowel due to bowel surgery. In this cases it may not even respond to large oral doses of vitami

n K. Water soluble vitamin K ( vitamin K3) may be useful in such cases. Deficiency Bleeding(hemorrhage) Abnormal bone formation Fat Soluble Vitamins • Vitamin K – DRI: 90(women) – 120(men) µg/day – Sources – Cabbage, spinach, soybean, cauliflower, lettuce, canola oil

chunks: LYMPHATIC SYSTEM By Professor Dr Imran Ishaque Shaikh Objectives • At the end student should able to: • Define lymphatic system. • Describes the classification of lymphoid tissue • Describes the line of defence • List the immunoglobulin and their functions • List the cells of immune system • Give the examples of diffuse and dense lymphatic tissue • Formation of MALT (Mucosa associated lymphoid tissue) • Discrete lymphoid organs (encapsulated) • Define lymphatic nodule • Difference between primary and secondary lymph nodule • Describes the structure of lymphoblast • Describes the structure of reticular epithelial cell • Describes the general architecture of lymphoid organ • Lymphatic system is a secondary circulatory system that collects excess interstitial fluid (lymph) from tissues, filters it, and returns it to the bloodstream, • Playing a key role in the body’s immune defense. Main Components • Lymph – clear fluid containing white blood cells (especially lymphocytes) • Lymphatic vessels – channels that carry lymph • Lymph nodes – filter lymph and trap pathogens • Lymphoid organs: 1. Thymus 2. Spleen 3. Tonsils 4. Peyer’s patches • The first line of defense is provided by the sur

face epithelium constituted by the epidermis of skin that covers the body and the mucous membrane that lines the hollow visceral tracts which are exposed to the external environment. • The second line of defense comes into effect when there is breach of the epithelial surface due to injury (abrasion, burning,). second line of defense is constituted by phagocytic cells. • The third line of defense is the specific immune response which gets activated when both the above mentioned lines of defense fail to check the invasion of pathogenic organisms. Cells of the immune system • Distributed throughout the body in the blood, lymph, and epithelial and C.T • Arranged in small spherical nodules called lymphoid nodules found in connective tissues and inside several organs; and • Organized in larger lymphoid organs—the 1. Lymph node 2. Spleen 3. Thymus 4. Bone marrow Cells of the Immune System • The primary cells that participate in the immune response are: 1. Lymphocytes 2. Plasma Cells 3. Mast Cells 4. Neutrophils 5. Eosinophils 6. cells of the Mononuclear 7. Phagocyte System. • Lymphocytes can be classified into three major types based on their immunologic 1. T lymphocytes (T cells) 2. Nul

l cells 3. B lymphocytes (B cells) • Lymphocytes originate in the bone marrow and develop and mature in primary lymphoid organs. Plasma cells • Are derived from B lymphocytes. • Are oval cells with basophilic cytoplasm. • Have eccentrically placed nucleus with clumps of heterochromatin distributed around the periphery of the nucleus— giving a cartwheel appearance. • Are involved in the defense of the body by producing antibodies (immunoglobulins). • IMMUNOGLOBULINS • Five classes of immunoglobulins have been described in human beings. • IgG: Most abundant type forming 75% of serum immunoglobulin. • Is the only immunoglobulin that crosses the placental barrier. • Protects the newborn against infection. • IgA - - Is the main immunoglobulin found in secretions (nasal, bronchial, intestinal, vaginal and secretions, tears, colos- trum, saliva, etc.). Protects the mucous membrane and prevents the proliferation of microorganisms. • IgM - - Constitutes about 5–10% of serum immunoglobulins. Found on the surface of B lymphocytes. First immunoglobulin to be produced in an initial immune response. Activates complement system. • IgD - - 0.2% of serum immunoglobulins function is not completely u

nderstood. Like IgM, it is found on the surface of B lymphocytes • IgE - - serum immunoglobulins bind to the surface of mast cells, eosinophils and basophils. subject: Histology
chunks: Histology of Thymus By Professor Dr Imran Ishaque Shaikh Objectives • At the end student should able to: • Describes the general characteristic features of thymus • Describes the supporting framework of thymus • List the contents of stroma and parenchyma of thymus. • Describe the Interlobular Septae and list its contents. • Describes the cellular cytoplasmic retinaculum. • Origin or reticular epithelial cells. • Histological features of reticular epithelial cells. • Formation & function of blood–thymus barrier • Describes the characteristic feature of the medulla of thymus. • Define and describes the structures of Hassall’s Corpuscle • List the thymic hormones produce by thymus. General Features • Thymus is a central lymphoid organ. It is responsible for the development of immune system of body • It is a bilobed organ, the lobes being unequal in size, present in the superior and anterior mediastinum of thorax. • It has dual origin. Its lymphocytes arise from mesoderm, whereas the epithelial reticular cells arise from endoderm. • So it is called a ‘lympho-epithelial organ’. • Thymus is larger and well-developed in fetus and in early childhood. It attains its peak development at pube

rty and thereafter it starts involuting and is replaced by fi bro-fatty tissue. • It has only efferent and no afferent lymphatic vessels. • Thymus consists of two distinct lobes connected by a connective tissue isthmus. A thin connective tissue capsule surrounds each lobe and gives rise to septae, that partially subdivide the thymus into interconnecting lobules of variable size and orientation COMPONENTS/STRUCTURE A. Supporting framework • Capsule • Interlobular septae • Cellular cytoplasmic reticulum—formed by epithelial reticular cells. B. Lobules or Parenchyma • Cortex • Medulla and Hassall’s corpuscle. • Capsule is composed of an outer and inner layer of collagen and reticular fibres between which are occasional clusters of lymphocytes. • A thin connective tissue capsule surrounds each lobe and, gives rise to septae, that partially subdivide the thymus into interconnecting lobules • The capsule is composed of reticular cells & fibres between which are clusters of lymphocytes. • Fine trabeculae also extend from the capsule or septae into the centre of the lobules. • The bulk of the supporting framework in the thymus is composed of the network of epithelial-reticular cells. • Emb

ryologically, their origin is from the endodermal cells of the third pharyngeal pouch. • Their epithelial origin is confirmed by the presence of basement membrane and the desmosomes with tonofibrils. The cells become flat and spindle shaped. • Lymphocytes lie in this network of epithelial reticular cells. • The identity of these cells has been established by 1. Presence of tonofilaments and desmosomes, 2. Basal lamina associated with cell membrane. 3. These cells have long cytoplasmic process which connect with adjacent cells. CORTEX • Darkly staining cortex contains densely packed, small, immature lymphocytes. • Cortex stains more darkly (is more basophilic) than the medulla, because it contains more lymphocytes than the medulla. • Large, mitotically active lymphoblasts, may be found in the subcapsular cortex , divide by mitosis produce smaller lymphocytes. • These cells have a round to oval nucleus with one or two prominent nuclei and relatively abundant, strongly basophilic cytoplasm. It contains dividing cells (mitotic figures) Mitotic figure lymphocytes • The immature lymphocytes only differentiate in the cortex. • Differentiating T-cells accumulate between epithelial reticula

r cells. • They can then pass into the venules and efferent lymphatics along the border between the cortex and the medulla. • Or they pass into the medulla, where they are further selected by thymic dendritic cells and matured before passing out of the medullary venules and efferent lymphatics. CORTICOMEDULLARY JUNCTION • characterized by plentiful 1. Blood vessels 2. Scant perivascular connective tissue 3. Mature and immature T lymphocytes • MEDULLA -- Paler staining, less densely cellular than the cortex, and contains more mature T-cells, prominent epithelial cells. • Hassall’s corpuscles are round lamellated acidophilic bodies. • They have a central homogeneous hyaline material surrounded by concentric layers of fl attened epithelial cells. • These cells are filled with keratin filaments. • Epithelial cells form a sheath around the capillaries, to form a barrier to the entry of antigenic material into the spaces between the epithelial cells in the reticular network. This is known as the blood thymus barrier. CAPILARIES CHARACTERISTIC FEATURES • Central lymphoid organ—essential for development of other lymphoid organs. • Dual origin (lymphocytes from mesoderm and epithelial retic

ular cells from the endoderm). • Formed only by T lymphocytes/thymocytes (no B lymphocytes). 1. Divided into lobules of lymphoid tissue by interlobular septum (no lymphatic nodules). 2. Dark stain cortex (basophilic) 3. Light stain medulla (eosinophilic) 4. Hassall’s corpuscles. • Produces many thymic hormones. • Fully developed at birth. • Involutes after puberty.

chunks: HISTOLOGY OF SPLEEN By Professor Dr. Rais Ahmed M.B.,BS FCPS M.phil Professor of anatomy United medical and dental college FUNCTIONS OF THE SPLEEN 1. The spleen is the largest lymphoid organ of the body. 2. Normally spleen is a blood-forming organ in fetal life, but blood-destroying organ in postnatal life (graveyard of RBCs). Since it is in the blood stream, it filter the blood-born antigen and microorganisms. 3. Like other lymphoid tissues the spleen is a centre where both B-lymphocytes and T-lymphocytes multiply. 4. The spleen contains the largest aggregations of macrophages of the mononuclear phagocyte system. 5. In fetal life the spleen is a centre for production of all blood cells. In later life only lymphocytes are produced here. 6. The spleen is often regarded as a store of blood that can be thrown into the circulation when required. This function is much less important in man than in some other species. Connective tissue frame work Stroma 1. Capsule 2. Trabeculae 3. Reticular stroma Parenchyma 1. White pulp 2. Red pulp • Spleen is covered by a capsule consisting of dense, irregular connective tissue with elastic and smooth muscle fibers (it varies with the species). • Trab

eculae derived from the capsule carry blood vessels (trabecular arteries and veins) and nerves to and from the splenic red pulp . • The splenic artery enters the hilum, giving rise to trabecular arteries, which are distributed to the splenic pulp along the connective tissue trabeculae. • As an artery leaves the trabecula, it becomes invested by a sheath of T cells forming a periarteriolar lymphoid sheath (PALS) and penetrates a lymphatic nodule (the white pulp). • The blood vessel is designated the central artery. • The central artery leaves the white pulp to become the penicillar artery. • Penicillar arteries end as macrophage- sheathed capillaries (Elipsoid) Penicillar arteries (or penicillar arterioles) are small, straight terminal branches of the splenic artery located within the red pulp of the spleen, responsible for supplying blood to the splenic sinuse They arise from the centra arteriole's termination and are crucial for the splenic circulation process. Ellipsoid arteries (or sheathed capillaries/arterioles) are specialized microscopic vascular structures located in the spleen, specifically at the transition between penicilliary arterioles and capillaries. They consist of

a capillary surrounded by a cuff of specialized cells (fixed macrophages and reticular cells) and act as a filter for blood-borne pathogens and a transit system for lymphocytes. Splenic artery – trabecular artery – central artery – nodular artery The Red Pulp • The red pulp is like a sponge. It is permeated by spaces lined by reticular cells. The intervals between the spaces are filled by B- lymphocytes as well as T-lymphocytes, macrophages, and blood cells. These cells appear to be arranged as cords (splenic cords, of Billroth). The cords form a network. • The zone of red pulp immediately surrounding white pulp is the marginal zone. This zone has a rich network of sinusoids. • The red pulp occupies the majority of the stromal tissue of the spleen. • It consists of the cords of Billroth and splenic sinusoids. • The cords of Billroth (splenic cords) are the cellular aggregations supported by the reticular connective tissue. • They appear as stripes and consist of of macrophages, plasmocytes and blood cells Red Pulp – modified lymphoid tissue 1. Splenic cord 2. Splenic sinuses Splenic sinusoids • Splenic sinusoids are found between the cords of Billroth. They are filled with blood an

d give the red pulp its distinguishable red appearance. • Blood slowly flows through the sinusoids where it is exposed to macrophages from the cords of Billroth, patiently waiting for foreign antigens that can appear in the blood. • In a nutshell, the red pulp functions as a blood filter for various toxins, destroying them before they enter systemic circulation and get the chance to spread throughout the body and damage other organs White pulp • The white pulp of the spleen is made of three different compartments: – Periarterial lymphoid sheath (PALS), – lymphoid follicles and – the marginal zone Marginal zone - (Functional zone between white & red pulp) • White pulp – Aggregation of lymphoid tissue around a artery (central artery). 1. PALT – Population of T lymphocytes around artery. 2. Lymphatic nodule 3. Marginal zone - (Functional zone between white & red pulp) Marginal zone • The marginal zone is found on the very edge of the lymphoid follicles, containing different immune cells that are well equipped for starting an appropriate immune response. PALS • The PALS consists of a central artery (a branch of the splenic artery) surrounded by a sheath of lymphoid tissue. Here, the ly

mphoid tissue organized into two layers: – The inner layer and outer layer. – The inner layer is mainly composed of T lymphocytes which is why it is also called the T- zone. – The outer layer has a more diverse cellular morphology, containing T and B lymphocytes. Lymphoid follicles • The branches of central arterioles are surrounded by the sharply defined areas of B lymphocytes, comprising the lymphoid follicles of the spleen. There are two types of lymphoid follicles depending on the features of the B lymphocytes that comprise them: – Primary follicles and – secondary nodules. • A follicle that consists mainly of small, immature lymphocytes is called a primary follicle. • Most nodules found in the spleen are secondary nodules that arise from primary follicles as the lymphocytes mature and increase in size. • They differ from primary follicles by featuring a distinctive centrally positioned zone called the germinal center. – The germinal centers are the sites where lymphocytes mature and acquire the ability to produce antibodies. So, seeing the germinal center is a sign that lymphoid tissue is responding to an antigen. • Each arteriole is surrounded by a dense sheath of lymphocytes
. These lymphocytes constitute the white pulp of the spleen. • The part of splenic tissue, which is infiltrated with blood in this way is called the red pulp.

subject: Histology
chunks: General Architecture of Lymphoid Organs Lymphoid organs consist of;  Supporting framework (connective tissue) and  Parenchyma (lymphocytes).  The supporting framework includes the capsule that covers the organ at the periphery; trabeculae/interlobular septae which enter into the organ carrying blood vessels and nerves, and reticulum which supports the cellular parenchyma. GENERAL FEATURES:  Thymus is a central lymphoid organ. It is responsible for the development of immune system of body and is essential for the growth and development of other lymphoid organs.  It is a bilobed organ, the lobes being unequal in size, present in the superior and anterior mediastinum of thorax.  It has dual origin. Its lymphocytes arise from mesoderm, whereas the epithelial reticular cells arise from endoderm of III pharyngeal pouch. So it is called a  ‘lympho-epithelial organ’.  Thymus is larger and well-developed in foetus and in early childhood. It attains its peak development at puberty and thereafter it starts involuting and is replaced by fi bro-fatty tissue. Its weight is 12–15 gm at birth, 30–40 gm at puberty and 10–15 gm at 60 years.  It has only efferent and no afferent lymphatic ve

ssels. COMPONENTS/STRUCTURE: A. Supporting framework 1. Capsule 2. Interlobular septae 3. Cellular cytoplasmic reticulum—formed by epithelial reticular cells. B. Lobules or Parenchyma 1. Cortex 2. Medulla and Hassall’s corpuscle. Supporting Framework: Capsule and Interlobular Septae:  Thin connective tissue capsule covers the thymus completely.  The capsule sends septae into the interior dividing the lobe into incomplete lobules. The interlobular connective tissue septae carry blood vessels, nerves and lymphatics.  Each lobule has a darkly stained cortex at the periphery and a lightly stained medulla in the centre  The medulla of one lobule becomes continuous with the medulla of neighbouring lobules, as seen in serial sections, and this confirms the presence of a central medulla for the lobe,while forming an interconnected, branching structure throughout the thymic lobe. Cellular Cytoplasmic Reticulum/Epithelial Reticular Cells:  The supporting stroma of the organ within the lobule is formed by epithelial reticular cells (endodermal in origin).  These are stellate cells and their cytoplasmic processes come in contact with the processes of neighbouring cells by means of desmos

omes.  Thus they form a cellular cytoplasmic reticulum giving support to the lymphocytes of thymic lobules. (This reticulum is different from the reticulum of other lymphoid organs where it is formed by reticular fibres.)  They can be easily identified by their large pale staining oval nuclei and eosinophilic cytoplasm.  The cytoplasm contains secretory granules which are believed to liberate hormones, thymosin and thymopoietin. Lobules or Parenchyma: 1. Cortex:  Each lobule shows a darkly stained cortex and a lightly stained medulla.  The cortex is densely packed with lymphocytes (thymocytes), few macrophages and epithelial reticular cells.  The outer part of cortex contains larger lymphocytes (lymphoblasts) which divide by mitosis to produce smaller lymphocytes which are pushed into the deeper part of the cortex.  Of the vast number of lymphocytes produced in the cortex, only very few leave the thymus via post-capillary venules in the medulla as immunocompetent T lymphocytes and the rest (majority) die in the thymus itself. The reason for this cell death is not fully understood.  The capillaries present in the cortex show a distinct, thick basement membrane and are surrou

nded by processes of epithelial reticular cells forming the so called blood–thymus barrier. It is believed that this barrier does not allow any blood borne antigen to come in contact with the maturing T lymphocytes, which otherwise may influence the developing T lymphocytes. Medulla and Hassall’s Corpuscle:  Medulla is lightly stained because the lymphocytes are less densely packed. For this reason the epithelial reticular cells in the medulla appear to be numerous.  The most characteristic feature of the medulla is the presence of Hassall’s corpuscles.  Hassall’s corpuscles are round lamellated acidophilic bodies (30–100 mm). They have a central homogeneous hyaline material surrounded by concentric layers of flattened epithelial cells. These cells are filled with keratin filaments.  The number of Hassall’s corpuscles increases with age and may show traces of calcification. Their function is crucial in immune system maturation. They are essential for T-cell development, specifically in the differentiation of natural regulatory T-cells, which prevents autoimmune diseases. and are the last one to undergo involution. CHARACTERISTIC FEATURES: Thymus has the following characteristic

features by which it is differentiated from other lymphoid organs:  Central lymphoid organ—essential for development of other lymphoid organs.  Dual origin (lymphocytes from mesoderm and epithelial reticular cells from the endoderm).  Supporting stroma is formed by ‘cytoplasmic reticulum’ derived from epithelial reticular cells.  Formed only by T lymphocytes/thymocytes (no B lymphocytes).  Divided into lobules of lymphoid tissue by interlobular septum (no lymphatic nodules).  Has Hassall’s corpuscles.  Produces many thymic hormones.  Fully developed at birth.  Involutes after puberty. FUNCTIONS  It is a central lymphoid organ and is essential till puberty for the development of the immune system of the organism. After puberty the other lymphoid organs of the body are fully developed and thereafter it undergoes involution.  Removal of thymus in newborn → failure of seeding of other lymphoid organs with immunocompetent T cells → deficiency in immunological competence to fight invading pathogens → infection → death.  Epithelial reticular cells secrete hormones like thymulin, thymosin, thymopoietin, etc., which are involved in stimulation, proliferation and differentiation

of T lymphocytes.  Produces immunocompetent T lymphocytes which are involved in cell mediated immunity. GENERAL FEATURES:  Oval or bean-shaped structures situated along the course of the lymphatic vessels.  They serve as filters of lymph, removing particulate matter and bacteria from lymph before it enters the CVS, thereby localizing and preventing the spread of infection.  Lymph nodes are usually found in groups, especially in the axilla, inguinal region, root of lung, etc.  Lymph node has many afferent lymphatic vessels which enter through the convex surface, whereas the efferent lymphatic vessels are one or two in number and leave through the concave depression, the hilum. The hilum also transmits nerves and blood vessels. The lymphatic vessels are provided with valves in such a way that lymph fl ows in one direction. COMPONENTS/STRUCTURE: A. Connective tissue framework 1. Capsule 2. Trabeculae 3. Reticular stroma (fibres) B. Parenchyma 1. Cortex 2. Paracortex (inner cortex) 3. Medulla Connective Tissue Framework: 1. Capsule and Trabeculae:  The organ is surrounded by a thin connective tissue capsule which sends trabeculae into the interior.  Beneath the capsule is the s

ubcapsular sinus which is traversed by reticular fibres and cells.  The subscapsular sinus receives afferent lymphatic vessels and is continuous with trabecular sinuses found around the trabeculae.  The trabecular sinuses become continuous with the medullary sinuses. Reticular Stroma: It is made of reticular fibres and associated phagocytic reticular cells, forming a meshwork throughout the organ and is particularly dense in the cortex. Gives structural support to lymphoid cells (parenchyma). PARENCHYMA: “It is the lymphoid tissue present in cortex, paracortex and medulla.” Cortex: The outer cortex is the peripheral part of the lymph node situated deep to the capsule. It contains the following structures: 1. Subcapsular sinus—found beneath the capsule. 2. Lymphatic nodules—with or without germinal centres formed mainly of B lymphocytes. A lymphatic nodule without a pale staining germinal centre is called primary nodule, whereas one with germinal centre is called secondary nodule. Paracortex:  It is the inner cortical zone, which does not have precise boundary with the outer cortex.  It consists mainly of T lymphocytes and is called the thymus-dependent zone.  Normally no nod

ules can be seen in the paracortex but sometimes discrete lymphatic nodules are seen.  The dense lymphoid tissue in the paracortex becomes continuous with the medullary cords. Medulla:  Medulla has two components, the medullary cords and medullary sinuses.  The medullary cords are branching and anastomosing cords of typical lymphoid tissue—made primarily of ‘B’ lymphocytes, few plasma cells and macrophages.  The medullary sinuses are atypical lymphoid tissue disposed between the medullary cords. As in the subcapsular and trabecular sinuses, the medullary sinuses are traversed by reticular fibres providing support to macrophages, B lymphocytes and plasma cells. The medullary sinuses are lightly stained compared to the darkly stained medullary cords (with H & E). The medullary sinuses drain into the efferent lymphatic vessels found at the hilum. FUNCTIONS: Filters the microorganisms from lymph, thereby localizing and preventing the spread of infection (defense). Produces lymphocytes. Produces antibodies.

RAIS AHMED M.B.,B.S FCPS (SURGERY) M.phil(anatomy) PROF. of ANATOMY UMDC Learning Objectives • Define cartilage, • Describe its microscopic structure, • Identify cells and matrix components, • Compare cartilage types, and • Understand clinical relevance. INTRODUCTION What Is Cartilage? ●Definition: a specialised, resilient connective tissue made of cells (chondrocytes) embedded in a firm, gel-like extracellular matrix. ●Origin: derived from mesenchyme, mainly of paraxial and lateral plate mesoderm and neural crest in the head. ●Avascular tissue: lacks blood vessels, lymphatics and nerves; matrix allows diffusion of nutrients. ●Mechanical role: combines tensile strength with elasticity, resisting compression while permitting some deformation. ●Clinical importance: forms the fetal skeleton, articular surfaces, and the template for most bone formation (endochondral ossification). Chondrocytes embedded in extracellular matrix 2 General Characteristics • Firm but flexible tissue. • Avascular, aneural, alymphatic: all nutrition, gas exchange and waste removal occur purely by diffusion through the matrix. • Nourished by diffusion. • Covered by perichondri

um: a dense connective tissue sheath present on most cartilage, except articular cartilage and fibrocartilage. • Dual growth pattern: grows by both appositional (surface) and interstitial (internal) mechanisms, unlike bone. Location • Cartilage is found in: – Respiratory tract – External ear – Intervertebral disc – Articular surface of bones (in joints) Ends of long bone. – Skeleton of fetus – Ossification Components • Cartilage consists of three components: – Cells – Matrix (between the cells) – Perichondrium (outer layer) • Cartilage contains three types of cells: – Chondrogenic cells – Chondroblast – chondrocyte Cells of Cartilage: Chondrogenic Cells • Located in perichondrium. • Stem-cell-like cells that differentiate into chondroblasts during growth and repair. MATRIX & CELLS Chondroblasts and Chondrogenesis ●Origin: mesenchymal cells aggregate and round up to form chondrogenic cells, which differentiate into chondroblasts. ●Chondroblasts: actively secrete collagen and ground substance; as they become surrounded by their own matrix they mature into chondrocytes. ●Timing: chondrification begins around the fifth week of intra- uterine life at sites called chondrification centres

. ●Outcome: the resulting hyaline cartilage model serves as the template for most bones formed by endochondral ossification. Mesenchymal cell Chondrogenic cell Chondroblast (secretes matrix) Chondrocyte (in lacuna) 8 Cells of Cartilage: Chondrocytes • Mature cartilage cells residing in lacunae. • Maintain cartilage matrix and metabolic activity. MATRIX & CELLS Chondrocytes ●Definition: mature cartilage cells occupying spaces called lacunae within the matrix. ●Shape: oval or rounded, becoming flattened near the perichondrium and rounder deeper in the tissue. ●Cytoplasm: basophilic, with well- developed rough endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus for active protein and glycosaminoglycan synthesis. ●Arrangement: single peripheral cells versus clustered isogenous groups (2–8 cells) centrally, from recent mitotic division. Lacuna Nucleus 6 Cartilage Matrix • The matrix is an avascular extracellular material secreted by chondroblast & chondrocyte. • Cartilage matrix consists of: – Fibers: collagen type I or type II or elastic fibers. – Ground substance: glycoproteins & chondroitin sulphate. subject: Histology
chunks: Histology of Mammary Gland Prof Dr Imran Ishaque • Glands within the breasts are classified as compound tubuloalveolar glands, • Consisting of 15 to 20 lobes radiating out from the nipple and separated from each other by adipose and collagenous connective tissue. • Each lobe is drained by its own lactiferous duct leading directly to the nipple, where it opens onto its surface. • Before reaching the nipple, each of the ducts is dilated to form a lactiferous sinus for milk storage and then narrows before passing through the nipple. STRUCTURE • STROMA – Supporting frame work of gland. • Partly fibrous and fatty • PARENCHYMA – made of glandular tissue consist of lobes cluster of alveoli lactiferrous duct MAMMARY GLANDS • Amount of parenchymal tissue & stromal tissue define the state of mammary gland. • They are found in two state Resting Lactating Resting Mammary Glands Alveoli are not developed in the resting mammary gland. • More CT and less glandular tissue. • Underdevelop alveoli • Entensive branching of ducts. • Smaller ducts are lined by simple columnar epithelium, which become stratified cuboidal in lactiferous duct up to lactiferous sinus. • Stellate myoepithelial cells locat

ed between the epithelium and the basal lamina also wrap around the developing alveoli and become functional during pregnancy. Lactating (Active) Mammary Glands During pregnancy, the terminal portions of the ducts branch and grow and develop secretory units known as alveoli. • During pregnancy under the influence of constant high level of sex hormone the terminal portion of ducts multiplies & alveoli are develop. • Enlargement of secretory portion gradually regresses CT stroma in the form of strands. • Within a few days after birth, when estrogen and progesterone secretions have subsided, prolactin, secreted by acidophils of the anterior pituitary gland, activates the secretion of milk, which replaces the colostrum. • Less CT and more glandular tissue. • Comactely packed alveoli with distended lumen. • Entensive branching of ducts. • Smaller ducts are lined by simple cuboidal epithelium. Alveoli of Mammary gland • The alveoli of the lactating (active) mammary glands are composed of cuboidal cells partially surrounded by a meshwork of myoepithelial cells. • These secretory cells possess abundant RER and mitochondria, several Golgi complexes, many lipid droplets, and numerous vesicle

s containing caseins (milk proteins) and lactose. • The secretions of the alveolar cells are of two kinds: lipids and proteins. • Protein secretion are merocrine while lipid secretions are apocrine. Areola and Nipple • Circular, heavily pigmented skin in the center of the breast is the areola. • Contains sweat glands and sebaceous glands at its margin as well as areolar glands (of Montgomery) that resemble both sweat and mammary glands. • Center of the areola is the nipple, a protuberance covered by stratified squamous epithelium containing the terminal openings of the lactiferous ducts. • Their color is imparted by fair blood supply. • Core of the nipple is composed of dense collagenous connective tissue with abundant elastic fibers connected to the surrounding skin or interlaced within the connective tissue and a rich component of smooth muscle cells. • Abundant smooth muscle fibers are arranged in two ways: circularly around the nipple and radiating longitudinally along the long axis of the nipple. The contraction of these muscle fibers is responsible for erection of the nipple.

chunks: Shoulder joint By Professor Dr. Rais Ahmed Professor of anatomy United medical and dental college Learning Objectives • Define the shoulder joint. • Describe its type, articular surfaces, capsule, ligaments, movements, muscles, blood supply, nerve supply, and clinical importance. Introduction • The shoulder joint is the most mobile joint in the human body. • It connects the upper limb to the trunk and • Allows a wide range of movements. Articular Surfaces • Large spherical head of humerus articulates with shallow glenoid cavity. • Only a small part of the humeral head contacts the glenoid at one time. Glenoid Labrum Articular Cartilage: • The Labrum: Made of dense, tough fibrocartilage, it acts like a gasket to seal the joint and stabilize the humerus. (rim attached to margin of glenoid cavity.) – Deepens the socket and improves stability. • Articular Cartilage: The actual articulating surface of the humeral head (the "ball" of your shoulder) is covered in hyaline cartilage, which is smooth and allows the joint to glide easily without friction. • Definition: a musculotendinous cuff formed by four muscles whose tendons blend with the joint capsule. • Function: dynamically stabilises

the shoulder by holding the head of the humerus in the glenoid cavity during movement – the most important stabiliser of the joint. • Mnemonic – SITS: – Supraspinatus – superior, initiates abduction. – Infraspinatus – posterior, lateral rotator. – Teres minor – posterior, lateral rotator. – Subscapularis – anterior, medial rotator. The Rotator Cuff — SITS Muscles Sub- scapularis Sub- scapularis LIGAMENTS • Accessory ligaments: – The coracoacromial ligament extends between the coracoid process and the acromion. • Its function is to protect the superior aspect of the joint. • The coracohumeral ligament strengthens the capsule from above and stretches from the root of the coracoid process to the greater tuberosity of the humerus. – The transverse humeral ligament strengthens the capsule and bridges the gap between the two humeral tuberosities. – The glenohumeral ligaments are three weak bands of fibrous tissue that strengthen the front of the capsule. The ligaments of the shoulder joint. The transverse humeral ligament is not shown on this diagram NERVE SUPPLY • Articular branches of the axillary & the suprascapular nerves. Movements • The following movements are possible: – Flexion

– Extension – Abduction – Adduction – Lateral rotation – Medial rotation – Circumduction MOVEMENTS • Normal flexion is about 90° – It is performed by the: Anterior fibers of the deltoid Pectoralis major Biceps brachii Coracobrachialis • Normal extension is about 45° It is performed by the: Posterior fibers of the deltoid, Latissimus dorsi Teres major. • Abduction: – Abduction of the upper limb occurs both at the shoulder joint and between the scapula and the thoracic wall. – It is initiated by supraspinatus from 0 to 18 – Then from 19 to 120 by the middle fibers of the deltoid. – Then above90 by rotation of the scapula by 2 muscles ( Trapezius & S.A..) The supraspinatus muscle: • Initiates the movement of abduction(from 0 to 19) and holds the head of the humerus against the glenoid fossa of the scapula; – This latter function of the supraspinatus allows the deltoid muscle to contract and abduct the humerus at the shoulder joint. The rotator cuff muscles, which act to stabilise the shoulder joint.

Introduction • The gluteal region forms the buttock and lies posterior to the hip joint. • It contains strong muscles that stabilize the pelvis and produce movements of the hip. Surface Landmarks • Iliac crest • Posterior superior iliac spine (PSIS) • Greater trochanter • Ischial tuberosity • Sacrum and coccyx ORGANISATION Gluteal Muscles — Three Layers 6 ●Superficial layer — gluteus maximus, the largest and most powerful muscle in the body ●Middle layer — gluteus medius, piriformis, and the upper parts of obturator internus with the gemelli ●Deep layer — gluteus minimus and quadratus femoris SUPERFICIAL MUSCLE Gluteus Maximus — Origin & Insertion 7 Gluteus maximus, the largest and coarsest muscle of the body, originates from the posterior gluteal line of ilium, t

he dorsal surface of sacrum and coccyx, the sacrotuberous ligament, and the aponeurosis of erector spinae. Its fibres run obliquely downward and laterally. About three-fourths of the muscle inserts into the iliotibial tract, while the deeper one-fourth inserts directly into the gluteal tuberosity of the femur. This dual insertion lets it act both directly on the femur and indirectly through the iliotibial tract on the tibia — vital for climbing, rising from sitting, and running. STRUCTURES UNDER THE COVER OF GLUTEUS MAXIMUS MUSCLE Tensor Fasciae Latae • Located on lateral side of hip. • Tenses fascia lata. • Stabilizes hip and knee through iliotibial tract. ANTEROLATERAL HIP Tensor Fasciae Latae 13 Tensor fasciae latae is a short muscle at the anterolateral hip, arising from the anterior part of the iliac crest and the anterior superior iliac spine. It inserts into the iliotibial tract about one-third of the way down the thigh. Supplied by the superior gluteal nerve, it flexes, abducts, and medially rotates the hip, and through the iliotibial tract also stabilises the extended knee. Working with gluteus maximus via the shared iliotibial tract, it helps maintain balance while walkin

g and running, particularly during the single-leg stance phase of gait. A) Structures passing through the greater sciatic foramen: Arterial Supply • Superior gluteal artery supplies gluteus medius and minimus. • Inferior gluteal artery mainly supplies gluteus maximus. Venous Drainage • Gluteal veins accompany arteries. • Drain into internal iliac vein. Lymphatic Drainage • Superficial lymphatics drain to superficial inguinal nodes. • Deep lymphatics drain to internal iliac nodes.

Popliteal fossa • Definition: The popliteal fossa is a diamond-shaped intermuscular depression located at the back of the knee joint. • It serves as an important passage for nerves and blood vessels traveling between the thigh and the leg. • Roof • Is formed by skin, superficial fascia and deep fascia (popliteal fascia). • The deep fascia in the roof is pierced by posterior cutaneous nerve of thigh and small saphenous vein. Side Boundaries 1. Superolateral: Bic

eps femoris muscle. 2. Superomedial: Semitendinosus and semimembranosus muscles. 3. Inferolateral: Lateral head of gastrocnemius and plantaris muscles. 4. Inferomedial: Medial head of gastrocnemius muscles. • Floor: Is formed by 1. Popliteal surface of femur 2. Capsule of knee joint 3. Fascia over popliteus muscle (from above downwards). • Origin: lateral femoral condyle and posterior horn of lateral meniscus • Insertion: posterior surface of proximal tibia at the medial 2/3rd aspect, just superior to the soleal line • Action: Unlocks the knee joint 1. In a weight-bearing (fixed foot) position, it laterally rotates the femur on the tibia. 2. In a non-weight-bearing (free leg) position, it medially rotates the tibia on the femur. • Arterial supply: popliteal artery • Innervation: tibial nerve, Root value: L4, L5, S1 • Origin: As a continuation of the femoral artery as it passes into the popliteal fossa through the adductor canal at the junction of the middle and lower thirds of the thigh. RELATIONS • Anterior (deep): • Floor of the popliteal fossa 1. Popliteal surface of femur 2. Posterior aspect of the knee joint 3. Fascia covering the popliteus muscle • Posterior (superficial): 1.

Popliteal vein 2. Tibial nerve 3. Fascial roof 4. Superficial fascia, and skin (from deep to superficial). Branches • Superior medial and lateral genicular arteries - course around the femoral condyles as part of the genicular anastomosis • Inferior medial and lateral genicular arteries - course around the tibial condyles as part of the genicular anastomosis • Middle genicular artery - pierces oblique popliteal ligament • Muscular branches - supply hamstrings, adductor magnus • Cutaneous branches - supply skin over knee joint Baker’s cyst (popliteal cyst) • Popliteal cysts in adults are often secondary to degenerative or inflammatory knee joint disease (arthritis) or joint injury. • There is protrusion of synovial membrane with fluid into the popliteal fossa through the joint capsule. • It is a cystic swelling in the popliteal fossa caused due to inflammation of synovial bursa beneath the tendon of semimebranosus or between medial head of gastrocnemius and semimbranousus. Popliteal artery aneurysm • It is abnormal dilation of popliteal artery. It usually causes edema and pain in the popliteal fossa. • The aneurysm may stretch the tibial nerve as the artery lies deep to the nerve,

resulting in pain along the medial aspect of the calf, ankle or foot (area supplied by tibial nerve). • A popliteal aneurysm can be distinguished from other masses by Type & Articular Surfaces Knee joint is formed of: ▪Three bones. ▪Three articulations. ▪Femoro-tibial articulation: between the 2 femoral condyles & upper surfaces of the 2 tibial condyles (Type: synovial, modified hinge). ▪Femoro-patellar articulation: between posterior surface of patella & patellar surface of femur (Type: synovial, plane). ▪ The medial meniscus is large & oval. ▪ Its outer border is attached to the capsule & medial collateral ligament. Menisci ▪ They are 2 C-shaped plates of fibro-cartilage attached by anterior & posterior horns, to the articular surface of tibia. FUNCTION: ▪ They deepen articular surfaces of tibial condyles. ▪ They serve as cushions between tibia & femur. ▪ The lateral meniscus is small & circular. ▪ Its outer border is separated from lateral collateral ligament by popliteal tendon. ▪Medial meniscus is less mobile & more liable to be injured. Capsule ▪Is deficient anteriorly & is replaced by: quadriceps femoris tendon, patella & ligamentum patellae. ▪Possesses 2 openings: one for p

opliteus tendon & one for communication with suprapatellar bursa. Ligaments: 4 Extracapsular 1. Ligamentum patellae (patellar ligament): from patella to tibial tuberosity. 2. Medial (tibial) collateral ligament: from medial epicondyle of femur to upper part of medial surface of tibia (firmly attached to medial meniscus). 3. Lateral (fibular) collateral ligament: from lateral epicondyle of femur to head of fibula (separated from lateral meniscus by popliteus tendon). 4. Oblique popliteal ligament: extension of semimembranosus tendon. Ligaments: 2 Intracapsular Anterior cruciate ligament: • Extends from anterior part of intercondylar area of tibia to posterior part of lateral condyle of femur. • Prevents posterior displacement of femur on tibia. Posterior cruciate ligament: • Extends from posterior part of intercondylar area of tibia to anterior part of medial condyle of femur. • Prevents anterior displacement of femur on tibia. The Cruciate Ligaments: • Two in number, situated in the middle of the joint. • They are called cruciate because they cross each other • Have received the names anterior and posterior, from the position of their attachments to the tibia. Bursae Related to Kne

e ▪ Suprapatellar bursa: between femur & quadriceps tendon, communicates with synovial membrane of knee joint (Clinical importance?) ▪ Prepatellar bursa: between patella & skin. ▪ Deep infrapatellar bursa: between tibia & ligamentum patella. ▪ Subcutaneous infrapatellar bursa: between tibial tuberosity & skin. ▪ Popliteal bursa (not shown): between popliteus tendon & capsule, communicates with synovial membrane of knee joint. Movements ▪FLEXION: ▪Mainly by hamstring muscles: biceps femoris , semitendinosus & semimembranosus. ▪Assisted by sartorius , gracilis & popliteus. ▪EXTENSION: ▪Quadriceps femoris. ▪ACTIVE ROTATION (PERFORMED WHEN KNEE IS FLEXED): A) MEDIAL ROTATION: ▪ Mainly by semitendinosus & semimembranosus. ▪ Assisted by sartorius & gracilis. B) LATERAL ROTATION: ▪ Biceps femoris. ▪INACTIVE (DEPENDANT) ROTATION: A) LOCKING OF KNEE: ▪Lateral rotation of tibia, at the end of extension ▪Results mainly by tension of anterior cruciate ligament. ▪In locked knee, all ligaments become tight. B) UNLOCKING OF KNEE: ▪Medial rotation of tibia, at the beginning of flexion. ▪Performed by popliteus to relax ligaments & allow easy flexion.

chunks: The Lumbosacral Plexus Nerves and Injuries The Lumbosacral Plexus • Major nerve supply structure for the pelvis and the lower limb • Divided into two separate plexuses: • The lumbar plexus (L1-L4) • The sacral plexus (L4-S4) • Majority of nerves originate from the anterior rami of the lumbar and sacral roots Lumbar Plexus • Lies within/beneath the psoas major muscle • Extends from the anterior rami of L1 to L4, with contributions from T12 • Supplies the abdominal, pelvic, and lower limb regions • Branches include: • Iliohypogastric • Ilioinguinal • Genitofemoral • Lateral cutaneous • Femoral • Obturator Iliohypogastric Nerve (L1; T12) • Innervates the internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles • Innervates skin around the posterolateral gluteal and pubic regions Ilioinguinal Nerve (L1) • Innervates the internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles • Innervates skin around the anteromedial thigh • In males, supplies skin over penis root and anterior scrotum • In females, supplies skin over mons pubis and labia majora Genitofemoral Nerve (L1-L2) • Innervates the cremasteric muscle • Genital branch innervates anterior scrotum/mons pubis and labia majora • Femoral branch i

nnervates upper anterior thigh Lateral Cutaneous Nerve (L2-L3) • No motor function • Innervates anterior and lateral thigh down to the knee • Enters thigh at the lateral aspect of the inguinal ligament Obturator Nerve (L2-L4) • Innervates all muscles of the medial thigh: • Adductor longus; adductor brevis; adductor magnus; gracilis; obturator externus • Innervates skin over medial thigh Obturator Nerve (L2-L4) • Descends through the fibers of the psoas major • Travels posteriorly towards obturator foramen • Enters obturator canal; divides into anterior and posterior branches • Anterior branch: enters between adductor longus and brevis • Innervates adductor longus, brevis, and gracilis; continues as cutaneous branch • Posterior branch: enters between adductor brevis and magnus • Innervates adductor magnus and obturator externus Femoral Nerve (L2-L4) • Innervates all muscles of the anterior thigh: • Iliacus; pectineus; quadriceps femoris; sartorius • Innervates skin over anterior thigh and medial leg Femoral Nerve (L2-L4) • Largest branch of the lumbar plexus • Femoral nerve moves inferiorly to the psoas major muscle • Supplies the iliacus muscle; enters thigh • Passes underneath the

inguinal ligament to enter the femoral triangle • Lies lateral to the femoral artery and vein • Divides into anterior and posterior branches • Anterior supplies the sartorius and pectineus muscles • Posterior supplies the quadriceps femoris Sacral Plexus (L4-S4) • Located on the surface of the posterior pelvic wall • Most nerves exit via the greater sciatic foramen • 5 major branches: • Superior gluteal • Inferior gluteal • Sciatic • Posterior femoral cutaneous • Pudendal Superior Gluteal Nerve (L4-S1) • Innervates the gluteus medius, minimus, and tensor fascia lata • No sensory function • Enters the gluteal region by exiting the greater sciatic notch • Lies superior to the piriformis muscle Inferior Gluteal Nerve (L5-S2) • Innervates the gluteus maximus • No sensory function • Exits greater sciatic foramen; enters gluteal region inferior to the piriformis Sciatic Nerve (L4-S3) • Innervates muscles of the posterior thigh (biceps femoris; semitendinosus; semimembranosus; hamstring part of adductor magnus) • Indirectly innervates all muscles of the leg and foot • Terminal branches innervate skin of lateral leg, heel, and both dorsal + plantar surfaces of the foot Sciatic Nerve (L4-S

3) • Exits pelvis via greater sciatic foramen • Enters gluteal region inferior to the piriformis • Enters posterior thigh deep to the long head of the biceps femoris • Innervates all hamstrings and hamstring part of adductor magnus • Bifurcates into tibial and common peroneal/fibular nerves at the apex of the popliteal fossa Posterior Femoral Cutaneous Nerve (S1-S3) • No motor function • Innervates skin over posterior thigh, posterior leg, and the perineum • Leaves pelvis via greater sciatic foramen Pudendal Nerve (S2-S4) • Innervates perineal muscles (external urethral sphincter, levator ani, external anal sphincter) • Innervates skin overlying the perineum, penis, and clitoris • Nerve exits the pelvis via the greater sciatic foramen • Re-enters via the lesser sciatic foramen Sciatica • Damage to the sciatic nerve typically caused by compression via: • Herniated disc • Spinal stenosis • Piriformis syndrome • Presents with pain shooting downwards from the posterior thigh • Pain gets worse upon sitting • Typically seen in older, obese patients Intramuscular Injections • Always given in the upper lateral quadrant of the gluteal region • The reason is to avoid direct damage to the sci

atic nerve • Gluteal region divided via two lines: • One descends vertically from the highest point of the iliac crest • One moves horizontally, crossing the midpoint between the highest point of the iliac crest and the ischial tuberosity

chunks: DEEP FASCIA OF THIGH MODIFICATION AND INGUINAL LIGAMENT By Professor Dr. Rais Ahmed M.B.,BS FCPS M.phil Professor of anatomy United medical and dental college Introduction to Fascia • Fascia is connective tissue surrounding muscles, vessels and nerves. It provides support, compartmentalization and protection. DEFINITION OF DEEP FASCIA OF THIGH • The deep fascia of the thigh is called fascia lata. It forms a strong fibrous sleeve around the thigh. OVERVIEW Introduction & Definition • Fascia lata = deep fascia of the thigh; the strongest, thickest deep fascia in the entire body. • A dense, glistening sheet of fibrous connective tissue lying just deep to the superficial (fatty) fascia. • Completely encircles the thigh like a firm fibrous stocking, investing every muscle group. • Binds muscles into compartments, preventing outward bulging and improving contraction efficiency. • Gives partial origin to several muscles; continuous with crural fascia below and gluteal fascia above. fascia lata (fibrous sleeve) LOCATION General Extent of Fascia Lata • Forms one continuous fibrous sleeve from the pelvic brim down to the leg. • Above: continuous with fascia over external oblique aponeurosis,

inguinal ligament and gluteal fascia. • Below: continues directly as the crural (deep) fascia of the leg — no interruption at the knee. • Circumferentially surrounds anterior, medial and posterior groups of thigh muscles. femur Anterior Medial Posterior ATTACHMENT OF FACIA LATA Superiorly, it is attached to the boundary line between the lower limb and the pelvis. Anteriorly, it is attached to the inguinal ligament; laterally to the iliac crest and Posteriorly, through the gluteal fascia to the sacrum, coccyx and sacrotuberous ligament. Medially, to the pubis, the pubic arch and the ischial tuberosity and Inferiorly, on the front and sides of the knee, the fascia lata is attached to subcutaneous bony prominences and the capsule of the knee joint. Posteriorly, the fascia lata forms the strong popliteal fascia which is continuous below with the fascia of the back of the leg. Extends from iliac tubercle to lateral condyle of tibia (Gerdy's tubercle). The importance of the iliotibial tract is as follows: • Two important muscles are inserted into its upper part, between the superficial and deep laminae. These are the three-fourths part of the gluteus maximus; and the tensor fasciae lata

e. • The iliotibial tract stabilizes the knee both in extension and in partial flexion: and is therefore used constantly during walking and running. In leaning forwards with slightly flexed knees, the tract is the main support of the knee against gravity. Saphenous Opening • Oval gap in fascia lata located below the medial end of inguinal ligament. SAPHENOUS OPENING Cribriform Fascia • The saphenous opening is not a bare gap — closed by a thin, sieve-like cribriform fascia (a superficial fascia condensation). • Perforated by numerous small openings transmitting: great saphenous vein, superficial lymphatics to superficial inguinal nodes, and small branches of superficial external pudendal & circumflex iliac vessels. Summary • Fascia lata is the deep fascia of thigh. Its key modifications are iliotibial tract, saphenous opening and septa.

chunks: FEMORAL ARTERY & VEIN PROF DR IMRAN ISHAQUE Objectives • By the end of the lecture, the student should be able to describe the: • Describes the course, relations and branches of femoral artery. • Describes the course, relations and tributaries of femoral vein. • It is the main artery of the lower limb. • It enters the femoral triangle behind the inguinal ligament at the midinguinal point. • It runs downward and medially successively via the femoral triangle and adductor canal. • At the lower end of the adductor canal , it leaves the thigh via the adductor hiatus to go into the popliteal fossa where it continues as the popliteal artery. • It passes downwards and medially. • First in the femoral triangle • Then in the adductor canal. • At the lower end of the adductor canal at the junction of the middle and lower thirds of the thigh it passes through an opening in the adductor magnus (adductor hiatus) to become the popliteal artery • EXTENT AND COURSE BRANCHES OF FEMORAL ARTERY FEMORAL ARTERY In the femoral triangle 3 deep branches Profunda femoris artery Deep external pudendal artery Muscular branches 3 superficial branches Superficial epigastric artery Superficial external pudendal

artery Superfic ial circumflexiliac artery In the adductor canal Muscular branches Descending genicular artery. ➢In the femoral triangle, the profunda femoris artery arises from the posterolateral aspect of the femoral artery. ➢It travels posteriorly and distally, giving off three main branches: ➢Perforating branches – Consists of three or four arteries that perforate the adductor magnus, contributing to the supply of the muscles in the medial and posterior thigh. ➢Lateral femoral circumflex artery – Wraps round the anterior, lateral side of the femur, supplying some of the muscles in the lateral side of the thigh. ➢Medial femoral circumflex artery – Wraps round the posterior side of the femur, supplying the neck and head of the femur.
