chunks: CALCIUM Sources and RDA Metabolism of calcium Functions of calcium Hormonal Regulation of plasma calcium Disorders of calcium metabolism CALCIUM Calcium is the most abundant mineral in the body Human body contain about 1-1.5 kg of calcium DAILY REQUIREMENTS OF CALCIUM Children 1000mg/day Adults 500mg/day Pregnancy and lactation 1500mg/day METABOLISM OF CALCIUM Absorption Factors affecting absorption Mechanism of absorption Excretion of calcium Distribution and storage METABOLISM OF CALCIUM - ABSORPTION Site Efficiency Upper small intestine 20-35% of dietary Ca Absorption and excretion • Usual intakes is 1000 mg/day • About 35 % is absorbed (350 mg/day) by the intestines • Calcium remaining in the intestine is excreted in the feces • 250 mg/day enters intestine via secreted gastrointestinal juices and sloughed mucosal cells • 60-70 % of the daily intake is excreted in the feces • 10 % of the ingested calcium is excreted in the urine • Calcium must be in a soluble and ionized form before it can be absorbed FACTORS AFFECTING CALCIUM ABSORPTION Calcium absorption is increased by Calcitriol PTH High protein diet Optimum Ca:P ratio Acidic pH Bile salts Absorption is decreased by Alkaline

pH Phytates and oxalates Steatorrhea Vitamin D deficiency Excess phosphate in diet Factors causing increased absorption • Vitamin D: • Calcitriol induces the synthesis of carrier protein (Calbindin) in the intestinal epithelial cells & facilitates the absorption of calcium • Parathyroid hormone: • It increases calcium transport from the intestinal cells by enhancing 1α-hydroxylase activity • Acidity: • Favors calcium absorption because the Ca-salts, particularly PO4 & carbonates are quite soluble in acidic solutions • In alkaline medium, the absorption of calcium is lowered due to the formation of insoluble tricalcium PO4 • High protein diet: • A high protein diet favors calcium absorption • If the protein content is low, only 5% may be absorbed • Amino acids: • Lysine & arginine increases calcium absorption • Amino acids increase the solubility of Ca-salts & thus its absorption • Sugars and organic acids: • Organic acids produced by microbial fermentation of sugars in the gut, increases the solubility of Ca- salts & increases their absorption • Citric acid may also increase the absorption of calcium Factors causing decreased absorption • Phytic acid: Cereals contain phytic acid (

Inositol hexaphosphate) forms insoluble Ca-salts & decreases the absorption • Oxalates: Present in some leafy vegetables, causes formation of insoluble calcium oxalates • Malabsorption syndromes: • Causing formation of insoluble calcium salt of fatty acid • Glucocorticoids: • Diminishes intestinal transport of calcium • Phosphate: • High phosphate content will cause precipitation as calcium phosphate • Magnesium: High content of Mg decreases the absorption • Ca: P Ratio: 3:1 MECHANISM OF CALCIUM ABSORPTION Calcium absorption occurs by 1,25(OH)2D3 mediated mechanism. • Calcitriol increases the intestinal absorption of calcium and phosphate • In the intestinal cells, calcitriol binds with a cytosolic receptor to form a calcitriol-receptor complex • This complex interacts with a specific DNA leading to the synthesis of a specific calcium binding protein • This protein increases calcium uptake by intestine • The mechanism of action of calcitriol is similar to that of steroid hormone Biochemical functions • Development of bones and teeth: • Bone is regarded as a mineralized connective tissue • Bones also act as reservoir for calcium • The bulk quantity of calcium is used for bone and te

eth formation • Osteoblasts induce bone deposition and osteoclasts produce demineralization FUNCTIONS OF CALCIUM Formation of bone and teeth Nerve conduction Muscle contraction Activation of enzymes Blood coagulation Secretion of hormones As a second messenger Action on myocardium EXCRETION OF CALCIUM Stools Unabsorbed calcium in the diet 60 – 70% Urine 50- 200mg/day Sweat 15mg/day DISTRIBUTION AND STORAGE OF CALCIUM Human body contain about 1-1.5 kg of calcium 99% present in bone and teeth 1% in soft tissue and extracellular fluid Plasma calcium : 8.5-10.2mg/dl REGULATION OF ENZYME ACTIVITY Ca++ activates •Glycogen phosphorylase kinase •Amylase Ca++ Inhibits •Pyruvate kinase •Trypsin REGULATION OF PLASMA CALCIUM 50% 40% 10% % Free or ionized calcium Protein bound complex with anions REGULATION OF PLASMA CALCIUM 3 Organs Gut Bone Kidney 3 Hormones Calcitriol PTH Calcitonin Vitamin D promotes intestinal calcium absorption • Vitamin D acts via steroid hormone like receptor to increase transcriptional and translational activity • One gene product is calcium-binding protein (CaBP) • CaBP facilitates calcium uptake by intestinal cells Parathyroid Hormone • PTH is synthesized and secrete

d by the parathyroid gland which lie posterior to the thyroid glands. • The blood supply to the parathyroid glands is from the thyroid arteries. • The Chief Cells in the parathyroid gland are the principal site of PTH synthesis. Regulation of PTH • The dominant regulator of PTH is plasma calcium. • Secretion of PTH is inversely related to calcium. • Maximum secretion of PTH occurs at plasma Ca2+ below 3.5 mg/dL. • At Ca2+ above 5.5 mg/dL, PTH secretion is maximally inhibited. PTH action • The overall action of PTH is to increase plasma Ca++ levels and decrease plasma phosphate levels. • PTH acts on the bones to stimulate Ca++ resorption • In kidney PTH stimulates Ca++ reabsorption in the distal tubule of the kidney and to inhibit reabsorption of phosphate (thereby stimulating its excretion). • In kidney PTH stimulates 1,α-hydroxylase enzyme which results in increased synthesis of 1,25,dihydroxy cholicalciferol • PTH also acts indirectly on intestine by stimulating 1,25-(OH)2-D synthesis. Calcitonin • Calcitonin acts to decrease plasma Ca++ levels. • While PTH and vitamin D act to increase plasma Ca++ only calcitonin causes a decrease in plasma Ca++. • Calcitonin is synthesized and

secreted by the parafollicular cells of the thyroid gland. • They are distinct from thyroid follicular cells by their large size, pale cytoplasm, and small secretory granules Calcitonin • The target cell for calcitonin is the osteoclast. • Calcitonin acts via increased cAMP concentrations to inhibit osteoclast motility and inactivates them. • The major effect of calcitonin administration is a rapid fall in Ca2+ caused by inhibition of bone resorption • Calcinotonin also inhibits the enzyme 1-α hydroxylase thus decreasing the synthesis of calcitriol and calcium absorption DISORDERS OF CALCIUM METABOLISM Hypocalcemia Hypercalcemia HYPOCALCEMIA Inadequate intake Impaired absorption Increased excretion Magnesium deficiency Acute pancreatitis Causes of hypocalcaemia 1) Increased Phosphate levels – Chronic kidney disease – Phosphate therapy 2) Hypoparathyroidism – Post thyroidectomy hypocalcaemia – Congenital deficiency (Di George Syndrome) – Idiopathic hypoparathyroidism – Severe hypomagnesaemia 3) Vitamin D deficiency – Osteomalacia/rickets – Vitamin D resistance • Hypoparathyroidism associated with other diseases states: - Addison’s disease - Pernicious Anemia -Fungal disease like can

didiasis • Other causes: – Acute pancreatitis – Citrate blood in massive transfusion – Low plasma albumin eg. Malnutrition, Chronic liver disease – Malabsorption eg. Coeliac disease – Osteomalacia & Rickets – Magnesium Defeciency HYPOCALCEMIA - FEATURES Muscle cramps and tetany Laryngospasm Convulsion Cardiac arrhythmias Prolongation of QT interval Cataract Chronic hypocalcemia HYPOCALCEMIA – SIGNS OF TETANY Contraction of facial muscle in response to tapping the facial nerve Chvostek’s sign Carpal spasm occurring after occlusion of the brachial artery with BP cuff for 3 min Trousseau’s sign • Hypercalcaemia:-when the serum calcium level exceeds 11.0mg/dl it is called as hypercalcaemia (normal serum calcium level is 8.5 to 10.2mg/dl). HYPERCALCEMIA Increased intake Increased absorption Decreased excretion Malignancy Hyperparathyroidism: causes ❖Primary Hyperparathyroidism – Solitary Adenomas (85%) – Multiple Adenomas(2%) – Parathyroid Carcinoma (<1% cases) – Familial benign hyperplasia of chief cells (FBH) ❖Secondary Hyperparathyroidism – Renal failure – Vitamin D deficiency Malignant hypercalcemia: major causes • PTHrP – mediated Parathyroid hormone-related protein (or PTHrP) is a

protein member of the parathyroid hormone family. It is occasionally secreted by cancer cells --Breast carcinoma – Squamous carcinoma (lung, head & neck, esophagus) – Renal carcinoma • Cytokine - mediated – Myeloma (lymphoma, leukemia) • Endocrine causes: Hyperthyroidisim, Acromegaly • Granulomatous diseases: Tuberculosis, sarcoidosis • Over Dosage of Vitamins: Hypervitaminosis D • Drug-induced Hypercalcaemia: Thiazide diuretics, spironlactone HYPERCALCEMIA - FEATURES Metastatic calcification Neurological symptoms Renal symptoms Gastrointestinal symptoms Cardiac arrhythmias

chunks: Phosphate • Calcium is tightly regulated with Phosphorous in the body . • Phosphate is an essential mineral • PHOSPHATE: 90% of daily dietary phosphate is absorbed. • The absorption is stimulated by both PTH(from bone resorption along with calcium) and vitamin D3(from intestine and to small extent from bone). • Phosphate is the constituent of bone and teeth. • Uptake of phosphate by the kidneys is sodium dependent about 85% of phosphate is reabsorbed by the proximal tubules. • Phosphate reabsorption is increased when dietary intake is reduced by a PTH mechanism ABSORPTION • 90% of daily dietary phosphate is absorbed • The absorption is stimulated by both PTH and vit D3. • The Ca: P ratio in diet affects the absorption and excretion of phosphorus • If one is excess in diet the excretion of other is increased Role of Kidney • 1. Phosphate uptake is sodium dependent, about 85% of filtered PO4 is reabsorbed by proximal tubules. Phosphate reabsorption is increased when dietary intake is reduced by a by PTH-dependent mechanism • 2. Increased vitamin D(calcitriol) increases PO4 absorption. Decreased vitamin D (Calcitriol) decreases PO4 absorption REGULATION OF SERUM PHOSPHATE • PTH reduce

s the reabsorption of phosphate from the proximal tubule of the kidney, which means more phosphate is excreted through the urine. • PTH enhances the uptake of phosphate from the intestine and bones into the blood. • In the bone, slightly more calcium than phosphate is released from the breakdown of bone. • In the intestines, absorption of both Calcium and Phosphate is mediated by an increase in activated vitamin D. • The absorption of phosphate is not as dependent on vitamin D as is that of calcium. Functions of Phosphate • Phosphate is the constituent of bone and teeth • Energy transfer: The free energy produced by metabolic reactions may be stored as high energy phosphate ATP, Creatine phosphate • Acid base balance: The buffer which is effectively handled by kidney is a phosphate buffer. It is a mixture of dibasic and monobasic phosphates • Phosphorylation/dephosphorylation involves phosphate • Enzyme Action: Phosphate of several co enzyme such as NADP,TPP is involved in enzymatic reactions. • Constitute of phospholipids, nucleotide/nuleic acid, lipoproteins, phosphoproteins is phosphate Normal serum phosphate • Ranges 2.5 - 4.5 mg/dL RDA and Sources • For Adults 19 years or olde

r 700 mg/day • For children 9-18 years old 1250 mg/day Sources: dairy, red meat, poultry, seafood, legumes, and nuts. CLINICAL CONDITIONS RELATED TO PHOSPHATE • Primary hyperparathyroidisim =increased Ca and decreased phospahte • Malignancy= increased Ca and Increased PO4 • Hypoparathyrodisim = Decreased Ca and increased PO4 • Vitamin D defeciency= decreased calcium and decreased phosphate HYPOPHOSPHATEMIA CAUSES Alcoholism Burns Respiratory Alkalosis Malnutrition/Starvation Hyperparathyroidism Vitamin D deficiency Diuretics Hypothyroidism and Cushing syndrome Symptoms • Muscle weakness • Softening or weakening of bones • Depletion of muscles • Altered mental state • Seizures • Numbness • Reflexive weakness • Heart failure • Muscle pain HYPERPHOSPHATEMIA CAUSES: • Renal failure • Hypoparathyroidism • High vitamin D level • Diabetic ketoacidosis Symptoms • Asymptomatic unless hypocalcemia occurs. Then it will have symptoms of hypocalcemia.

chunks: LEARNING OBJECTIVES By the end of lecture student should be able to : • Discuss the metabolism of Sulphur containing amino acids • Describe the functions of Sulphur containing amino acids • List the steps of formation of Cysteine and Methionine • Explain clinical significance of disorders of Sulphur containing amino acids The sulfur – containing amino acids are methionine, cysteine & cystine. METHIONINE • Glucogenic as well as an essential amino acid. • Serves as a precursor for the synthesis of cysteine and cystine which are non-essential. • It is required for the initiation of protein biosynthesis. INTRODUCTION INTRODUCTION • Cystine is reduced to cysteine. • Cystine is found exclusively in protein. • The sulfur - containing amino acids are almost an exclusive dietary source of sulfur to the body. METABOLISM OF METHIONINE Methionine metabolism may be divided into two parts. 1. Utilization of methionine for trans methylation reactions 2. Conversion of methionine to cysteine and cystine. • The synthesis of SAM (S Adenosyl Methionine) occurs by the transfer of adenosyl group from ATP to sulphur atom of methionine. • The activation of methionine is unique as the sulfur becomes a sulf

onium atom (SAM is a sulfonium compound) by the addition of a third carbon. • This reaction is catalyzed by methionine adenosyltransferase (MAT). • Three high energy phosphates (3 ATP) are consumed in the formation of SAM. (2 ATP break bonds of first ATP) STEP 1: Activation of methionine to SAM STEP 2 SAM (S Adenosyl Methionine) transfers the methyl group to an acceptor and gets itself converted to S-adenosyl homocysteine (SAH). The transfer of methyl group ( CH3) from active methionine to an acceptor is known as transmethylation. Functions of S-adenosylmethionine • S-Adenosylmethionine is highly reactive due to the presence of a positive charge. • S-Adenosylmethionine transfers the methyl group to an acceptor and gets itself converted to S-adenosylhomocysteine. • The loss of free energy in this reaction makes the methyl transfer essentially irreversible. • S-Adenosylhomocysteine is hydrolysed to homocysteine and adenosine. • Homocysteine can be remethylated to methionine by N5-methyl tetrahydrofolate. In this manner, methionine can be regenerated for reuse. Biochemical Significance of transmethylation 1. Transmethylation is of great biological significance since many compounds bec

ome functionally active only after methylation. 2. Methylation helps to control protein turnover. In general, methylation protects the proteins from immediate degradation. 3. In plants, S-adenosylmethionine is the precursor for the synthesis of a plant hormone, ethylene, which regulates plant growth and development and is involved in the ripening of fruits Synthesis of cysteine • Homocysteine formed from methionine is a precursor for the synthesis of cysteine. • Homocysteine condenses with serine to form cystathionine. This reaction is catalysed by a Pyridoxal phosphate-dependent cystathionine synthase. • The enzyme cystathioninase (PLP-dependent) cleaves and deaminates cystathionine to cysteine and α-ketobutyrate. • The sum of the reactions catalysed by cystathionine synthase and cystathioninase is a good example of transsulfuration (transfer of sulfur from one compound to another). Hypermethioninemia • Hypermethioninemia is an excess of a particular protein building block (amino acid), called methionine, in the blood. This condition can occur when methionine is not broken down (metabolized) properly in the body. • People with hypermethioninemia often do not show any symptoms. • S

ome individuals with hypermethioninemia exhibit intellectual disability and other neurological problems; delays in motor skills such as standing or walking; sluggishness; muscle weakness; liver problems; unusual facial features; and their breath, sweat, or urine may have a smell resembling boiled cabbage. • Hypermethioninemia can occur with other metabolic disorders, such as homocystinuria, tyrosinemia and galactosemias, which also involve the faulty breakdown of particular molecules. • It can also result from liver disease or excessive dietary intake of methionine from consuming in large quantity. Cysteine • Non essential and glucogenic amino acid • Present in large quantity in keratin of hair and nails. Synthesis • It is formed from the degradation of methionine with the carbon skeleton contributed by serine and sulphur comes from methionine. Metabolic Functions of Cysteine Cysteine is a part of glutathione. Functions of glutathione • Amino acid transport • Glutathione keeps the enzymes in reduced, active state. • RBC membrane integrity. • Necessary for the reduction of met hemoglobin to normal hemoglobin. • Conjugation for detoxification. Degradation of Cysteine • Cystine & cyst

eine are interconvertible by an NAD+ dependent enzyme Cystine reductase. • Cysteine on decarboxylation produces mercapto-ethanolamine which is involved in the biosynthesis of coenzyme A from the vitamin B5 or pantothenic acid. • The enzyme cysteine dioxygenase oxidizes cysteine to cysteine sulfinate which, on further oxidation, is converted to cysteic acid. • Cysteic acid undergoes decarboxylation to produce taurine which conjugates with bile acids. • Cysteic acid can also be degraded to pyruvate, which is glycogenic . Oxidation Cysteine dioxygenase • Cysteine sulfinate cleaves off alanine to produce sulfite which is converted to sulfate and excreted in urine. • Some amount of sulfate condenses with ATP to form active sulfate or 3-phosphoadenosine 5-phosphosulfate (PAPS). Active sulfate (PAPS) is utilized for the synthesis of mucopolysaccharides (sulfation), besides being used in detoxification. • Cysteine can be degraded by desulfhydrase to liberate sulfur (as H2S), ammonia and pyruvate. Cysteine is a component of tripeptide glutathione (synthesis described in glycine metabolism). Inborn Errors of Sulphur amino acids metabolism Cystinuria (cystine-lysinuria) • The most common inhe

rited disease. • It is characterized by increased excretion of cystine (25-40 times normal). • Elevation in the urinary output of lysine, arginine & ornithine is also observed. • A specific carrier system exists in kidney tubules for the reabsorption of amino acids, namely cysteine, ornithine, arginine & lysine . COAL mneumonic) • In cystinuria, this carrier system becomes defective leading to the excretion of all these four amino acids in urine. • Cystine is relatively insoluble & increased concentrations leads to precipitation & formation of cystine stones in kidney & urinary tract. • Cystinuria is usually identified in the laboratory by cyanide nitroprusside test. • The treatment includes restricted ingestion of dietary cystine & high intake of fluids. Cystinosis (cystine storage disease) • Under normal conditions, the amino acid cysteine is converted to cystine in the lysosomes, then they move out of the lysosomes. Cystinosis occurs when the proteins that send cystine out of the lysosomes become defective. • Also a defect in the enzyme Cystine reductase (interconverting enzyme). • Cystine crystals are deposited in spleen, lymph nodes, liver, kidney, bone marrow etc. • It is cha

racterized by generalized aminoaciduria. • The affected patients die within 10 years, mostly due to renal failure. Homocysteine and heart attacks • Homocysteine is an intermediate in the synthesis of cysteine from methionine. • Elevation in plasma homocysteine (normal < 15 µ mol/litre) has been implicated in coronary artery diseases. • Homocysteine reacts with collagen to produce reactive free radicals, besides interfering with collagen cross links. • Homocysteine is also involved in the aggregation of LDL particles. • All this leads to an increased tendency for atherogenesis, and consequently heart complications. • Hyperhomocysteinemia in pregnancy increases the risk of neural tube defects in fetus. • Supplementation of diet with folic acid, vitamin B12 and vitamin B6 have some beneficial affects in lowering plasma homocysteine levels . Homocystinuria • Homocystinurias are a group of metabolic disorders characterized by the accumulation & increased urinary excretion of homocysteine & S-adenosylmethionine (SAM). • Plasma concentration of methionine is increased. • Enzyme defect: Cystathionine synthase. • Accumulation of homocysteine. • It results in various complications-thrombosis
, osteoporosis & mental retardation. • The deficiency of cystathionine is associated with damage to endothelial cells which might lead to atherosclerosis.

Brachial Plexus — Basics • Formed by: ventral rami of C5, C6, C7, C8, T1 (+ small twigs from C4 / T2). • Location: starts in the neck (between scalenus anterior & medius) → crosses posterior triangle → ends in the axilla. • Order: Roots (5) → Trunks (3) → Divisions (6) → Cords (3) → Branches. Mnemonic: “Randy Travis Drinks Cold Beer”. • Trunks: Upper (C5+C6), Middle (C7), Lower (C8+T1). • Divisions: each trunk splits into anterior + posterior. Anterior → flexor compartments; posterior → extensor compartments. • Cords (named by relation to 2nd part of axillary artery): Lateral = ant. div. of upper + middle trunk (C5–7); Medial = ant. div. of lower trunk (C8, T1); Posterior = post. div. of all 3 trunks (C5–T1). ⚠ Exam: Roots lie between scalenes • Trunks in posterior triangle • Divisions behind clavicle • Cords in axilla. popliteal fossa into two terminal nerves 1. Tibial nerve (L4–S3) • Runs down popliteal fossa → posterior leg • Supplies posterior compartment of leg (calf muscles) • Behind medial malleolus, divides into medial plantar and lateral plantar nerves • Branch: Sural nerve (joined by communicating branch of common peroneal) → lateral foot skin 2. Common peroneal (fibular) nerve (L4–S2) • Winds around neck of fibula (vulnerable site) • Superficial peroneal → lateral compartment (peroneus longus and brevis), dorsum of foot skin • Deep peroneal → anterior compartment (dorsiflexors), skin of first web space Quick Recap 1 Lumbar plexus → femoral (anterior thigh) + obturator (medial thigh) 2 Sacral plexus → sciatic + gluteal nerves 3 Sciatic → tibial + common peroneal at popliteal fossa 4 Tibial → medial + lateral plantar 5 Common peroneal → superficial + deep peroneal Common Mistake: Sciatic nerve divides in the popliteal fossa, not at the thigh midpoint (though high division can occur). Clinical: Common peroneal injury at the fibular neck → foot drop.

chunks: Dorsum, Sole and Arches of Foot Short notes with mnemonics 1. Muscles of the Dorsum of Foot Extensor digitorum brevis (EDB) is the only intrinsic muscle on the dorsum. • Origin: upper surface of calcaneus (front part) • Insertion: 4 tendons. Medial one (extensor hallucis brevis) → big toe; other three join EDL tendons of toes 2–4 • Nerve: deep peroneal • Action: extends toes 1–4 • Tendons of EHL, EDL and peroneus tertius cross the dorsum, but they are leg muscles Clinical: a swollen EDB belly in front of the lateral malleolus can look like an ankle sprain swelling. 2. Dorsal Venous Arch • Lies in subcutaneous tissue over the metatarsal bases • Formed by the dorsal digital veins (via dorsal metatarsal veins) • Medial end → medial marginal vein → great saphenous vein (in front of medial malleolus) • Lateral end → lateral marginal vein → small saphenous vein (behind lateral malleolus) • Connected to deep veins by perforating veins 3. Architecture of the Sole (skin to deep) 1 Skin: thick, hairless, many sweat glands 2 Superficial fascia: fibro-fatty pad; fibrous septa bind skin to deep fascia, so it does not slide and absorbs pressure 3 Plantar aponeurosis: strong central sheet from th

e calcaneal tuberosity, splitting into 5 slips to the toes. It acts as a tie-beam for the longitudinal arch. Two septa divide the sole into medial, central and lateral compartments 4 Four layers of muscles 4. Layers of the Sole Layer Contents 1 (superficial) Abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis, abductor digiti minimi 2 Quadratus plantae, 4 lumbricals, tendons of FDL and FHL 3 Flexor hallucis brevis, adductor hallucis, flexor digiti minimi brevis 4 (deep) 3 plantar + 4 dorsal interossei, tendons of tibialis posterior and peroneus longus Mnemonic: Layer 1 = A F A | Layer 3 = F A F | Interossei = PAD and DAB (Plantar ADduct, Dorsal ABduct) 5. Arches of Foot: Architecture and Functions • Medial longitudinal: high and springy; summit = talus • Lateral longitudinal: low and flat; mainly for weight-bearing • Transverse: across the tarsal and metatarsal bases; a full arch only when both feet are together Functions: bear and spread body weight, absorb shock, give spring for push-off, protect vessels and nerves of the sole. 6. Bones Forming the Arches Arch Bones Medial Calcaneus, talus, navicular, 3 cuneiforms, medial 3 metatarsals Lateral Calcaneus, cuboid, 4th and 5th metatarsals Tr

ansverse Cuboid, 3 cuneiforms, bases of the metatarsals 7. Ligaments Holding the Arches Arch Ligaments (static) Muscles (dynamic) Medial Spring ligament (most important, holds head of talus), plantar aponeurosis, deltoid Tibialis posterior, tibialis anterior, FHL, peroneus longus Lateral Long and short plantar ligaments Peroneus longus and brevis Transverse Deep transverse metatarsal ligaments Peroneus longus, adductor hallucis (transverse head) Mnemonic: Bones shape it, ligaments tie it, muscles sling it. 8. Plantar Fasciitis and Related Injuries • What: inflammation or degeneration of the plantar aponeurosis at the calcaneal tuberosity • Features: heel pain, worst with the first steps in the morning; tenderness at the medial heel; pain on dorsiflexing the toes • Causes: overuse, obesity, long standing, tight Achilles tendon, flat or high arch • Treatment: rest, calf and fascia stretching, arch support, NSAIDs Related conditions • Heel spur: bony outgrowth, often seen on X-ray but not the actual cause of the pain • Flat foot (pes planus): lost medial arch from weak spring ligament or tibialis posterior • Pes cavus: high arch • Tibialis posterior rupture: causes acquired flat foot

Quick Recap 1 EDB is the only dorsal muscle (deep peroneal) 2 Dorsal venous arch drains to great saphenous (medial) and small saphenous (lateral) 3 Sole = skin, fat pad, plantar aponeurosis, then 4 muscle layers 4 3 arches; the spring ligament is the key support of the medial arch 5 Plantar fasciitis = heel pain at the fascia's origin, worst on first steps Exam favourites: EDB is the only dorsal muscle; the spring ligament holds the head of the talus; plantar fasciitis pain is at the calcaneal tuberosity.

The understanding of the structures, their functions and biochemical aspects are crucial for physicians. This module attempts to build a solid foundation regarding knowledge of the Locomotor system and its clinical applications. chunks: By PROFESSOR DR. RAIS AHMED M.B.,B.S FCPS M.PHIL PROFESSOR OF ANATOMY UNITED MEDICAL AND DENTAL COLLEGE Learning Objectives By the end of this lecture, students will be able to: 01 Define The thoracic duct and its embryological origin 02 Describe The precise course and relations from abdomen to neck 03 List Major tributaries and the lymphatic territories they drain 04 Explain The cisterna chyli and its formation 05 Identify Key anatom ical landm arks for surg ical approaches 06 Discuss Clinical implications of duct injury, chylothorax, and lymphadenopathy Introduction to the Lymphatic System One-Way Network Returns interstitial fluid to blood via capillaries, vessels, vessels, nodes, and ducts Largest Vessel The thoracic duct measures 40–45 cm, draining lower body, left thorax, and left upper limb Origin Begins at L1–L2 as continuation of the cisterna chyli preencoded.png Course of the Thoracic Duct Abdomen to Thorax Through aortic hiatus at T12; between aorta and azygos; covered by esophagus Superior Mediastinum Crosses left at T4–T5; behind aortic arch and left subclavian; ascends along side esophag us Posterior Mediastinu m Ascends on vertebral bodies behind esophagus; receives

left intercostal trunks From the cisterna chyli, the duct ascends through the aortic hiatus, gradually inclines leftward, and crosses at T4–T5 to enter the superior. Origin & Cisterna Chyli Origin Site: Begins in the abdomen as a direct upward continuation of the Cisterna Chyli at the lower border of T12 vertebra. Cisterna Chyli Location: A dilated lymphatic sac lying retroperitoneally in front of L1–L2 vertebral bodies, immediately to the right of the abdominal aorta. Primary Inflow: Receives lymph from the right and left lumbar lymph trunks (draining lower extremities, pelvis) and the intestinal lymph trunk (draining GI tract lipid-rich chyle). Diaphragmatic Entry: Ascends into the posterior mediastinum by passing through the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm at T12, accompanied by the descending aorta and azygous vein. Drainage Territory: Thoracic vs Right Duct Thoracic Duct Coverage (75%): Drains lymph from both lower extremities, abdomen, pelvis, perineum, left side of thorax, left upper extremity, and left side of head and neck. Right Lymphatic Duct Coverage (25%): Drains only the right upper quadrant—right upper limb, right half of thorax, right lung/pleura, right side of heart

, and right half of head and neck. Clinical Implication: Obstruction or lesions of the thoracic duct cause widespread systemic effects compared to localized right duct impairment. preencoded.png Cisterna chyli at L1–L2; enters thorax via aortic hiatus at T12 Ascends posterior mediastinum, crosses left at T4–T5, terminates at left venous ang le Entire body except right head, neck, thorax, and upper limb Injury → chylothorax; Virchow's node sig nals abdominal m alig nancy Understanding the thoracic duct's course, relations, and variations is essential knowledge for every surgeon.

subject: Anatomy
chunks: Thoracic AORTA By PROFESSOR DR. RAIS AHMED M.B.,B.S FCPS M.PHIL PROFESSOR OF ANATOMY UNITED MEDICAL AND DENTAL COLLEGE Learning Objectives – Trace the course, divisions and branches of the thoracic aorta from the aortic orifice to the aortic hiatus. – Describe the formation, course, tributaries and termination of the thoracic duct. – Identify the parts, constrictions, relations and blood supply of the esophagus. – Relate vertebral levels to surface anatomy — a favourite examination theme. – Correlate structure with clinical conditions: coarctation, chylothorax, dysphagia and varices. THE AORTA Overview & Divisions • The aorta is the largest and main arterial trunk of the body, carrying oxygenated blood from the left ventricle to every systemic organ. • It begins at the aortic orifice, behind the left half of the sternum at the level of the third costal cartilage. • Conventionally it is divided into the ascending aorta, the arch of aorta, and the descending aorta — itself split into thoracic and abdominal parts at the diaphragm. • Each division carries its own course, relations and branches, making this a heavily examined region of gross anatomy. left ventricle Arch of aorta Ascendi

ng aorta Descending thoracic aorta Three divisions of the aorta — schematic Ascending Aorta • Origin: aortic orifice of the left ventricle, opposite the 3rd intercostal space. – Extent: about 5 cm long, ending at the sternal angle (2nd costal cartilage). – Enclosure: lies within the fibrous pericardium, sharing a sheath with the pulmonary trunk. – Aortic sinuses: three dilations at the root — right, left and posterior. – Branches: only two — right and left coronary arteries, from the right and left sinuses. Ascending Aorta: Originates at aortic vestibule (left ventricle) at level of 3rd left costal cartilage; extends upward to sternal angle (T4/T5). Aortic Sinuses: Gives off right and left coronary arteries from anterior and left posterior aortic sinuses. Arch of Aorta: Situated in superior mediastinum, begins behind right 2nd sternocostally joined joint; arches posteriorly over left principal bronchus to end at lower border of T4 vertebra. Key Relations: Anterolateral to left phrenic and vagus nerves; inferiorly loops around left recurrent laryngeal nerve. Ascending Aorta & Arch Arch of Aorta — Course Continuation: begins where ascending aorta ends, at the sternal angle (T4/T5 dis

c). – Course: arches upward, backward and to the left, over the root of the left lung and left main bronchus. – Highest point: about 2.5 cm below the upper border of the manubrium sterni. – Termination: at the lower border of T4, continuing as the descending thoracic aorta. – Location: begins in the superior mediastinum, curves into the posterior mediastinum. THE AORTA Arch of Aorta — Branches – Brachiocephalic trunk: divides into right common carotid and right subclavian arteries. – Left common carotid a.: supplies the left side of the head and neck. – Left subclavian a.: supplies the left upper limb; contributes to vertebral circulation. – Variant: a fourth branch, thyroidea ima, may arise directly from the arch. – Clinical note: a common origin of brachiocephalic trunk and left carotid (“bovine arch”) matters for angiography. Brachiocephalic trunk Left common carotid a. Left subclavian a. Three branches, right → left, from the convexity Descending Thoracic Aorta — Course – Start: lower border of T4, continuing the arch of aorta. – Path: descends through the posterior mediastinum, initially left of the vertebral column. – Shift: inclines forward and medially, lying anterior to th

e vertebral bodies by T12. – End: passes through the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm (T12) as the abdominal aorta. – Esophagus relation: the esophagus crosses from its right side to its anterior/left side as both descend. THE AORTA Branches of Descending Thoracic Aorta – Visceral: pericardial, bronchial, esophageal (4–5 small branches) and mediastinal branches. – Parietal: posterior intercostal arteries (3rd–11th spaces), subcostal and superior phrenic arteries. – Anastomosis: posterior intercostals join anterior intercostal branches of the internal thoracic artery. – Clinical significance: this collateral network enlarges markedly in coarctation of the aorta. chunks: A N A T O M Y · T H O R A X · 1 S T Y E A R M B B S The Azygos Venous System Development, course, tributaries and applied anatomy of the azygos, hemiazygos and accessory hemiazygos veins R A Professor Dr. Rais Ahmed Professor of Anatomy · United Medical & Dental College Learning Objectives By the end of this session, the student should be able to 01 Define the azygos venous system and name its three components 02 Trace its development from the embryonic cardinal veins 03 Describe the origin, course, relations and termination of the azygos vein 04 Describe the hemiazygos and accessory hemiazygos veins 05 List the tributaries draining into each of the three veins 06 Explain the applied and radiological anatomy of the azygos system INTRODUCTION What is the Azygos Venous System? It drains, ultimately, into the superior vena cava — and forms one of the body's most important natural collateral pathways between the SVC and IVC. Azygos vein Hemiazygos vein Left side, lower — crosses over at T9 Accessory hemiazygos vein Left side, upper — crosses over at T7 WHY IT MATTERS Greek azygos = “unpaired” Unpaired, asymmetric venous drainage — Bypasses an obstructed SVC or IVC, carrying blood the l

ong way round Site of clinically important developmental variation (azygos continuation of IVC) THE AZYGOS VEIN Origin & Course 1 ORIGIN Union of the right ascending lumbar vein and the right subcostal vein, anterior to the T12 vertebra (occasionally arises directly from the IVC) 2 ENTRY INTO THORAX Passes into the thorax through the aortic opening of the diaphragm, or by piercing the right crus 3 ASCENT Ascends in the posterior mediastinu m along the right side of the vertebral column — right of the aorta, thoracic duct and oesophagus 4 ARCH At T4/T5, arches forward over the root of the right lung, above the right main bronchus 5 TERMINATIO N Drains into the superior vena cava, just before it pierces the pericardium BIG PICTURE The System at a Glance 1 One continuous vein on the right (azygos) draining directly into the SVC 2 Two veins on the left (hemiazygos + accessory hemiazygos) that must cross the midline to reach the azygos vein 3 Each of the three great veins begins by union of a subcostal vein with an ascending lumbar vein 4 The azygos vein arches over the root of the right lung at T4/T5 before entering the SVC T H E A Z Y G O S V E I N · I I FROM THE BODY WALL Right poste

rior intercostal veins (4th–11th) Right subcostal vein Right superior intercostal vein (2nd & 3rd spaces) Hemiazygos vein — joins at T9 Accessory hemiazygos vein — joins at T7 Oesophageal, mediastinal, pericardial & right bronchial veins The azygos vein is unique in receiving the entire venous return of the right posterior chest wall — plus both left-sided “hemiazygos” veins. chunks: Muscles, Fascia and Movement of the Thoracic Wall Transversus Thoracis — Three Parts 1 Subcostalis Confined to the posterior part of the lower intercostal spaces only. Runs from the inner surface of the rib near the angle to the inner surface of the 2nd–3rd rib below. 2 Intercostalis Intimi The innermost intercostal — confined to the middle two-fourths of all intercostal spaces. Lies deep to the intercostal vessels and nerve. 3 Sternocostalis Present in relation to the anterior parts of the upper intercostal spaces, from the sternum and xiphoid to the costal cartilages of ribs 2–6. WALLS OF THORAX 4 Attachments of the Intercostal Muscles Muscle Origin Insertion External intercostal Lower border of the rib above the space Outer lip of the upper border of the rib below Internal intercostal Floor of the costal groove of the rib above Inner lip of the upper border of the rib below Subcostalis Inner surface of the rib near the angle Inner surface of two or three ribs below Intercostalis intimi Middle two-fourths of the ridge above the costal groove Inner lip of the upper border of the rib below Sternocostalis Lower 1/3 of posterior body of sternum · posterior xiphoid · posterior costal

cartilages of lower 3–4 true ribs Costal cartilages of the 2nd to 6th ribs 5 Nerve Supply & Actions NERVE SUPPLY All intercostal muscles are supplied by the intercostal nerves of the spaces in which they lie. 1 Stabilising role (main action) Prevent the intercostal spaces from being drawn in during inspiration and from bulging outwards during expiration. 2 Elevate the ribs The external intercostals, the interchondral part of the internal intercostals, and levator costae may elevate the ribs during inspiration. 3 Depress the ribs The internal intercostals (except interchondral part) and transversus thoracis may depress the ribs / cartilages during expiration. 6 Fascia of the Thoracic Wall 1 Superficial fascia Subcutaneous layer containing fat, cutaneous vessels and nerves. In females it encloses the mammary gland and its fibrous septa (suspensory ligaments of Cooper). 2 Deep fascia A thin sheet investing the external intercostal muscles and rib periosteum. It is continuous above with the deep fascia of the neck and below with that of the abdominal wall. 3 Endothoracic fascia A thin fibroareolar layer lining the inner aspect of the thoracic wall, between the innermost (intercostalis

intimi) muscle and the parietal pleura. Allows the pleura to glide freely; continuous with the fascia over the diaphragm and with the clavipectoral fascia. 4 Suprapleural membrane (Sibson's fascia) A thickened dome-shaped part of the endothoracic fascia over the cervical pleura, attached to the inner border of the 1st rib and the transverse process of C7. Resists the piston-like negative pressure of breathing and protects the apex of the lung. 7 Pump-Handle Movement 3 BONES & JOINTS OF THORAX 9 RESPIRATORY MUSCLES Inspiration Quiet inspiration Diaphragm, external intercostal muscle, and interchondral part of the internal intercostal of the contralateral side. Deep inspiration Additionally recruits erector spinae, scalene muscles and pectoral muscles. Forced inspiration Scapulae are elevated and fixed by trapezius, levator scapulae and rhomboids — so serratus anterior and pectoralis minor can act on the ribs; action of erector spinae is markedly increased. chunks: Intercostal Nerves BY PROFESSOR DR. RAIS AHMED PROFESSOR OF ANATOMY UNITED MEDICAL AND DENTAL COLLEGE B E F O R E W E B E G I N Learning Objectives 1 Describe the formation of a thoracic spinal nerve and the typical course of an intercostal nerve. 2 List the boundaries and neurovascular contents of a typical intercostal space, including the VAN order. 3 Enumerate the branches of a typical intercostal nerve and the structures each one supplies. 4 Identify the atypical intercostal nerves (1st, 2nd, 7th–11th, subcostal) NERVE SUPPLY OF THE INTERCOSTAL SPACE TYPICAL NERVE Course of a Typical Intercostal Nerve The 3rd–6th intercostal nerves are “typical” • Enters the intercostal space near the neck of its corresponding rib, running below and parallel to the intercostal vessels. • Passes forward initially between the pleura and the internal intercostal membrane, then gains the costal groove along the lower border of the rib above. • Travels in the plane between the internal intercostal muscle and the innermost intercostal muscle for most of its course. • Continues to the front of the chest wall, ending as the anterior cutaneous branch near the sternum. Intervertebral foramen Costal groov

e Between internal & innermost intercostals Anterior cutaneous branch NERVE SUPPLY OF THE INTERCOSTAL SPACE ATYPICAL NERVE 1 The First Intercostal Nerve • Main diversion: the bulk of the anterior ramus of T1 leaves the intercostal space and joins the brachial plexus via a branch to its lowest trunk. • Remaining part: only a small portion continues as the true 1st intercostal nerve, running along the first rib without a well-formed costal groove for part of its course. • Missing branches: it typically has no lateral cutaneous branch, and often no anterior cutaneous branch either, unlike typical nerves. • Why it matters: this diversion explains why lower brachial plexus injuries can occasionally produce sensory change over the upper chest wall. T1 ANTERIOR RAMUS Large part → Brachial plexus (lowest trunk) Small part → True 1st intercostal nerve Roughly a 4:1 split — most T1 fibres are recruited by the upper limb plexus rather than the thoracic wall. NERVE SUPPLY OF THE INTERCOSTAL SPACE ATYPICAL NERVE 2 The Second Intercostal Nerve • Key feature: its lateral cutaneous branch is unusually large and given its own name — the intercostobrachial nerve. • Course: crosses the floor of the a

xilla and joins the medial cutaneous nerve of the arm (a branch of the brachial plexus). • Distribution: supplies skin over the floor of the axilla and the medial side of the upper arm. • Clinical significance: frequently divided during axillary lymph node clearance for breast cancer, producing numbness or paraesthesia along the inner arm — patients should be counselled about this before surgery. 2nd intercostal nerve Lateral cutaneous branch Intercostobrachial nerve Floor of axilla → medial arm skin NERVE SUPPLY OF THE INTERCOSTAL SPACE ATYPICAL NERVES 3 The 7th–11th Intercostal Nerves Called thoraco-abdominal nerves because they cross from the thoracic to the abdominal wall. • Leave the intercostal space by passing deep to the costal margin, entering the anterior abdominal wall. • Continue in the same plane as in the thorax — between the internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles. • Supply the abdominal wall muscles and overlying skin, ending as anterior cutaneous branches near the linea alba. • Their dermatomes give the standard surface landmarks: T7 at the xiphisternum, T10 at the umbilicus. Intercostal space Deep to costal margin Between int. oblique & transversus Line

a alba region NERVE SUPPLY OF THE INTERCOSTAL SPACE ATYPICAL NERVE 4 The Subcostal Nerve (T12) • Identity: the anterior primary ramus of T12, following a course similar to an intercostal nerve but lying below the 12th rib rather than between two ribs. • Course: passes behind the lateral arcuate ligament and kidney, then enters the abdominal wall in the same muscular plane as the lower intercostal nerves. • Communication: often exchanges fibres with the iliohypogastric nerve, the first branch of the lumbar plexus. • T12 the only anterior ramus below the last rib — it has no rib above it to form a costal groove. Surgical flank incisions for the kidney run close to this nerve — careful retraction protects it from stretch injury. NERVE SUPPLY OF THE INTERCOSTAL SPACE Q U I C K R E C A P Typical vs Atypical Intercostal Nerves Nerve Type Distinguishing feature Nerve Type Distinguishing feature 1st (T1) Atypical Mostly joins brachial plexus; small remainder, no lateral cutaneous branch 2nd (T2) Atypical Large lateral cutaneous branch = intercostobrachial nerve 3rd–6th Typical Follows the standard three-part course and full branch pattern 7th–11th Atypical Thoraco-abdominal — cross into th

e anterior abdominal wall Subcostal (T12) Atypical Lies below the 12th rib; may join the iliohypogastric nerve NERVE SUPPLY OF THE INTERCOSTAL SPACE SUMMARY Intercostal Nerves — Recap 1 12 pairs: anterior rami of T1– T12 (T12 = subcostal nerve, outside the intercostal space). 2 Typical nerves T3–T6 follow the standard 3-part course; T1, T2, T7–T11, and T12 are atypical. 3 VAN order in the costal groove, from above down: Vein, Artery, Nerve — nerve is most exposed. 4 Five branches: rami communicantes, collateral, muscular, lateral cutaneous, anterior cutaneous. 5 Motor to intercostal & (in lower nerves) abdominal wall muscles; sensory in a clear dermatomal pattern. 6 Clinically vital for nerve blocks, chest drains, herpes zoster localisation, and thoracoabdominal surgery. 25

chunks: The Diaphragm • Dome-shaped musculotendinous sheet (TWO domes) • Separates abdomen from thorax • Assists breathing The Diaphragm • Origin: • Arises from circumference of inner thoracic outlet • Fibers are grouped into sternal, costal, and lumbar parts • Insertion • Central tendon Lumbar Origin • Vertebral originating parts are tendinous • Referred to as the left and right crura (singular crus) • Right crus: L1-L3 and associated intervertebral discs • Left crus: L1-L2 and associated intervertebral discs • The two crura form a tendinous arch in front of the aorta called the median arcuate ligament Insertion • Into the central tendon • Tendon is made up of three leaflets: • Right, left, and middle leaflets • Middle leaflet: triangular in shape; towards xiphisternum • Right and left leaflets: tongue-like, protruding backwards Innervation • Phrenic nerve bilaterally (C3, C4, C5) • 3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive • Sensory: • Phrenic nerve- central part • Lower six thoracic nerve- peripheral part Relations • Right dome reaches 4th costal space (during expiration) • Left dome reaches 5th rib during expiration • Superior – pericardium, basal lung segments • Inferior: • Right – liver, sup

rarenal region, kidney • Left – stomach, suprarenal, kidney, and spleen • Posterior – Aorta, azygous vein, esophagus, vagii, •Actions: • The diaphragm is the principal muscle of inspiration. On contraction, the diaphragm descends increasing the vertical diameter of the thorax.

Anterior: Thin space in front of the pericardium — areolar tissue, lymph nodes, sternopericardial l

chunks: The Pleura • Continuous double-layered serous membrane covering the lungs • Two broad parts: • Parietal • Visceral • These two parts are continuous with each other at the lung’s hilum Visceral Pleura • In direct contact with the outer surface of the lungs • Continuous with the parietal pleura at the hilum • Firmly adherent to the lungs; inseparable Parietal Pleura • Parietal pleura is further subdivided into four parts according to location: • Diaphragmatic • Costal • Mediastinal • Cervical Cervical Pleura • Dome of the parietal pleura • Extends into the neck • Boundaries: • Anterior – Subclavian vessels • Posterior – neck of rib 1 • Medial – ICA • Lateral – Scalene muscles Suprapleural Membrane • Also called Sibson’s fascia • Derived from the scalene muscles and endothoracic fascia • Attachment points: • C7/T1 vertebra • Inner border of rib 1 • Separates the cervical pleura and lung apex from root of the neck structures • Subclavian artery/vein Pulmonary Ligament • False ligament – made by pleural folds • Hangs beneath the lung hilum • Allows for movement of structures in lung root during inspiration Pleural Recesses • Excessive space in the pleural cavity • Allows for lung expans

ion during inspiration • Two spaces: • Costodiaphragmatic • Costomediastinal Costodiaphragmatic Recess • Lies between the costal and diaphragmatic pleurae • Lies opposite ribs 8-10 in the midaxillary line • Lies opposite ribs 6-8 in the midclavicular line • Common site of pleural fluid collection • Related structures: • Right side – Liver and right kidney • Left side – Stomach fundus, spleen, and left kidney Costomediastinal Recess • Lies between costal and mediastinal pleurae • Positioned anteriorly • Left recess is larger than the right recess • Due to cardiac notch • This wide region is located at ribs 4-6 Clinical Correlations • Pleurisy • Inflammation of the pleura • Friction between the parietal and visceral pleura produces: • Pain • Friction rub (sound) • Pneumothorax Pneumothorax • Pathological introduction of air into the pleural cavity • Resulting change in pressure causes lung collapse • Different types: • Traumatic • Spontaneous • Both types can further devolve into tension pneumothorax Needle Decompression • Done to remove air from pleural cavity • Done to reverse symptoms of pneumothorax • Typical sites are: • 2nd intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line • 5th int

ercostal space in the mid-axillary line (newer guidelines) Thoracentesis • Tap done to remove excessive fluid from the pleural cavity • Done in posterior axillary/mid-scapular line • Between ribs 8 and 9 • Both diagnostic and therapeutic

chunks: The Lung • Organs of respiration • Located within the thorax, on either side of the mediastinum • Related to multiple important structures within the thorax The Lung • Roughly cone shaped, with an apex, a base, three surfaces, three borders, and two (left)/three (right) lobes • Surfaces – Costal, Mediastinal, Diaphragmatic • Borders – Anterior, Inferior, Posterior • The apex – projects above rib 1, into the neck root • The base – sits on the diaphragm Surfaces • The costal surface: • Smooth and curved • Related directly to the costal pleura • Separated from the chest wall and intercostal muscles • The diaphragmatic surface: • Concave shape • Concavity is deeper in the right lung • Rests on the diaphragm • The mediastinal surface: • Faces the lateral aspect of the middle mediastinum • Contains the lung hilum Lung Lobes • The right and left lung are not mirror images • The right lung has three lobes, separated via two fissures • Oblique • Horizontal • The left lung has two lobes, separated by an oblique fissure Lung Lobes • The left lung contains within itself an indentation called the cardiac notch • This notch deprives the left lung of space needed for a third lobe • In place of a

third lobe, the left lung has an extension called the lingula The Lung Root • A collection of structures that suspend the lung • The hilum is an opening that allows for the passage of these structures • Inferior to the hilum lies the pulmonary ligament • Structures within the hilum include: • Principal bronchi (bronchus in the left lung) • Pulmonary vessels (artery and vein) • Bronchial vessels • Hilar lymph nodes • Autonomic nerve fibers Vasculature • Each lung is supplied by a single pulmonary artery • Carries deoxygenated blood • Blood leaves each lung via two pulmonary veins • Carries oxygenated blood • The bronchi, surrounding lung tissue, and visceral pleura is supplied by the bronchial vessels from the aorta • Right bronchial vein drains into the azygous vein • Left bronchial vein drains into the accessory hemiazygos vein Nerve Supply • Parasympathetic – Vagus Nerve (CN X) • Sympathetic – Derived from the sympathetic trunk (T1-T5) • Visceral afferents – Conduct pain to CN X’s sensory ganglion Tracheobronchial Tree • Four parts: • Trachea • Bronchi • Bronchioles • Alveoli The Trachea • The trachea starts as an extension of the larynx • Starts below the cricoid cartilage (C6-T

4/5) • Bifurcates at the sternal angle, within the middle mediastinum • Located anteriorly to the esophagus The Trachea • Is held open by C-shaped hyaline cartilaginous rings • Both the trachea and the bronchi are lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells • At the bifurcation, a layer of cartilage called the carina runs between the bronchi • Frequent trigger site of cough reflex Trachea • Relations (in the chest): • Anterior – Manubrium, thymus, aortic arch, right CCA, brachiocephalic trunk • Posterior – Esophagus • Laterally – Left and right vagus nerves, left and right recurrent laryngeal nerves, Left CCA, arch of the azygous vein Trachea • Arterial supply – Inferior thyroid artery • Venous drainage – Brachiocephalic, azygous, and accessory hemiazygous veins • Nerve supply – Recurrent Laryngeal Nerve Tracheostomy • Emergency life-saving procedure • Incision given in the trachea to pass tracheostomy tube • Allows for breathing in cases of obstruction, prolonged ventilation • Incision given between tracheal rings 2-3 Bronchi • The trachea divides into a right and left bronchus • Right bronchus is wider, shorter, and steeper • Common site of foreign bo

dy inhalation • Left bronchus passes inferiorly to the aortic arch Bronchi • Primary bronchi divide into 2/3 secondary bronchi • One for each lobe (2 in the left, 3 in the right) • Secondary bronchi divide into tertiary bronchi • Supply individual bronchopulmonary segments Bronchioles & Alveoli • Bronchi terminate into smaller bronchioles • Two major types: • Conducting bronchioles – conduct air; no glands or alveoli • Respiratory bronchioles – contain alveoli; allow for gaseous exchange • Unlike bronchi, bronchioles do not contain cartilage • They instead have layers of smooth muscle

azygous/hemiazygous veins Bronchopulmonary Segment • Smallest functionally independent unit of the lung • Smallest area that can be removed without damaging surrounding structures • Each is supplied by one terminal bronchus and one pulmonary artery • 10 segments in each lung Bronchopulmonary Segment • Principal bronchi arise from the trachea bifurcation • Divide into lobar/secondary bronchi • Lobar bronchi divide into segmental/tertiary bronchi, which supply these segments • Tributaries of the pulmonary veins pass around the margins of the segments Lymphatic Drainage • Lymphatic drainage of the chest wall and lungs is conducted via the tracheobronchial lymph nodes • These ultimately drain into the right and left bronchomediastinal lymph trunks

chunks: Classify ribs. Discuss the features of typical and a typical ribs. Describe the attachments and relations of ribs. OBJECTIVES: There are twelve pairs of ribs, each terminating anteriorly in a costal cartilage. Although all ribs articulate with the vertebral column, only the costal cartilages of the upper 7 ribs , known as true ribs, (articulate directly with the sternum). The remaining 5 pairs of ribs are false ribs: The costal cartilage of rib VIII to X articulate anteriorly with the costal cartilages of the rib above; Ribs XI and XII have no anterior connection with other ribs or with the sternum and are called floating ribs. RIBS Key facts about ribs Classificatio n Based on articulations - true (1 to 7), false (8 to 10), and floating (11 and 12) ribs Based on structure - typical (3 to 9) and atypical (1, 2, 10, 11, and 12) ribs Structure Typical (3 to 9) and atypical (1, 2, 10, 11, and 12) ribs Structure of typical ribs Head (contains two articular facets), neck, tubercle (has an articular and non articular part), and body (curves at the costal angle, the internal surface contains the costal groove and it joins with the costal cartilage) Structure of atypical ribs First

- widest, shortest, it has the sharpest curve and only one articular surface, contains two grooves for the subclavian vessels Second - it has two facets and a roughened tuberosity on its posterior surface Tenth, eleventh, twelfth - they have only one facet and neither a neck or tubercles Clinical Chest drain insertion (superior border of rib), fractures, flail chest Ribs three to nine are the ‘typical’ ribs and the major landmarks are the head, neck, tubercle and body. Side Determination: The anterior end bears a concave depression . The posterior end bears a head, a neck, and a tubercle. The shaft is convex outwards and there is a costal groove situated along the lower part of its inner surface The lower border is thin and the upper border rounded. TYPICAL RIBS A typical ribs consists of a curved shaft with the anterior and posterior ends.  The anterior end is continuous with its costal cartilage. The posterior end articulates with the vertebral column and is characterized by a head, neck, and a tubercle. FEATURES: The head is expanded and typically presents two articular surfaces separated by a crest. The smaller superior surface articulates with the inferior costal f

acet on the vertebra above, whereas the larger inferior facet articulates with the superior costal facet of its own vertebra. The neck is a short flat region of bone that separates the head from tubercle. The tubercle projects posteriorly from the junction of the neck and the shaft and consists of two regions, an articular and non-articular part; The articular part is medial and has an oval facet for the articulation with the transverse process of the associated vertebra; The raised non-articular part is roughened by ligament attachments. The shaft is thin and flat . It has: 2 surfaces: outer and inner surfaces. 2 borders: Upper or superior margins is smooth and rounded  lower or inferior margin is rough. The shaft bends forward just laterally to tubercle at a site termed as angle. The inferior margin of the internal surface is marked by a distinct costal groove. The body ends with a cup for the costal cartilage, which allows the rib to articulate with the sternum. Anteriorly head provides attachment to the radiate ligament. The crest of head provides attachment to intra- articular ligament of costovertebral joint. Attachments to the neck: Anterior surface is cove

red by costal pleura. Inferior costotransverse ligament is attached to rough posterior surface. The two laminae of superior costotransverse ligament are attached to the crest of neck ATTACHMENTS OF A TYPICAL RIB The lateral non-articular part of tubercle gives attachment to lateral costotransverse ligament. FIRST RIB It is the shortest, broadest and most curved rib. The shaft is not twisted and there is no costal groove. It is flattened from above downwards so that it has superior and inferior surfaces; and outer and inner border. SIDE DETERMINATION: The anterior end is larger, thicker and pitted . The posterior end is small and rounded. The outer border is convex . The upper surface of shaft is crossed obliquely by two shallow grooves separated by a ridge. The ridge is enlarged at inner border of rib to form the scalene tubercle. When the rib is placed on a horizontal, i.e. with the superior facing upwards, both the ends of rib touch the surface. FEATURES: The anterior end is larger and thicker then the other ribs. The posterior end comprises of : Head: small and rounded. Articulates with body of vertebra T1 and therefore has only one articular surface. Neck: rounded

Tubercle: large. Articulates with the transverse process of 1st thoracic vertebra to form the costotransverse joint. Shaft: has 2 surfaces(superior and inferior ) and 2 borders(outer and inner). The superior surface is marked by two shallow grooves, separated near the inner border by the scalene tubercle. The lower surface is smooth and has no costal groove. ATTACHMENTS AND RELATIONS: Anteriorly, neck is related from medial to lateral side to: Sympathetic chain Posterior intercostal vein Superior intercostal artery Ventral ramus of 1st thoracic nerve (Mnemonic- Chain pulling a VAN) Superiorly, neck is related to: The deep cervical vessels. The 8th cervical nerve Anterior groove on superior surface of shaft lodges subclavian vein, The posterior groove lodges the subclavian artery and the lower trunk of brachial plexus. Structures attached to upper surface of shaft are: Origin: Subclavius muscle – anterior end Insertion: 1.Scalenus anterior – scalene tubercle.  2. Scalenus medius – behind groove for subclavian artery. Attachment of costoclavicular ligament at anterior end behind the subclavius. The outer border gives origin to: The external intercostal muscle; T

he upper part of first digitation of serratus anterior , just behind the groove for subclavian artery. The tubercle gives attachment to lateral costotransverse ligament. SECOND RIB Features : The second rib is thinner and length is twice that of the 1st rib. There are two facets present on the head to allow articulation with the T1(superior) and T2 (corresponding) vertebrae. Its unique feature is a roughened tuberosity on its superior surface(near middle). ATTACHMENTS: Origin: Serratus anterior(one and half digitations): outer surface of tubercle. Insertion: Scalenus posterior: upper border TENTH RIB The 10th rib is closely resembles a typical rib, but is; Shorter Has only one facet on the head, for the body of 10th thoracic vertebra. ELEVENTH AND TWELFTH RIBS 11th and 12th ribs are shorts. They have pointed ends. The necks and tubercles are absent. The angle and costal groove are poorly marked in 11th rib; and are absent in 12th rib. CLINICAL ANATOMY: Cervical Ribs: A cervical rib is an accessory rib articulating with vertebra C VII; the anterior end attaches to the superior border of anterior aspect of rib I. Plain radigraphs demonstrate cervical rib as small h

orn-like structure. A fibrous band extends from the anterior tip of cervical rib to rib I , producing cervical band. It may cause pressure on lower trunk of brachial plexus. Resulting in paraesthesia along the medial border of forearm and wasting of intrinsic muscles of hand. It may also cause pressure on the subclavian artey. RIB FRACTURE: Weakest area of rib is the region of its angle. This is the commonest site of fracture. Flail Chest: After severe trauma, rib may be broken into two or more places. If enough ribs are broken a flail segment, or flail chest, can occur. When the patient takes a deep inspiration, the flail segments moves in opposite direction to chest wall, preventing full lung expansion.

chunks: CONTENTS ▪Bony Features ▪Muscle attachments ▪Jugular Notch ▪Joints ▪Sternal Angle – Clinical Significance INTRODUCTION ▪The adult sternum consists of three major elements: ▪the broad and superiorly positioned manubrium of sternum, ▪the narrow and longitudinally oriented body of sternum, and ▪the small and inferiorly positioned xiphoid process BONY FEATURES Flat bone with three divisions: • Manubrium: • Upper portion • 2 inches • Indentations (jugular, clavicular, costal) • Body: • Middle portion • 5 inches • Costal notches • Xiphoid process: • Lower portion • Small • Vary in size and shape MANUBRIUM OF STERNUM ▪The manubrium of sternum forms part of the bony framework of the neck and the thorax. ▪The superior surface of the manubrium is expanded laterally and bears a distinct and palpable notch, the jugular notch (suprasternal notch), in the midline. ▪On either side of this notch is a large oval fossa for articulation with the clavicle. ▪Immediately inferior to this fossa, on each lateral surface of the manubrium, is a facet for the attachment of the first costal cartilage. ▪ ▪At the lower end of the lateral border is a demifacet for articulation with the upper half of the anterior

end of the second costal cartilage . Manubrium Body (gladiolus) Xiphoid process Suprasternal notch (jugular) 4 5 Sternal angle BODY OF THE STERNUM ▪The body of the sternum is flat. ▪The anterior surface of the body of the sternum is often marked by transverse ridges . ▪The lateral margins of the body of the sternum have articular facets for costal cartilages. ▪Superiorly, each lateral margin has a demifacet for articulation with the inferior aspect of the second costal cartilage. ▪Inferior to this demifacet are four facets for articulation with the costal cartilages of ribs III to VI. ▪At the inferior end of the body of the sternum is a demifacet for articulation with the upper demifacet on the seventh costal cartilage. ▪The inferior end of the body of the sternum is attached to the xiphoid process. XIPHOID PROCESS ▪The xiphoid process is the smallest part of the sternum. ▪Its shape is variable: it may be wide, thin, pointed, bifid, curved, or perforated. ▪It begins as a cartilaginous structure, which becomes ossified in the adult. ▪On each side of its upper lateral margin is a demifacet for articulation with the inferior end of the seventh costal cartilage. STERNAL ANGLE ▪The ste

rnal angle is used to find the position of rib II as a reference for counting ribs (because of the overlying clavicle, rib I is not palpable); ▪The sternal angle lies on a horizontal plane that passes through the intervertebral disc between vertebrae TIV and TV. CLINICAL SIGNIFICANCE ▪Second costal cartilage articulates, on each side, with the sternum at this level, therefore this level is utilized for counting the ribs. ▪It is located at the level of intervertebral disc between T4 and T5 vertebrae. ▪Horizontal plane going through this level divides superior mediastinum from inferior mediastinum. ▪Ascending aorta finishes at this level. ▪Arch of aorta starts and finishes at this level. ▪Descending aorta starts at this level. ▪Trachea bifurcates into left and right main bronchi at this level. ▪Pulmonary trunk splits into left and right pulmonary arteries at this level. ▪Upper border of heart is located at this level. ▪Azygos vein arches over the root of right lung to finish in the superior vena cava. ▪Thymus is located posterior to the manubrium of sternum JOINTS ▪All ribs articulate with the vertebral column, only the costal cartilages of the upper seven ribs, known as true ribs ,

articulate directly with the sternum. STERNOCOSTAL JOINTS ▪The sternocostal joints are joints between the upper seven costal cartilages and the sternum. ▪The joint between rib I and the manubrium is not synovial and consists of a fibrocartilaginous connection between the manubrium and the costal cartilage. ▪The second to seventh joints are synovial and have thin capsules reinforced by surrounding sternocostal ligaments. MANUBRIOSTERNAL AND XIPHISTERNAL JOINTS ▪The joints between the manubrium and body of sternum and between the body of sternum and the xiphoid process are usually symphyses ▪Only slight angular movements occur between the manubrium and body of sternum during respiration. ▪The joint between the body of sternum and the xiphoid process often becomes ossified with age.

chunks: Surface Anatomy of Lung and Thoracic Wall Anatomy & Clinical Correlations Introduction • Overview of lungs and thoracic wall anatomy. • Importance in clinical practice. Thoracic Wall: Overview • Bony framework: sternum, ribs, thoracic vertebrae. • Muscular component: intercostal muscles, diaphragm. • Surface landmarks used in clinical examination. Surface Landmarks • Jugular notch (T2), Sternal angle (T4), Xiphisternum (T9). • Costal margins and intercostal spaces. Thoracic Wall Muscles • External intercostal muscles. • Internal intercostal muscles. • Innermost intercostal muscles. Surface Anatomy of Lungs • Right lung: 3 lobes, 2 fissures. • Left lung: 2 lobes, 1 fissure + lingula. Lung Borders • Apex: 2–3 cm above clavicle. • Anterior border: right – straight; left – cardiac notch. • Inferior border: 6th rib (MCL), 8th rib (MAL), 10th rib (scapular line). Oblique Fissure • Runs from T3 spine posteriorly to 6th rib anteriorly. • Separates upper/middle from lower lobes (right), upper from lower lobe (left). Horizontal Fissure • Present only in right lung. • Runs along 4th rib anteriorly, joining oblique fissure at mid-axillary line. Surface Projection: Right Lung • Upper lobe – abo

ve 4th rib anteriorly. • Middle lobe – between 4th and 6th rib. • Lower lobe – below 6th rib, posterior thorax. Surface Projection: Left Lung • Upper lobe – extends down to 6th rib anteriorly. • Lingula – near cardiac notch, 5th intercostal space. • Lower lobe – posterior thorax below 6th rib. Pleura vs Lung Borders • Pleural reflections extend lower than lung borders. • Pleura: 8th rib (MCL), 10th rib (MAL), 12th rib (scapular line). • Creates costodiaphragmatic recess. Auscultation Points • Upper lobes: anterior chest above 4th rib. • Middle lobe (right): anterior, 4th–6th rib. • Lower lobes: posterior chest below T3 scapular spine. Percussion & Clinical Relevance • Dullness – consolidation, effusion. • Hyperresonance – pneumothorax. • Surface anatomy guides interpretation. Thoracentesis Surface Landmark • Needle insertion: above 9th rib, mid-axillary line. • Avoid neurovascular bundle (runs under ribs). Chest Tube Insertion • 5th intercostal space, mid-axillary line. • Triangle of safety: lateral border of pec major, anterior border of lat dorsi, nipple line. Clinical Correlations • Pneumonia – localized to lobes. • Pleural effusion – fluid in costodiaphragmatic recess. • Pneumo
thorax – air in pleural cavity. Summary • Thoracic wall provides landmarks. • Surface anatomy helps guide examination and procedures. • Vital for clinical practice.
