chunks: Thoracic vertebrae, Joints of thoracic wall and anomalies Thoracic Vertebrae • Characteristic Features • The thoracic vertebrae have four features which distinguish them from other vertebrae: • Vertebral body is heart shaped. • Presence of demi-facets on the sides of each vertebral body – these articulate with the heads of the ribs. • Presence of costal facets on the transverse processes – these articulate with the tubercles of the ribs. They are present on T1-T10 only. • The spinous processes are long and slant inferiorly. This offers increased protection to the spinal cord, preventing an object such as a knife entering the spinal canal. Joints of thoracic wall • The articulations between the vertebrae and the ribs are unique to the thoracic spine. For each rib, there are two separate articulations – costovertebral and costotransverse. • Each costovertebral joint consists of the head of the rib articulating with: • Superior costal facet of the corresponding vertebra • Inferior costal facet of the superior vertebra • Intervertebral disc separating the two vertebrae • Within this joint, the intra-articular ligament of head of rib attaches the rib head to the intervertebral disc. Onl

y slight gliding movements can occur at these joints, due to the close articulation of their components. • The costotransverse joints are formed by the articulation of transverse processes of a thoracic vertebra and the tubercle of the adjacent rib. They are present in all vertebrae except T11 and T12. Ligaments • The thoracic spine is strengthened by the presence of numerous ligaments. • Unique to Thoracic Spine • A number of small ligaments also support the costovertebral joints: • Radiate ligament of head of rib – Fans outwards from the head of the rib to the bodies of the two vertebrae and intervertebral disc. • Costotransverse ligament – Connects the neck of the rib and the transverse process. • Lateral costotransverse ligament – Extends from the transverse process to the tubercle of the rib. • Superior costotransverse ligament – Passes from the upper border of the neck of the rib to the transverse process of the vertebra superior to it Review • The Thoracic Cage relies on several key joints to remain stable yet flexible during breathing: • Costovertebral joints: Connect the head of a rib to the bodies of the vertebrae. • Costotransverse joints: Connect the bump (tubercle) of

a rib to the side transverse process of the vertebra. • Intervertebral joints: Fibrocartilage discs sit between vertebral bodies to absorb shock. • Sternocostal joints: Connect the upper rib cartilages directly to the breastbone (sternum). • Manubriosternal and xiphisternal joints: The joints connecting the different parts of the sternum together CLINICAL • Thoracic Kyphosis • Kyphosis is an excessive curvature of the thoracic spine, causing the back to appear “hunched”. It may occur for a number of reasons early in life. These include poor posture, abnormally wedge-shaped shaped vertebrae (Scheuermann’s kyphosis), and fusing of vertebrae during development. • Various diseases can also lead to kyphosis in adults. The most common cause is osteoporosis – a condition whereby bone mass is lost (mostly in older people). This leaves the spine less able to support the weight of the body, thus resulting in characteristic kyphosis. Common Anomalies • Developmental and genetic variations can change the shape of the chest and spine: • Pectus excavatum: A sunken or "funnel" chest where the breastbone sinks inward, which can crowd the heart and lungs. • Pectus carinatum: A "pigeon chest" where

the breastbone pushes outward. • Hemivertebra: A failure of one side of a vertebra to form properly, causing sideways curving of the spine (scoliosis). • Rib fusion or absence: Neighboring ribs or vertebrae fuse together or fail to grow, as seen in rare conditions like Jarcho-Levin syndrome

subject: Anatomy
chunks: Introduction • The vertebral column is a series of approximately 33 bones called vertebrae, which are separated by intervertebral discs. • The column can be divided into five different regions, with each region characterized by a different vertebral structure. Structure of a Vertebrae • All vertebrae share a basic common structure. They each consist of an anterior vertebral body, and a posterior vertebral arch. Vertebral Body • The vertebral body forms the anterior part of each vertebrae. • It is the weight-bearing component, and vertebrae in the lower portion of the column have larger bodies than those in the upper portion (to better support the increased weight). • The superior and inferior aspects of the vertebral body are lined with hyaline cartilage. Adjacent vertebral bodies are separated by a fibrocartilaginous intervertebral disc. Vertebral Arch • The vertebral arch forms the lateral and posterior aspect of each vertebrae. • In combination with the vertebral body, the vertebral arch forms an enclosed hole – the vertebral foramen. The foramina of all the vertebrae line up to form the vertebral canal, which encloses the spinal cord. • The vertebral arches have several bony pr

ominences, which act as attachment sites for muscles and ligaments: • Spinous processes – each vertebra has a single spinous process, centered posteriorly at the point of the arch. • Transverse processes – each vertebra has two transverse processes, which extend laterally and posteriorly from the vertebral body. In the thoracic vertebrae, the transverse processes articulate with the ribs. • Pedicles – connect the vertebral body to the transverse processes. • Lamina – connect the transverse and spinous processes. • Articular processes – form joints between one vertebra and its superior and inferior counterparts. The articular processes are located at the intersection of the laminae and pedicles. Clinical Relevance • Intervertebral Disc Herniation • The intervertebral disc is a fibro cartilaginous cylinder that lies between the vertebrae, joining them together. They permit the flexibility of the spine, and act as shock absorbers. In the lumbar and thoracic regions, they are wedge–shaped – supporting the curvature of the spine. • Each vertebral disc has two parts: the nucleus pulposus and annulus fibrosus. The annulus fibrosus is tough and collagenous, and it surrounds the jelly-like

nucleus pulposus. • Herniation of an intervertebral disc occurs when the nucleus pulposus ruptures, breaking through the annulus fibrosus. The rupture usually occurs in a posterior-lateral direction, after which the nucleus pulposus can irritate nearby spinal nerves – resulting in a variety of neurological and muscular symptoms. Cervical Vertebrae • There are seven cervical vertebrae in the human body. They have three main distinguishing features: • Bifid spinous process – the spinous process bifurcates at its distal end. • Exceptions to this are C1 (no spinous process) and C7 (spinous process is longer than that of C2- C6 and may not bifurcate). • Transverse foramina – an opening in each transverse process, through which the vertebral arteries travel to the brain. • Triangular vertebral foramen • Two cervical vertebrae that are unique. C1 and C2 (called the atlas and axis respectively), are specialised to allow for the movement of the head. Thoracic Vertebrae • The twelve thoracic vertebrae are characterized by their articulation with the ribs – forming the bony thorax. They increase in size from superior to inferior. • Typical thoracic vertebrae (T2–T9) have two demi-facets on ea

ch side of the vertebral body, superiorly and inferiorly placed. These articulate with the heads of adjacent ribs. • The transverse processes contain costal facets for articulation with the tubercle of a single rib. For example, the head of Rib 2 articulates with the inferior demi-facet of T1 and the superior demi-facet of T2, while the tubercle of Rib 2 articulates with the transverse costal facet of T2. • The spinous processes are oriented obliquely inferiorly and the vertebral foramen is circular. Lumbar Vertebrae • There are five lumbar vertebrae in most humans, which are the largest in the vertebral column. They are structurally specialized to support the weight of the torso. • Lumbar vertebrae have very large vertebral bodies, which are kidney shaped. They lack the characteristic features of other vertebrae, with no transverse foramina, costal facets, or bifid spinous processes. • However, like the cervical vertebrae, they have a triangular- shaped vertebral foramen. Their spinous processes are shorter than those of thoracic vertebrae and do not extend inferiorly below the level of the vertebral body. • Their size and orientation permits needle access to the spinal canal and

spinal cord (which would not be possible between thoracic vertebrae). Examples include epidural anesthesia administration and lumbar puncture. Sacrum and Coccyx • The sacrum and coccyx lie at the caudal (tail) end of the vertebral column. They are composed of fused vertebrae, and are referred to as the ‘false’ vertebrae. • Sacrum – formed by five fused vertebrae. It is shaped as an inverted triangle, and forms the posterior wall of the bony pelvis. On the lateral walls of the sacrum are facets for articulation with the ilium at the sacroiliac joints. • Coccyx – formed by four fused vertebrae. It is a small bone which articulates with the apex of the sacrum. It is recognized by its absent vertebral canal and vertebral arches. • Separation of S1 from the sacrum is termed “lumbarisation”, while fusion of L5 to the sacrum is termed “sacralisation”. These conditions are congenital abnormalities Joints and Ligaments • The mobile vertebrae articulate with each other via joints between their bodies and articular facets: • Left and right superior articular facets articulate with the vertebra above. • Left and right inferior articular facets articulate with the vertebra below. • Vertebral bo

dies indirectly articulate with each other via the intervertebral discs. • The vertebral body joints are cartilaginous joints, designed for weight-bearing. The articular surfaces are covered by hyaline cartilage, and are connected by the intervertebral disc. • Two ligaments strengthen the vertebral body joints: the anterior and posterior longitudinal ligaments, which run the full length of the vertebral column. The anterior longitudinal ligament is thick and prevents hyperextension of the vertebral column. The posterior longitudinal ligament is weaker and prevents hyper flexion. • The joints between the articular facets, called facet joints, allow for some gliding motions between the vertebrae. They are strengthened by several ligaments: • Ligamentum flavum – extends between lamina of adjacent vertebrae. • Interspinous and supraspinous – join the spinous processes of adjacent vertebrae. The interspinous ligaments attach between processes, and the supraspinous ligaments attach to the tips. • Intertransverse ligaments – extends between transverse processes Abnormal Morphology of the Spine • There are several clinical syndromes resulting from an abnormal curvature of the spine: • Kyph

osis – excessive thoracic curvature, causing a hunchback deformity. • Lordosis – excessive lumbar curvature, causing a swayback deformity. • Scoliosis – lateral curvature of the spine, usually of unknown cause. • Cervical spondylosis – decrease in the size of the intervertebral foramina, usually due to degeneration of the joints of the spine. The smaller size of the intervertebral foramina puts pressure on the exiting nerves, causing pain

LEARNING OBJECTIVES Respiratory Compensation Respiratory mechanisms • In patients with chronically high PaCO2 (chronic Carbon dioxide behaves as an acid in aqueous solution. One way that the body controls the pH of extracellular fluid is by increasing or decreasing the rate and depth of respiration and thereby the amount of carbon dioxide expelled. • The partial pressure of carbon dioxide in arterial blood (PaCO2) reflects the amount of carbon dioxide in arterial blood. PaCO2 is determined by alveolar ventilation. Respiratory Compensation • Chemoreceptors located in medulla sense pH changes in extracellular fluid and changes in arterial carbon dioxide, altering ventilation to maintain normal pH. • In patients with chronically high PaCO2 (chronic hypercapnia); for example, owing to severe chronic obstructive pulmonary

disease (COPD), chemoreceptors may become desensitised. • The body then relies on PaO2 to detect inadequate ventilation (hypoxic drive). • In chronic hypercapnia, supplemental oxygen in emergency settings should be given in a controlled manner with ABG monitoring to avoid respiratory depression. Respiratory Compensation pH • Small changes in pH have a significant impact on wide range of physiological processes. • If the cause of an abnormal pH is the respiratory system, the body can increase/decrease HCO3 - production by the kidneys to try and normalize the pH. • If the cause of an abnormal pH is metabolic, the body can increase/decrease alveolar ventilation to retain/exhale CO2 to try and normalize the pH. Rules of compensation 1. The compensatory response depends upon the

proper functioning of the organ system involved in the response (lungs or kidneys) and on the severity of acid–base disturbance. For example, the likelihood of complete compensation in chronic respiratory acidosis is <15% when paCO2 exceeds 60 mmHg. 2. Acute compensation occurs within 6–24 h and chronic within 1–4 days. Respiratory compensation occurs faster than metabolic compensation. 3. In clinical practice, it is rare to see complete compensation. The maximum compensatory response in most cases is associated with only 50–75% return of pH to normal. However, in chronic respiratory alkalosis, the pH may actually completely return to normalcy in some cases. Rate of Compensation • Respiratory compensation for a metabolic disorder can occur rapidly. • Metabolic compensation for a respiratory disorder can occur slowly. chunks: The Delicate Balance: Acid-Base Regulation, Anion Gap & ABGs Lt Col®. Professor. Dr. Sarah Sadiq MBBS.M Phil. PhD Depart of Biochemistry UMDC Learning Objectives • Regulation of acid base balance • Mechanism of acid production • List of volatile & non-volatile acids • Henderson’s Hassel balch equation • Mechanisms of buffer in human body • Normal regulation of pH by buffers, respiratory and renal systems • Anion gap and its biochemical significance • Interpretation of the values of Arterial Blood Gases (ABGs) Case Scenario A 21-year-old male medical student is rushed to emergency after being found unresponsive in his dorm during exams. His roommate reports that he had been consuming black coffee, and complained of abdominal pain and was breathing rapidly over past 24 hrs. He had Type 1 DM but was skipping his Insulin doses because he "forgot to eat“ Case Scenario • Physical Examination: He was confused, lethargic with BP 100/60 mmHg, pulse 115 bpm (tachycardia), respiratory rate 32 breaths/min • Breathing Pattern: Deep, labored, and gasping (Kussmaul breathing) with a distinct fruity odor on his breath Case Scenario • Arterial Blood Gas (ABG) & Lab Results • pH: 7.15 (Normal: 7.35–

7.45) • pCO₂: 24 mmHg (Normal: 35–45 mmHg) • HCO₃⁻: 8 mEq/L (Normal: 22–26 mEq/L) • Blood Glucose: 450 mg/dL (Normal: <140 mg/dL) • Plasma Ketones: Strongly positive • What is the primary acid-base disorder? The Importance of Acid-Base Balance • Human body is a complex, enzyme-driven machine • Enzymes are proteins, and proteins are sensitive to changes in hydrogen ion concentration 𝐻+ • If blood pH drops below 6.8 or rises above 7.8, cellular functions halt, and death is imminent • Normal pH of arterial blood is tightly regulated between 7.35 and 7.45 • RBCs pH is 7.2, skeletal Muscle has 6.0 pH Mechanism of Acid Production & Types of Acids • An acid is a proton (H+) donor and a base is a proton acceptor • Metabolic processes generate acid daily, as a byproduct of living • Acids dissociate to form proton and base, while the base combines with proton to form acid • Strong acid has a weak conjugate base while a weak acid has a strong base • There are two types: 1. Volatile acids and 2. Non-Volatile (Fixed) acids 1. Volatile Acids • Cellular respiration produces 𝐶𝑂2,which combines with water, catalyzed by carbonic anhydrase, and becomes Carbonic acid (𝐶𝑂2 + 𝐻2𝑂⇌𝐻2𝐶𝑂3 ⇌𝐻+ + 𝐻𝐶𝑂3 −) • W

e produce about 15,000 millimoles volatile acid daily, it is expelled as a gas by lungs 2. Non-Volatile (Fixed) Acids • These cannot be expelled out by lungs and must be excreted by kidneys • Lactic acid (from anaerobic glycolysis) • Ketoacids like acetoacetate (from lipid metabolism) • Sulfuric acid (from oxidation of sulfur-containing amino acids e.g. methionine and cysteine • Phosphoric acid (from phosphoprotein breakdown) 12 The body produces more acids than bases • Acids we take in with foods • Cellular metabolism produces CO2 • Acids produced by metabolism of lipids and proteins Volatile acid H2CO3 CO2+ H2O CO2 CO2 CO2 Fixed acid H2SO4 H3PO4 Uric acid Lactic acid Ketone body The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation • It describes relationship between pH, dissociation constant (𝑝𝐾𝑎), and concentrations of an acid and its conjugate base • When a weak acid dissociates: 𝐻𝐴⇌𝐻+ + 𝐴− • Ka: Dissociation constant: 𝐾𝑎= 𝐻+ 𝐴− 𝐻𝐴 • Re-arrange for H⁺: 𝐻+ = 𝐾𝑎 𝐻𝐴 𝐴− • Take log of both sides pH = p𝐾𝑎+ log Salt/𝑏𝑎𝑠𝑒 Acid • Where “Ka” of an Acid is “Dissociation Constant” and pKa is -log 10(ka) (how strongly an acid releases protons) The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation • As long as body maintains it

, pH is 7.4 • More acid (HA) → more H⁺ released → lower pH • More salt/base (A⁻) → H⁺ is buffered → higher pH • Thus • More base (salt) → pH increases • More acid → pH decreases Body’s Defense mechanisms against pH changes There are three lines of defence in the body: Buffers Lungs Kidneys First Line: Chemical Buffers • Human body maintains normal pH by depending on chemical buffers They act instantly, within fractions of seconds, to sponge up excess 𝐻+ Chemical Buffers • Bicarbonate Buffer: Important in extracellular fluid, handles metabolic acids • Phosphate Buffer: Crucial in intracellular fluid and inside renal tubules • Protein Buffers: Intracellular proteins and Hb in RBC • Deoxygenated Hb is a buffer for 𝐻+generated during 𝐶𝑂2 transport Bicarbonate Buffer System • This system has Sodium bicarbonate and Carbonic acid (NaHCO3- H2CO3) • It is the most predominant buffer system of extracellular fluid and plasma • Carbonic acid dissociates into hydrogen and bicarbonate ions • H2CO3 H+ + HCO3 Applying HH Equation for Bicarbonate Buffer • Plasma HCO3̄ conc. is around 24 mmol/l • Carbonic acid (H2CO3) is a solution of CO2 in water, lts conc. is given by product of pCO2 (arterial par

tial pressure of CO2 = 40 mm Hg) and solubility constant of CO2 (0.03 mmol/L/mmHg) • Thus H2CO3 conc = 40 x 0.03 = 1.2 mmol/l • Substituting the values( blood pH = 7.4; pKa for H2CO3 = 6.1; HCO3 = 24 mmol/l; H2CO3̄ =1.2 mmol/l, in HH equation (pH = p𝐾𝑎+ log Salt Acid ) • 7.4 = 6.l + log 24/1.2 • = 6.1 + log 20 • = 6.1 + 1.3 • = 7.4 /Base Bicarbonate Buffer • At a blood pH 7.4, ratio of bicarbonate to carbonic acid is 20 : 1 • The bicarbonate concentration is 20 times than carbonic acid in blood • Bicarbonate buffer system serves as an index to understand the disturbances in acid-base balance of the body \ Phosphate Buffer • It has Sodium Di Hydrogen Phosphate and DiSodium Hydrogen Phosphate (NaH2PO4- Na2HPO4), as constituents • H2PO4 acts as a weak acid that donates H+ when fluid becomes too basic • HPO4² : Acts as a weak base that accepts H+ when fluid becomes too acidic • lt is intracellular buffer with low conc., so less important in plasma • Its pKa is 6.8 Protein Buffer • Constituents of this buffer are Plasma proteins and Hb • Buffering capacity of proteins is dependent on pKa of ionizable groups of amino acids • Imidazole group of histidine (pKa = 6.7), is most effective con

tributor of protein buffers Protein Buffer • Plasma proteins account for about 2% of total buffering capacity of plasma • Hb buffers fixed acids, and participates in transport of O2 and CO2 • When pH increases COOH group in Amino acid acts as weak acid and releases H+ • When pH decreases NH3 group acts as base and accepts H+ Second Line: Respiratory Regulation (Minutes to Hours) • Lungs regulate Carbonic Acid via 𝐶𝑂2 • If blood becomes acidic (pH drops), chemoreceptors in medulla are stimulated • Patient hyperventilates and exhales 𝐶𝑂2, acid levels drop, pH goes back, up • H2CO3 Carbonic Anhydrase CO2+H2O Second Line: Respiratory Regulation (Minutes to Hours) • If blood becomes alkaline, respiration depresses, retaining 𝐶𝑂2 to generate acid • Respiratory control of pH is short termed Third Line: Renal Regulation (Hours to Days) • Reabsorption of Bicarbonate: • Kidneys act slowly but give permanent solution and regulate HCO3 ̄ • Kidneys reabsorb almost 100% of 𝐻𝐶𝑂3 −, filtered at glomerulus • Kidneys excrete 𝐻+buffered by phosphate (𝑁𝑎2𝐻𝑃𝑂4 becomes 𝑁𝑎𝐻2𝑃𝑂4) Renal Regulation: Excretion of H+ (proximal convoluted tubules) • H+ excretion is coupled with regeneration of HCO3 • Carbonic

anhydrase catalyzes production of H2CO3 from CO2 and H2O in renal tubular cell • H2CO3 then dissociates to H+ and HCO3 • H+ ions are secreted into tubular lumen in exchange for Na+ • Na+ in association with HCO3 is reabsorbed into blood • H+ combines with a non-carbonate base and is excreted in urine Renal Regulation: Excretion of Titrable acid • It is a measure of acid excreted into urine by kidney • It is estimated by titrating urine back to normal pH 7.4 • (No of ml of N/10 NaOH required to titrate 1 liter of urine to pH 7.4) • H + is secreted into tubular lumen in exchange for Na+, obtained from base, Na2HPO4 • Na combines with H+ to produce acid,NaH2PO4 (major quantity of titratable acid in urine is in this form) Third Line: Renal Regulation (Hours to Days) Excretion of Ammonium (𝑁𝐻4 +): • Glutamine is deaminated in kidney to produce ammonia (𝑁𝐻3) • 𝑁𝐻3diffuses into urine, binds 𝐻+ to become 𝑁𝐻4 + and is excreted Anion Gap & Its Biochemical Significance • Principle of electroneutrality states that total cations must equal total anions in the blood We measure Na+ , Cl−and HCO3 − • Formula: AnionGap = Na+ −(Cl−+ HCO3 −) • Normal Value: 8 to 16 mEq/L (Average 12 mEq/L) • What mak

es up this 'gap'? It represents unmeasured anions—mostly albumin, phosphates, and sulfates Biochemical Significance of Anion Gap • If a patient has metabolic acidosis, we look at Anion gap • High Anion Gap Acidosis: >16 • This means a new, abnormal acid has entered the blood, consumed the bicarbonate, and left its own unmeasured anion behind e.g. Methanol, Diabetic Ketoacidosis (acetoacetate/beta-hydroxybutyrate), Lactic acidosis, Salicylates Normal Anion Gap (Hyperchloremic) Acidosis: • Bicarbonate is lost from the body (e.g., severe diarrhea), and kidneys hold onto Chloride to compensate • The gap stays normal, but the patient is acidic Interpretation of Arterial Blood Gases (ABGs) When we draw an ABG, we look at three main values: • pH: Normal 7.35 - 7.45 • Respiratory parameter: pCO2 Normal 35 - 45 mmHg • Metabolic parameter: HCO3 − Normal 22 - 26 mEq/L Interpretation of Arterial Blood Gases (ABGs) • If it's a Respiratory issue, pH and pCO2move in opposite directions e.g. pH goes down, pCO2 goes up = Respiratory Acidosis, like in COPD • If it's a Metabolic issue, pH and HCO3 −move in same direction e.g. pH goes down, HCO3 −goes down = Metabolic Acidosis, e.g. Diabetic Ketoacido

y tract Splanchnic mesoderm Smooth muscle Splanchnic mesoderm Connective tissue Splanchnic mesoderm Blood vessels Mesoderm DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 8 Endoderm forms the epithelial lining; splanchnic mesoderm forms the supporting tissues. A groove appears on the ventral wall of the foregut called the: • Laryngotracheal groove This groove evaginates to form the: • Laryngotracheal diverticulum / respiratory diverticulum The distal end enlarges to form the lung bud. evelops as the tracheoesophageal folds fuse. The laryngeal opening initially becomes narrowed because of epithelial proliferation. A temporary laryngeal epithelial occlusion occurs. DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 17 Later: Recanalization of the larynx → formation of laryngeal ventricles and vocal folds Clinical correlation: Failure of recanalization may cause: • Laryngeal atresia • Laryngeal stenosis DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 18 DEVELOPMENT OF TRACHEA The distal part of the laryngotracheal tube develops into the: Trachea Its epithelial lining is derived from endoderm. The trachea subsequently divides into the: Right main bronchus Left main bronchus DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 20 DEVELOPMENT OF BRONCHIAL TREE The distal end of the respiratory diverticulum develops into two primary

bronchial buds: Right and left primary bronchial buds • These give rise to the main bronchi. Secondary Bronchial Buds • The primary bronchi form secondary bronchial buds corresponding to the pulmonary lobes. DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 21 Right lung 3 secondary bronchial buds → 3 lobes: • Superior • Middle • Inferior Left lung 2 secondary bronchial buds → 2 lobes: • Superior • Inferior DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 22 TERTIARY BRONCHIAL BUDS Secondary bronchi further divide into: Tertiary / segmental bronchi These form the bronchopulmonary segments. DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 24 Primary bronchus ↓ Secondary bronchi ↓ Tertiary bronchi ↓ Smaller bronchi ↓ Bronchioles ↓ Terminal bronchioles ↓ Respiratory bronchioles ↓ Alveolar ducts ↓ Alveolar sacs ↓ Alveoli •By 24 weeks, about 17 orders of branches have formed and respiratory bronchioles have developed. •An additional seven orders of airways develop after birth. As the lungs develop they acquire a layer of visceral pleura from splanchnic mesenchyme. The thoracic body wall becomes lined by a layer of parietal pleura derived from the somatic mesoderm. DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 25 DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 26 DEVELOPMENT OF LUNGS The developing lungs grow into the: Pericardioperitoneal c

anals These canals are initially located on either side of the foregut. Later, the developing lungs expand into the thoracic cavity. The pleural cavities develop around the lungs. Pleural development The lung becomes covered by: Visceral pleura – derived from splanchnic mesoderm Parietal pleura – derived from somatic mesoderm DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 28 IMPORTANT DISTINCTION Pleura Origin Visceral pleura Parietal pleura DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 29 IMPORTANT DISTINCTION Pleura Origin Visceral pleura Splanchnic mesoderm Parietal pleura Somatic mesoderm DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 30 STAGES OF LUNG DEVELOPMENT (MATURATION OF THE LUNGS) The maturation of the lungs is classically divided into five stages. • 1. Embryonic stage: Weeks 4–7 • 2. Pseudoglandular stage: Weeks 5–17 • 3. Canalicular Stage: Weeks 16–25 • 4. Saccular Stage: Weeks 24–birth • 5. Alveolar Stage: Late fetal period → childhood DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 33 1. EMBRYONIC STAGE Weeks 4–7 Respiratory diverticulum forms Trachea develops Primary bronchi form Secondary bronchial buds develop DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 34 2. PSEUDOGLANDULAR STAGE Weeks 5–17 The lungs have a gland-like appearance. Major events: Branching of bronchi Formation of terminal bronchioles Importa

nt: No respiratory bronchioles or alveoli are present. Therefore, a fetus born during this stage cannot survive because effective gas exchange is impossible. DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 35 3. CANALICULAR STAGE Weeks 16–25 Important changes: Terminal bronchioles divide into respiratory bronchioles. Respiratory bronchioles form alveolar ducts. Vascularity increases markedly. SACCULAR STAGE Weeks 24–birth Terminal sacs develop. These are also called: Primitive alveolar sacs Major changes: • Terminal sacs increase in number. • Capillaries come into close contact with respiratory epithelium. • Blood-air barrier becomes thinner. DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 40 5. ALVEOLAR STAGE Late fetal period → childhood Mature alveoli continue to develop. At birth, only a fraction of the adult number of alveoli are

present. The number of alveoli increases substantially during: Postnatal life, particularly during early childhood. Important examination point: Alveolar development continues after birth. ALVEOLAR PERIOD (32 WEEKS – 8 YEARS) DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 41 DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 42 SURFACTANT Surfactant is produced by: Type II pneumocytes It is a phospholipid-rich substance that: • Reduces surface tension • Prevents alveolar collapse • Facilitates lung expansion Production increases significantly during the later fetal period. chunks: The Pericardium • External covering of the heart • Fibro-serous in nature • Outer, tough, fibrous layer is fibrous pericardium • Inner layer is serous pericardium: • Has two layers; outwards parietal and inner visceral (epicardium) Fibrous Pericardium • Inferiorly continuous with the central tendon of the diaphragm • As the pericardiophrenic ligament • Superiorly continuous with the tunica adventitia of great vessels • Anteriorly attached via the sternopericardial ligament to the sternum • Bound posteriorly via loose connective tissue Visceral Pericardium (Epicardium) • Space between the parietal and visceral pericardium is called the pericardial cavity • Epicardium extends upwards to cover the great vessels • Continuous with parietal layer at: • Exit point of aorta and pulmonary trunk • Entry point of SVC, IVC, and pulmonary veins Pericardial Sinuses • Formed by folds/reflections of the serous pericardium • Two major sinuses: • Transverse pericardial sinus • Between major blood vessels to and from the heart • Oblique pericardial sinus • J shaped sinus between pulmonary veins and SVC Transverse Pericardial Sinus • Passage between major vessels of the heart • Anterior to the SVC • P

osterior to the aorta and the pulmonary trunk • Separates arterial outflow from venous inflow • Of major clinical significance during CABG (coronary arterial bypass grafting) • Allows surgeons space to clamp aorta and pulmonary trunk Nerve and Blood Supply • The pericardium is innervated by: • The phrenic nerve (referred shoulder pain during MI) • Vagus nerve • Sympathetic trunk • Arterial supply comes from: • Pericardiophrenic artery; branch of the internal thoracic artery • Musculophrenic artery; internal thoracic • Bronchial and phrenic branches; internal thoracic Pericarditis • Inflammation of the pericardium • Most commonly secondary to viral infections • HIV • COVID • Influenza • Young/middle aged patient with sharp, stabbing pain and history of throat infection 2 weeks ago • Pain radiates to the back and shoulder • Pericardial rub (squeaky sound) on auscultation Pericardial Effusion • Persistent inflammation can result in pericardial effusion • Collection of fluid in pericardial cavity • Can result in difficulty in breathing • Specifically orthopnea (SOB on lying down) • Non-inflammatory causes include CHF Cardiac Tamponade • EMERGENCY CONDITION • Excessive blood/fluid aroun
d the heart • Compresses the heart • Patient presents with Beck’s Triad: • Raised JVP/Distended veins • Muffled heart sounds • Low blood pressure • Treatment requires pericardiocentesis

chunks: External Anatomy of the Heart Gross Features and Sulci The Heart • Blood pump of the body • Lies in the middle mediastinum • Between T5-T8; posterior to the body of the sternum • Inclined more towards the left side of the chest • 5 surfaces; 4 borders Surfaces of the Heart • Anterior – Sternocostal (right ventricle) • Posterior – Base of the heart (left atrium) • Inferior – Diaphragmatic (ventricles) • Right pulmonary – Right atrium • Left pulmonary – Left ventricle Borders of the Heart • Right border – right atrium • Inferior border – left and right ventricles • Left border – left ventricle and atrium • Superior border – right and left atrium with great vessels Points of Importance • The apex is located in the 5th intercostal space, in the midclavicular line • The base faces vertebral bodies T6-T9 • Right border spans between the IVC and SVC • Superior border forms the inferior border of the transverse pericardial sinus Layers of the Heart • Epicardium • Visceral pericardium – serous layer • Pericardium • Helical muscular layer • Endocardium • Thin, simple squamous layer Myocardium and Epicardium • The myocardium is the contractile, muscular layer of the heart • Muscle fibers are

arranged in a helical pattern • The Epicardium is the outer, serous part of the heart • Formed by the visceral pericardium • Layer between the epicardium and the myocardium is called the subepicardial layer Endocardium • Simple squamous layer • Plays a role in perfusion and regulation heart contractions • The subendocardial layer is a thin layer of connective tissue • Lies between endocardium and myocardium • Houses the Purkinje fibers, which regulate myocardial contractions • Ischemic damage to this layer can result in arrythmias Sulci of the Heart • Distinct from the pericardial sulci • Three major sulci: • Coronary sulcus • Anterior interventricular sulcus • Posterior interventricular sulcus Sulci of the Heart • The coronary sulcus: • Wraps around the heart • Separates atria from ventricles • Contains: • Right coronary artery • Left circumflex artery • Coronary sinus Sulci of the Heart • Anterior interventricular sulcus: • On anterior surface of the heart • Between left and right ventricles • Contains: • Left Anterior Descending (LAD) artery – also called anterior interventricular artery • Great cardiac vein • Posterior interventricular sulcus: • Posterior surface, between ventr
icles • Contains: • Posterior interventricular artery • Middle cardiac vein

chunks: Internal Features of the Heart The Chambers The Right Atrium • Receives blood from the SVC and IVC • Pumps blood to the right ventricle (via the tricuspid valve) • Forms the right border of the heart • Overlying the right atrium is a pouch called the right auricle • Muscular pouch • Increases atrial capacity and receives overflow Right Atrium • The atria has two embryologically distinct parts: • The sinus venarum • Smooth, thin, posterior part • SVC (3rd costal cartilage), IVC (5th costal cartilage), and coronary sinus drainage site • The atrium proper • Rough, muscular, anterior part • Comprised of pectinate muscles Right Atrium • Smooth and rough parts are divided by • The sulcus terminalis externally • The crista terminalis internally • Interatrial septum is marked by the fossa ovalis • Remnant of the embryological foramen ovale Right Ventricle • Receives blood from the right atrium • Pumps blood to the pulmonary artery (via the pulmonary valve) • Cone-shaped in appearance • Apical part leads into the pulmonary artery • Referred to as the conus arteriosus (smooth part of the RV) • Embryologically derived from the bulbus cordis • Internal surface has rough muscular projections ca

lled trabeculae carneae • Supraventricular crest separates the smooth and rough parts Right Ventricle • The trabeculae carneae can be classified into three components: • Ridges – formed by irregular muscular shapes and protrusions • Bridges – muscular rings that span the ventricle • Example is the moderator band – carries part of the right AV bundle • Papillae – muscular fingers that attach to the tricuspid valve • Anterior • Posterior • Septal Left Atrium • Receives blood from the four pulmonary veins • Pumps blood to the left ventricle (via the mitral valve) • Externally, the left auricle covers the root of the pulmonary trunk • Remnant of the primordial atrium • Similar function as the right auricle • Trabeculated internal surface • Common site for clot formation during atrial fibrillation Left Atrium • Semilunar depression is found on the interatrial septum • Floor of the fossa ovalis • Walls are slightly thicker than those of the right atrium • Two internal parts: • A smooth inflow tract that receives blood from the pulmonary veins • A trabeculated outflow tract (the left auricle is a part of this) Left Ventricle • Thickest walls of any of the chambers (3x of the right ventric

le’s walls) • Walls covered with trabeculae carneae • Long conical cavity • Larger anterior and posterior papillary muscles • A smooth, non-muscular outflow tract • Called the aortic vestibule • Outflow guarded by the aortic valve

subject: Anatomy
chunks: Valves of the Heart • Divided into two categories: • Atrioventricular • Tricuspid • Mitral/Bicuspid • Semilunar • Aortic • Pulmonary Atrioventricular Valves • Between atria and ventricles • Close during ventricular contraction • Produce S1 Heart Sound (the first “lub”) • Two valves: • Tricuspid • Mitral/Bicuspid • Attached to papillary muscles via chordae tendineae Atrioventricular Valves • Tricuspid valve: • Located between right atrium and ventricle • Three cusps; anterior, posterior, septal • Mitral valve: • Located between left atrium and ventricle • Two cusps; anterior, posterior Semilunar Valves • Both valves have three cusps • Between ventricles and outflow vessels • Close during ventricular relaxation • Produce S2 heart sound (the second “dub”) • Both valves form sinuses with their respective outflow vessels

chunks: Vasculature of the Heart The Coronary Vessels The Arterial Supply of the Heart • The myocardium and epicardium are supplied by the coronary arteries • Two coronary arteries: RCA and LCA • Originate within the right and left aortic sinuses • Pass around opposite sides of the pulmonary trunk • Most significant branches of the heart originate from the RCA and LCA The Right Coronary Artery • Originates in the right aortic sinus • Gives off a sino-atrial nodal branch near its origin • Passes to the right of the pulmonary trunk • Descends into the coronary sulcus • Gives off the right marginal branch • Turns left to the posterior heart (still in coronary sulcus) • Reaches the posterior crux of the heart • Point at which AV and coronary sulci meet • Gives off AV nodal branch The Right Coronary Artery • In 67% of patients, gives rise to the posterior interventricular artery • Descends into the posterior IV groove • Supplies both ventricles • Supplies IV septum via interventricular septal branches • Dominance of coronary artery is dependent on which CA gives off the posterior interventricular/posterior descending artery • RCA terminates as the left ventricular branch in the coronary sulcus

The Right Coronary Artery • The RCA supplies: • Right atrium • SA node (in 60% of patients) • Diaphragmatic part of the left ventricle • AV node (in 80% of patients) • Most of the right ventricle The Left Coronary Artery • Originates in the left aortic sinus • Passes between the left auricle and the left part of the pulmonary trunk • Runs in the coronary sulcus • At the superior end of the IV groove, divides into: • The LEFT ANTERIOR DESCENDING (LAD) branch • Circumflex branch of the LCA • LAD descends into anterior IV groove, reaches apex • Anastomoses with posterior IV branch of RCA The Left Coronary Artery • Circumflex branch of LCA travels backwards to posterior heart • Gives off left marginal branch • LCA terminates in coronary sulcus • Often just before reaching the crux of the heart • Supplies: • Left atrium • Most of left ventricle • Part of the right ventricle • Most of the IVS • The SA node (in 40% of patients) Coronary Arterial Dominance • Determined by which coronary artery forms the POSTERIOR DESCENDING ARTERY • 85% of hearts are right-dominant • The rest are either left-dominant or co-dominant • Dominance helps determine commonly involved vessels in MI • Despite the R

CA being commonly dominant the LCA supplies: • Majority of the ventricular myocardium • 2/3rd of the IVS Myocardial Infarction • Ischemic damage to the heart; informally labelled a heart attack • Most common cause is atherosclerosis • Most common artery involved is the LAD (anterior wall MI) • Patient typically presents with central chest pain, often radiating towards the left shoulder and back (phrenic nerve) Venous Drainage of the Heart • Drainage mainly carried out via the coronary sinus • Located on the posterior coronary sulcus • Receives venous drainage from: • Great cardiac vein – drains areas supplied by the LCA • Middle cardiac vein – drains areas supplied by the RCA • Small cardiac vein – drains areas supplied by the RCA Great Cardiac Vein • Main tributary of the coronary sinus • Begins as the anterior interventricular vein • Near apex of the heart • Ascends with the LAD artery • Turns left at coronary sulcus • Runs to the left of the heart with the left circumflex artery • Drains parts of the heart supplied by the LCA Middle & Small Cardiac Veins • Middle accompanies the posterior interventricular vein • Small accompanies the right marginal branch of the RCA • Remnant of

the left SVC is found in post-embryonic life: • Called the oblique vein of Marshal/left atrium • Merges with great cardiac vein to form coronary sinus • The smallest cardiac veins do not drain via the coronary sinus • Open directly into the right atrium • Veins is a misnomer; these are valveless structures

chunks: Sinoatrial Node • Pacemaker of the heart • Initiates and regulates heart contractions • Supplied by SA nodal branch (typically derived from RCA) • Location: • Anterolaterally to right atrium and SVC junction • Deep to the epicardium • Near superior end of sulcus terminalis Atrioventricular Node • Located in the posteroinferior region of the interatrial septum • Near opening of the coronary sinus • Transmits signals from the SA node to the ventricles via the AV bundle • AV bundle passes inferiorly through the fibrous skeleton of the heart Atrioventricular Bundle • The AV bundle reaches the junction of the membranous and muscular parts of the IVS • Divides into two smaller bundles: • The Right AV bundle • The Left AV bundle • These extend on either side of the IVS and divide into Purkinje fibers Purkinje Fibers • Right fibers stimulate: • IVS muscles (and posterior + septal papillary muscles indirectly) • Anterior papillary muscles (via moderator band) • Wall of the right ventricle • Left fibers stimulate: • Divides into six smaller tracts • Stimulate the IVS • Anterior and posterior papillary muscles • Wall of the left ventricle Arrhythmia • Irregularities in the conduction of the h
eart • Most common causes include: • Electrolyte abnormalities (hyperkalemia, hypokalemia) • Coronary vessel disease/Hx of MI • Chronic HTN • Excessive usage of caffeine

chunks: Lipids Digestion & Absorption Humaira Sharif Department of Biochemistry Consumption of Dietary Lipid • An adult man ingest about 60 – 100 gm of fat/day. • TAG Constitute more than 90%. The rest is made up of phospholipid, cholesterol, cholesterol ester and FFA. • Current recommendation are – Maximum 30% of energy intake as fat. • 10% each from SFA, MUFA & PUFA. Intake of cholesterol less than 300 mg/day. • The recommendations are aimed primarily to influence cholesterol metabolism. Digestion, Absorption, Secretion and Utilization of Dietary Lipids PROCESSING OF DIETARY LIPIDS IN STOMACH: Lipid digestion begins in mouth and then in stomach by LINGUAL LIPASE --- acid stable Primary target ----- fatty acids of short or medium chain length ( milk fat ). GASTRIC LIPASE ----- acid stable. Both enzymes ---- optimum pH 4 to 6. Particularly important in neonates and in patients with pancreatic insufficiency. Digestion, Absorption, Secretion and Utilization of Dietary Lipids Digestion, Absorption, Secretion and Utilization of Dietary Lipids Digestion, Absorption, Secretion and Utilization of Dietary Lipids Digestion, Absorption, Secretion and Utilization of Dietary Lipids Hormonal control of

lipid digestion CHOLECYSTOKININ Site of release: Blood in response to lipids and partially digested proteins entering small intestines. Actions: • Gall bladder: contraction & release of bile. • Pancreatic exocrine cells : release of digestive enzymes SECRETIN Site of release: Blood from other intestinal cells. -in response to low pH of chyme Actions: release of a watery solution by pancreas and liver, high in bicarbonate -appropriate pH for action of pancreatic enzymes. Hormonal control of lipid digestion Question? Which hormone primarily stimulates gallbladder contraction and pancreatic enzyme secretion in response to fatty acids and amino acids in the duodenum? A) Secretin B) Gastrin C) Cholecystokinin (CCK) D) Motilin CK is released from I cells of the duodenal mucosa in response to fatty acids and amino acids. It causes gallbladder contraction (bile release) and stimulates pancreatic acinar cells to secrete digestive enzymes, including lipase. Digestion, Absorption, Secretion and Utilization of Dietary Lipids PROCESSING OF DIETARY LIPIDS: Pancreatic Lipase: • Secreted by the acinar cells of the exocrine pancreas as an active enzyme (unlike trypsinogen, it does not require acti

vation by cleavage). • Released into the duodenum via the pancreatic duct in response to CCK (stimulates acinar secretion) and secretin (stimulates bicarbonate-rich fluid, providing the alkaline medium). • Requires colipase (activated from procolipase by trypsin) to remain anchored to the fat droplet surface in the presence of bile salts. Digestion, Absorption, Secretion and Utilization of Dietary Lipids PROCESSING OF DIETARY LIPIDS: Pancreatic Lipase: Hydrolyzes triglycerides at the sn-1 and sn-3 positions, producing: • 2 free fatty acids • 2-monoacylglycerol (2-MAG) Acts at the oil-water interface of emulsified fat droplets (emulsification by bile salts increases surface area for lipase action). The products (fatty acids + 2-MAG) combine with bile salts to form micelles, which transport them to the intestinal brush border for absorption. Digestion, Absorption, Secretion and Utilization of Dietary Lipids Pathology: Chronic pancreatitis (commonly from alcoholism) damages acinar cells, reducing pancreatic lipase, colipase, and bicarbonate secretion. This impairs triglyceride hydrolysis, causing undigested fat to pass into stool — steatorrhea. Floating, greasy, foul-smelling stools a

re classic for fat malabsorption. Hormonal control of lipid digestion Pathology: In cystic fibrosis, thick viscous secretions block pancreatic ducts, preventing pancreatic enzymes (lipase, colipase, proteases) from reaching the duodenum, causing exocrine pancreatic insufficiency and steatorrhea, along with fat- soluble vitamin deficiencies (A, D, E, K). Digestion, Absorption, Secretion and Utilization of Dietary Lipids Question? A 6-month-old infant presents with failure to thrive, distended abdomen, and pale, bulky stools. Sweat chloride test is positive, confirming cystic fibrosis. Which enzyme deficiency best explains the child's steatorrhea? A) Salivary lipase deficiency B) Pancreatic lipase deficiency due to thick mucus obstructing pancreatic ducts C) Lingual lipase deficiency D) Intestinal enterokinase deficiency Hormonal control of lipid digestion Question? A 45-year-old man presents with bulky, greasy, foul-smelling stools that float on water and are difficult to flush. He has a history of chronic alcoholism and recurrent abdominal pain. Stool fat estimation shows fat content >7 g/day. Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism for his symptoms? A) Incre

ased bile salt synthesis B) Deficiency of pancreatic lipase due to chronic pancreatitis C) Excess secretion of cholecystokinin D) Overactivity of intestinal brush border enzymes Emulsification of lipids in small intestine Emulsification increases the surface area of the hydrophobic fat droplets so that digestive enzymes can act effectively. • Site: duodenum • Done by: - peristalsis---- mechanical mixing - Bile salts ---- detergent properties as they decrease the surface tension and cause fat emulsification. Most common: Glycocholate Emulsification of lipids in small intestine Pathology: Reduced bile salt delivery (post-cholecystectomy bile flow dysregulation) impairs micelle formation, leading to fat malabsorption even if lipase activity is normal. Emulsification of lipids in small intestine Colipase: secreted as procolipase and activated by trypsin, binds both lipase and the lipid interface, anchoring lipase in place so it can effectively hydrolyze triglycerides at the sn-1 and sn-3 positions into 2-monoglycerides and free fatty acids. Anchors pancreatic lipase to the lipid-water interface, preventing its displacement by bile salts Emulsification of lipids in small intestine Quest

ion? Colipase is essential for efficient fat digestion because it: A) Directly hydrolyzes triglycerides into monoglycerides and fatty acids B) Anchors pancreatic lipase to the lipid-water interface, preventing its displacement by bile salts C) Forms micelles with fatty acids for intestinal absorption D) Converts cholesterol to bile acids Emulsification of lipids in small intestine Question? A patient who underwent cholecystectomy years ago now complains of intermittent diarrhea and fatty stools after high-fat meals. Investigations reveal reduced bile salt concentration reaching the duodenum. Which step in lipid digestion is primarily impaired in this patient? A) Emulsification and micelle formation B) Hydrolysis of triglycerides by lipase C) Chylomicron synthesis in enterocytes D) Activation of pancreatic lipase by colipase Digestion, Absorption, Secretion and Utilization of Dietary Lipids Micelles are composed of FA, MAGs & Bile salts 1 2 3 4 ① Large fat globules are emulsified (physically broken up into smaller fat droplets) by bile salts in the duodenum. ② Digestion of fat by the pancreatic enzyme lipase yields free fatty acids and monoglycerides. These then associate with bile

salts to form micelles which "ferry" them to the intestinal mucosa. ③ Fatty acids and monoglycerides leave micelles and diffuse into epithelial cells. There they are recombined and packaged with other lipoid substances and proteins to form chylomicrons. ④ Chylomicrons are extruded from the epithelial cells by exocytosis. The chylomicrons enter lacteals. They are carried away from the intestine by lymph. Digestion Of Lipids In Small Instestine Pancreatic enzymes are responsible to degrade: Phospholipids, Cholesteryl esters & TAG 1- Degradation of TAG:- Pancreatic Lipase ---- removes fatty acids at carbon 1 and 3 and forms 2-monoacylglycerol and free fatty acids. Digestion Of Lipids In Small Intestine 2- Degradation of cholesteryl esters:- Cholesteryl estrase produces cholesterol and free fatty acids. Activity is increased in presence of Bile salts. Degradation of dietary lipids by Pancreatic enzymes 3- Degradation of Phospholipids :- Phospholipase A2 in proenzyme form, activated by Trypsin, requires bile salts for activity. Removes one fatty acid from carbon 2 of a phospholipid lysophospholipid. Lysophospholipase removes fatty acid at carbon 1 and forms glycerylphosphoryl base t

hat is excreted, degraded or absorbed. Degradation of dietary lipids by Pancreatic enzymes Lipid Malabsorption Obstruction to transportation phase in lacteals Steatorrhea ----- • Increased lipid and fat soluble vitamin excretion in feces. • Loss of lipid in feces >6g/day • Caused by defects in lipid digestion and/or lipid absorption Obstruction due to cholesterol stones Obstruction to transportation phase in lacteals Chyluria ------ • Patients excrete milky urine • Caused by abnormal connection between urinary tract & lymphatic drainage system of intestine, forming chylous fistula ( leakage of lymphatic fluid from the lymphatic vessels). Chylothorax----- • Accumulation of lymph in pleural cavity giving milky pleural effusion. • An abnormal connection between pleural space & lymphatic drainage of small intestine results in accumulation of lymph in pleural cavity giving milky pleural effusion. Recommendation in fat malabsorption syndrome

subject: Biochemistry
chunks: CARDIAC BIOMARKERS Biochemical basis, clinical significance & interpretation Dr Hafsa Fayyaz | MBBS | Dept. of Biochemistry, UMDC 01 What is released after myocardial injury? 02 Why does the biomarker matter? 03 How do we interpret the result? 1 LEARNING OBJECTIVES By the end of this lecture, students should be able to: 1. Outline the major cardiac biomarkers and their biochemical basis. 2. Discuss the importance of cardiac biomarkers in cardiovascular disease. 3. Interpret laboratory investigation reports in relevant clinical conditions. 4. Correlate biomarker patterns with clinical conditions and timing. 2 Clinical Opening A patient presents with severe central chest pain. Clinical picture Chest pain Sweating Shortness of breath Investigation ECG : myocardial ischemia High-sensitivity cardiac troponin Question Why should a protein inside cardiac cells appear in blood? Myocardial injury → cellular disruption → biomarker release → bloodstream → measurable result 3 What Are Cardiac Biomarkers? Measurable substances in blood whose concentration changes with myocardial injury or cardiac stress. Some reflect myocardial cell injury; others reflect cardiac wall stress. Interpretation dep

ends on clinical context, timing and the assay-specific reference limit. Myocardial injury Troponin I/T CK-MB Myoglobin Cardiac stress BNP NT-proBNP Historical / non-specific LDH AST 4 Why Do Biomarkers Appear in Blood? Normal state: intracellular cardiac proteins remain within myocardial cells. Myocardial injury disrupts cells and can cause release of intracellular proteins. Proteins move from damaged myocardium into interstitial fluid and then the bloodstream. Blood concentration rises and can be detected by laboratory testing. 5 Classification of Cardiac Biomarkers Myocardial injury CARDIAC TROPONIN I/T CK-MB Myoglobin Cardiac stress BNP NT-proBNP Reflect myocardial wall stress Historical / non-specific LDH AST Largely replaced by troponin for acute MI assessment 6 Myoglobin An early, but non-specific, marker of muscle injury Small, heme-containing globular protein. Present in skeletal and cardiac muscle. Binds and stores oxygen within muscle cells. Rises early after muscle injury but cannot reliably distinguish cardiac from skeletal muscle injury. Approximate kinetics Myoglobin Onset ~1–2 h Peak ~4–12 h Returns toward baseline ~24 h 7 Causes of Increased Myoglobin Cardiac Acute

myocardial injury Skeletal muscle Trauma Rhabdomyolysis Muscular dystrophy Inflammatory myopathies Severe exercise Other Renal failure Shock Severe tissue injury 8 Exam shortcut Myoglobin = Early but non-specific Creatine Kinase (CK / CPK) Biochemical reaction Creatine + ATP ⇌ Phosphocreatine + ADP + H⁺ CK catalyzes reversible high-energy phosphate transfer. Why important? Phosphocreatine provides a rapidly available high-energy phosphate reserve in tissues with high energy demand. 9 CK is a dimer composed of M (muscle) and B (brain) subunits. CK Isoenzymes Isoenzyme Composition Major location CK-MM M + M Skeletal muscle CK-MB M + B Cardiac muscle; also skeletal muscle CK-BB B + B Brain and other tissues Exam point CK-MB is the CK isoenzyme historically associated most closely with myocardial injury. 10 CK-MB May increase after acute myocardial injury. Also rises with myocarditis, cardiac trauma, cardiac surgery, endomyocardial biopsy and cardioversion/defibrillation. Less specific than cardiac troponin. Feature CK-MB Onset ~4–6 h Peak ~24 h Returns toward baseline ~2–3 days Modern practice Cardiac troponin is preferred over CK-MB for routine diagnosis of acute myocardial injury w

hen troponin is available. 11 Troponin The principal biomarker of myocardial injury TnC Troponin C Binds calcium. TnI Troponin I Regulates/inhibits actin–myosin interaction. TnT Troponin T Anchors the troponin complex to tropomyosin. 12 Cardiac Troponin I and T Clinically measured cardiac isoforms are cTnI and cTnT. Cardiac troponins are highly sensitive and specific indicators of myocardial injury. High-sensitivity assays detect very low concentrations; saying troponin is simply 'absent' in all healthy people is an oversimplification. The assay-specific 99th percentile upper reference limit is central to interpretation. 13 Troponin Elevation: What Does It Mean? Troponin ↑ Myocardial injury This is the biochemical signal. Not automatically MI Troponin elevation can occur in many cardiac and systemic conditions. For MI Acute myocardial injury + evidence of acute myocardial ischemia. 14 Causes of Elevated Troponin Cardiac Acute MI Myocarditis Cardiomyopathy Heart failure Tachyarrhythmias Systemic / other Sepsis Pulmonary embolism Stroke Severe systemic illness Chronic kidney disease Key message Troponin is a marker of myocardial injury. Always correlate with symptoms, ECG and serial

measurements. 15 Troponin Kinetics Feature Approximate timing Rise ~3–6 h* Peak ~12–24 h Remains elevated ~7–14 days Why does it matter? Troponin stays elevated much longer than CK-MB. *Timing varies with assay, sampling time and extent of injury. 16 Why Serial Troponin? Acute myocardial injury often produces a change in biomarker concentration over time. Serial samples allow clinicians to identify a rise and/or fall pattern. One measurement gives a concentration; serial measurements add information about change over time. Interpret serial results with symptoms, ECG and the laboratory's reference limit. Concept: One result = concentration, Serial results = concentration + change over time Sample 1 → Sample 2 → Sample 3 = concentration + change over time 17 High-Sensitivity Cardiac Troponin What is hs-cTn? An assay designed to measure very low concentrations of cardiac troponin. 99th percentile The assay-specific upper reference limit used as the key decision limit for myocardial injury. Remember Reference limits are assay/laboratory-specific and may be sex-specific. 18 Always interpret the value using the laboratory's reported reference interval. Sample 1 → Sample 2 → Sample 3 = co

ncentration + change over time Troponin ≠ Myocardial Infarction MYOCARDIAL INJURY: cardiac troponin above the assay-specific 99th percentile. MYOCARDIAL INFARCTION: acute myocardial injury PLUS evidence of acute myocardial ischemia. Evidence of ischemia may include ischemic symptoms, new ischemic ECG changes, imaging evidence or coronary thrombus. Exam distinction Troponin = myocardial injury marker | MI = myocardial injury + ischemia 19 Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH) Reaction Pyruvate + NADH + H⁺ ⇌ Lactate + NAD⁺ Why not specific? LDH is widely distributed in many tissues. Historically used in myocardial infarction assessment. Today it is a non-specific, historical biomarker and is not a primary test for acute MI when troponin is available. 20 LDH Isoenzymes & the 'LDH Flip' Isoenzyme Composition LDH-1 H₄ LDH-2 H₃M LDH-3 H₂M₂ LDH-4 HM₃ LDH-5 M₄ Normal serum pattern LDH-2 > LDH-1 Historical MI finding LDH-1 > LDH-2 This reversal was called the 'LDH flip'. 21 LDH Kinetics & Other Causes Feature Approximate timing Onset ~6–12 h Peak ~24–48 h Duration ~6–8 days Other causes of ↑ LDH Hemolysis Liver/tissue injury Malignancy Muscle injury Infection/inflammation Modern practice - LDH is not

a primary biomarker for acute MI when cardiac troponin is available. 22 AST — A Historical Cardiac Biomarker Biochemical reaction Aspartate + α-ketoglutarate ⇌ Oxaloacetate + Glutamate AST was historically used in myocardial infarction assessment. It is highly non-specific and has largely been replaced by cardiac troponins. 23 BNP — Cardiac Wall Stress Biomarker BNP is produced predominantly by ventricular myocardium in response to increased myocardial wall stress. Volume or pressure overload can increase ventricular stretch and stimulate BNP release. BNP/NT-proBNP are useful in the evaluation of suspected heart failure. Remember BNP reflects cardiac wall stress — it is not a direct measurement of ventricular function. 24 BNP vs NT-proBNP proBNP Ventricular stretch ↓ proBNP release ↓ BNP + NT-proBNP The products BNP → biologically active peptide NT-proBNP → inactive cleavage fragment Both can be measured clinically. 25 The Big Comparison Biomarker Main significance Specificity Approx. duration Myoglobin Early muscle injury Low ~24 h CK-MB Myocardial injury; older/selected use Moderate 2–3 days cTnI / cTnT Myocardial injury High 7–14 days BNP / NT-proBNP Cardiac wall stress — Varia

ble LDH Historical tissue injury marker Low 6–8 days AST Historical tissue injury marker Very low Variable 26 Clinical Case 1 — Chest Pain Case 55-year-old man Severe chest pain ECG shows ischemic changes hs-cTnI: above 99th percentile CK-MB: elevated Interpretation The findings indicate myocardial injury. With compatible symptoms and ischemic ECG changes, the overall picture is consistent with acute myocardial infarction. chunks: Regulation of Blood Pressure Dr. Zulfiqar Department of Biochemistry Lecture objectives By the end of the lecture students will be able to • Define primary and secondary hypertention and their risk factors. • Relate role of minerals with hypertention. • List the interventions for the management of hypertention. • Explain dietary approaches to stop hypertention. Blood Pressure as a Cardiovascular Risk 4 Attributable Risk • Overall ½ of heart failure and stroke* • Stroke 60-70%* • Heart failure 50% • Heart attack 25% • Kidney failure 20% • Dementia • Sexual dysfunction • Hypertension is sustained elevation of BP – Systolic blood pressure  140 mm Hg – Diastolic blood pressure  90 mm Hg Hypertension Definition BP Classification SBP mmHg DBP mmHg Normal < 120 and < 80 Pre-hypertension* 120-139 or 80-89 Stage 1 Hypertension 140-159 or 90-99 Stage 2 Hypertension > 160 or > 100 Blood Pressure Classification • Primary (Essential) Hypertension - Elevated BP with unknown cause - 90% to 95% of all cases • Secondary Hypertension - Elevated BP with a specific cause - 5% to 10% in adults Classification of Hypertension Risk Factors for Primary Hypertension • Age (> 55 for men; > 65 for women) •

Being overweight or obese • Cigarette smoking • Diabetes mellitus • Elevated serum lipids • Excess dietary sodium • Gender • Excessive alcohol intake • Stress • Heredity • Coarctation of aorta • Renal disease • Endocrine disorders • Neurologic disorders Risk Factors for Secondary Hypertension Sodium What are sodium and salt? – Sodium is a chief extracellular cation – About 90 percent of sodium consumed is in form of sodium chloride, table salt Functions: chief role is regulation of fluid balance – Necessary for normal nerve and muscle function • Studies link excess sodium intake to the development of elevated blood pressure, which increases the risk of heart attacks, stroke, and kidney disease. Sodium Higher dietary salt increases death from stroke Adapted from Perry IJ et al. J Hum Hypertens. 1992;6:23-25. International scientific and health organizations conclude that high dietary salt: • Increases blood pressure • Is a health risk WHO/FAO technical report recommends less than 5 g of salt per day Nishida C et al. Public Health Nutr. 2003;7:245-50. • Potassium regulates the activity of muscles and nerves. • Decrease your chances of developing kidney stones Best sources of Potassiu

m: • Avocados • Yams • Papaya • Lentils • Dark leafy greens Potassium • A consistent body of evidence from observational studies and clinical trials indicates that high levels of potassium are associated with lower BP. • Meta-analyses do reveal a dose response relationship between BP lowering and potassium intake. Evidence of Benefits of Potassium on BP Calcium • Most abundant mineral in body – More than 99 percent located in bones and teeth • Functions: – Helps strengthen bones and teeth – Plays a role in muscles, nerves, and blood – May reduce risk of kidney stones (dietary calcium) Calcium Food sources: – Milk, yogurt – cheese, broccoli, – calcium –fortified soy milk, – calcium-fortified juices and – cereals • Population studies indicate that high intakes of calcium from the diet are linked with low BP, where as clinical trials using calcium supplements to lower BP have been less compelling. • Calcium supplementation has not been shown to prevent an increase in BP or hypertension. • The evidence relating calcium and BP reduction is weak. Calcium • Contributes to the relaxation of muscles and nerves. Best sources of Magnesium: • Pumpkin & Sunflower seeds • Dark leafy greens • Sal

mon • Black beans Magnesium • Epidemiologic, observational, and clinical trial data results are inconsistent to indicate that a diet high in magnesium may lower BP. • In most epidemiologic studies, an Inverse relationship has been shown between dietary magnesium intake and BP. • clinical studies have been less convincing, and the therapeutic value of magnesium in the prevention of hypertension remains unclear. Effect of Magnesium on BP The DASH: (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension) DASH DIET (DIETARY APPROACHES TO STOP HYPERTENSION) • Follows heart healthy guidelines to limit saturated fat and cholesterol. • Focuses on increasing intake of foods rich in nutrients that are expected to lower blood pressure, mainly minerals (like potassium, calcium, and magnesium), protein, fiber. • DASH demonstrated that a diet rich in fruit and vegetables and low-fat dairy products with reduced saturated and total fat can result in a clinically significant reduction in BP • A subgroup analysis of the DASH trial also found that the BP-lowering effects were more pronounced in hypertensive individuals DASH DIET (DIETARY APPROACHES TO STOP HYPERTENSION) • Weight reduction • Dietary changes (DASH di

et: Dietary Approaches to Stop HTN) • Sodium restriction • Regular physical activity • Avoidance of tobacco and alcohol use • Stress management Lifestyle Modifications • Vasopressin (Anti-diuretic Hormone) which controls water balance by regulating the loss and elimination of water into urine. • The Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone system which regulates the amount of sodium ion (Na+) lost and eliminated in urine • Atrial Natriuretic Peptides (ANP) that counter the actions of Vasopressin and the Renin-Angiotensin- Aldosterone system. Blood pressure is primarily maintained by three systems: What alters blood volume? • Removing H2O from the body decreases the volume of blood; along with blood pressure. Vasopressin stimulates the kidney distal tubules to recapture the H2O in urine passing through the tubules. • Sodium ion recovery from urine is stimulated by the Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone system which is stimulated by low blood pressure. • Brain, heart, & kidney respond to changes in blood pressure via pressure receptors, baroreceptors(Juxtaglomerular cells in kidneys), & to changes in ionic composition of blood via macula densa(in kidney). How are changes in blood pressure detected?

Barorecepter Baroreceptors are located mainly in: Carotid sinus Aortic arch When arterial pressure increases: ↑ BP → ↑ baroreceptor firing → medullary cardiovascular centers → ↓ sympathetic + ↑ parasympathetic activity This causes: ↓ HR ↓ contractility Arteriolar dilation ↓ venous return Therefore, BP falls toward normal. When BP decreases, the opposite occurs. • Aldosterone is a steroid hormone, secreted from adrenal cortex • Aldosterone regulates both the reabsorption sodium and secretion of potassium in proximal tubule, distal tubule, and collecting duct Aldosterone & Sodium Reabsorption • ANP released from the atrium in response to increased atrial stretch via mechanoreceptors. In other words, when plasma volume increases. • The effect of ANP are to: 1) Dilate the renal blood vessels to increase the GFR 2) Inhibit the reabsorption of Na+ from collecting ducts. 3) Inhibit the release of renin, aldosterone and ADH. • The result is to increase the kidney’s ability to excrete both water and sodium. Though natural BP reducers they are not widely employed clinically. Non Pharmacological Treatment of Hypertension DASH diet Regular exercise Loose weight , if obese Reduce salt and high fat diets

chunks: Role of Oxidative Stress and Free Radicals in Cardiovascular Disease From Molecular Insult to Clinical Manifestation Humaira Sharif Lecture Objectives • Classification of Oxidants & Anti-oxidants • List of Oxidants & Anti-oxidants sources • Biochemical role of Oxidants & Anti-oxidants • Role of Oxidants & Anti-oxidants in CVS diseases A biochemical state characterized by a disruption of the redox (reduction-oxidation) balance in favor of oxidants. This leads to a potential destruction of cellular structures, including: Lipids, Proteins and DNA. Oxidative Stress Free Radicals: Contain unpaired electron(s). E.g: Superoxide (O₂•⁻), Hydroxyl (•OH), Nitric Oxide (NO•) Non-Radicals: Powerful oxidizing agents. E.g: Hydrogen Peroxide (H₂O₂), Hypochlorous Acid (HOCl) Classification The Unstable Agents Free Radical: A molecule with one or more unpaired electrons in its outer orbit, making it highly unstable and reactive. Superoxide anion (O₂•⁻) Hydroxyl radical (•OH) Reactive Oxygen Species (ROS): A broader term that includes both free radicals and other reactive, non-radical molecules (e.g., Hydrogen Peroxide. ROS: Not Always the Villain Normal Physiological Roles: ●Cell signaling ●Immune d

efense (phagocytes use ROS to destroy pathogens) ●Regulation of vascular tone Problem: Excessive, unregulated ROS production leads to damage Sources of Free Radicals in CVD Endogenous Sources: ●Mitochondrial Electron Transport Chain (primary source) ●Enzymes: NADPH oxidase, Xanthine oxidase ●Inflammation (activated immune cells) Exogenous Sources: ●Cigarette smoke ●Air pollution ●Radiation ●Processed foods Lipid Peroxidation - Lipid peroxidation is oxidative degradation of lipids, resulting in the formation of reactive aldehydes and other products. - Contributes to the formation of foam cells, which accumulate in the arterial wall, leading to atherosclerosis. Mechanism: ROS initiate lipid peroxidation, leading to the oxidation of low- density lipoprotein (LDL) and its subsequent uptake by macrophages, forming foam cells. Consequence: Lipid peroxidation promotes atherosclerotic plaque formation, inflammation, and CVD progression. Protein Modification Protein modification impairs vascular function, promoting inflammation and CVD progression. Mechanism: ROS modify proteins, leading to: - Enzyme inactivation - Receptor dysfunction - Signaling pathway disruption Consequence: Protein mod

ification contributes to vascular dysfunction, inflammation, and CVD development. Inflammation Inflammation is a complex biological response to tissue damage or infection, characterized by the activation of immune cells and the release of pro-inflammatory mediators. Role in CVD: Inflammation promotes CVD development and progression by: - Enhancing atherosclerotic plaque formation - Impairing vascular function - Increasing thrombogenicity Inflammation Mechanism: ROS promote inflammation by: - Activating immune cells - Inducing pro-inflammatory gene expression - Enhancing cytokine release Consequence: Inflammation contributes to CVD progression and increased risk of cardiovascular events. DNA Damage DNA damage contributes to vascular cell apoptosis, CVD progression, and increased risk of cardiovascular events. Mechanism: ROS damage DNA, leading to: - Genetic mutations - Epigenetic changes - Vascular cell apoptosis Consequence: DNA damage promotes CVD progression, vascular dysfunction, and increased risk of cardiovascular events. Antioxidants Endogenous antioxidants: Enzymes (superoxide dismutase, catalase, glutathione peroxidase) and non-enzymatic antioxidants (glutathione, vitamins

C and E). Dietary antioxidants: Fruits, vegetables, and whole grains rich in antioxidants (polyphenols, flavonoids), reduce CVD risk. Mechanisms: Antioxidants scavenge ROS, reduce oxidative stress, and promote vascular health. Therapeutic Potential in CVDs Antioxidants may reduce CVD risk by improving vascular function, reducing inflammation, and preventing oxidative damage. Clinical trials: Some studies suggest benefits of antioxidant supplements (e.g., vitamin E, omega-3 fatty acids) in reducing CVD risk, but results are inconsistent. Future directions: Further research is needed to determine the efficacy and safety of antioxidant therapies in CVD prevention and treatment. Two lipids are the exception. Free fatty acids and lysophospholipids are carried by plasma ALBUMIN, not by lipoproteins. Steroid hormones and fat-soluble vitamins also ride on their own binding proteins. 3 Structure of a lipoprotein particle A spherical droplet: oily inside, w

ater-friendly outside SURFACE MONOLAYER 1 Core Non-polar lipids only: triacylglycerol and cholesteryl ester. Completely hidden from water. 2 Surface (outside) A single layer of phospholipid with its water-liking heads facing the plasma. 3 Free cholesterol Sits in the surface layer and keeps it flexible. 4 Apolipoproteins Proteins stuck in the surface.
