s ON the enzyme LCAT; binds the ABCA1 transporter Apo B-48 Chylomicron Needed to build and release chylomicrons from the intestine Apo B-100 VLDL, IDL, LDL The key that fits the LDL receptor on cells Apo C-II Chylomicron, VLDL, HDL Switches ON lipoprotein lipase - without it TAG is not unloaded Apo C-III Chylomicron, VLDL, HDL Switches OFF lipoprotein lipase (a brake) Apo E Chylomicron remnant, VLDL, IDL, HDL The key for remnant uptake by the liver Apo(a) Lipoprotein(a) Looks like plasminogen; blocks clot breakdown - raises clot risk 6 Transport systems 1 Exogenous Gut to tissues Dietary fat leaves the intestine as chylomicrons and is unloaded by LPL. 2 Endogenous Liver to tissues Liver-made fat leaves as VLDL, is stripped down and becomes LDL. 3 Reverse transport Tissues to liver HDL collects spare cholesterol and brings it back for excretion in bile. 4 Free fatty acids Fat cells to tissues FFA travel bound to albumin during fasting - no lipoprotein needed. Routes 1 and 2 send fat out to the tissues. Route 3 brings cholesterol back to the liver. Route 4 is the quick fasting fuel line. 7 Route 1 - Exogenous pathway (dietary fat) 1 Digestion in the gut Bile salts emulsify fat. Pancr

eatic lipase and colipase break triacylglycerol into 2-monoacylglycerol and free fatty acids. 2 Absorption into enterocyte These products enter the intestinal cell inside micelles, then are re-joined back into triacylglycerol in the smooth ER. 3 Chylomicron assembly Microsomal triglyceride transfer protein (MTP) loads the new TAG onto apo B-48. The nascent chylomicron is formed. 4 Release by lymph Chylomicrons are too big for capillaries. They enter lacteals, travel up the thoracic duct and empty into the left subclavian vein. Why lymph? Because chylomicrons bypass the liver first - this is why a fatty meal makes plasma look milky (lipaemia) 2 to 6 hours later. 8 Route 1 - Exogenous pathway continued Steps 5 to 8: unloading the fat and clearing the leftovers 5 Maturation by HDL In plasma, HDL donates apo C-II and apo E to the nascent chylomicron. Now it is a mature chylomicron. 6 Unloading at the capillary Lipoprotein lipase (LPL) sits on capillary walls of muscle and fat tissue. Apo C-II switches it on. TAG is broken into free fatty acids and glycerol. 7 Fate of the fatty acids Muscle burns them for energy. Adipose tissue re-esterifies and stores them. Glycerol goes to the liver.

8 Remnant clearance The shrunken particle returns apo C-II to HDL and becomes a chylomicron remnant, rich in cholesterol. The liver takes it up through apo E receptors (LRP). 9 Clinical correlation Two classic disorders of the exogenous pathway + Type I hyperlipoproteinaemia • Cause: deficiency of LPL or of its activator apo C-II. • Result: chylomicrons cannot be unloaded and pile up in plasma. • Findings: very high triacylglycerol, milky (creamy) serum on standing. • Signs: eruptive xanthomas, lipaemia retinalis, hepatosplenomegaly. • Danger: acute pancreatitis. • Treatment: strict low-fat diet; medium-chain triglycerides (they go straight to portal blood, no chylomicrons needed). + Abetalipoproteinaemia • Cause: mutation in MTP, so apo B cannot be loaded with lipid. • Result: no chylomicrons and no VLDL can be made at all. • Findings: very low plasma TAG and cholesterol; absent apo B. • Signs: fat malabsorption, steatorrhoea, failure to thrive. • Blood film: acanthocytes (spiky red cells). • Late: retinitis pigmentosa and spinocerebellar degeneration from vitamin E deficiency. • Treatment: low fat diet plus large doses of vitamins A, D, E and K. Note • Creamy top layer on serum k

ept overnight in the fridge = chylomicrons = type I. Uniformly milky serum = VLDL = type IV. 10 Route 2 - Endogenous pathway (liver fat) VLDL is slowly stripped down into LDL 1 VLDL is built in the liver When carbohydrate or fatty acid supply is high, the liver packs its own TAG onto apo B-100 using MTP, and releases VLDL directly into blood. 2 HDL donates the labels HDL gives apo C-II and apo E to the new VLDL particle. 3 LPL strips the TAG Again apo C-II switches on lipoprotein lipase. TAG leaves; the particle shrinks into IDL (VLDL remnant). 4 IDL has two fates About half is taken up by the liver via apo E. The rest is further stripped by hepatic lipase and loses apo E, becoming LDL. 5 LDL is cholesterol-rich Now the particle carries mostly cholesteryl ester and only apo B-100. It delivers cholesterol to any cell with an LDL receptor. 11 How a cell takes up LDL Receptor-mediated endocytosis 1 Binding Apo B-100 on LDL binds the LDL receptor sitting in a clathrin-coated pit. 2 Internalisation The pit pinches off into an endosome. Low pH releases LDL from the receptor. 3 Recycling and digestion The receptor returns to the surface. LDL goes to the lysosome, where cholesteryl ester i

s hydrolysed to free cholesterol. PCSK9 - the receptor destroyer • PCSK9 is a liver protein that binds the LDL receptor and sends it to the lysosome instead of back to the surface. • Fewer receptors on the cell = more LDL left in blood. • Blocking PCSK9 with antibodies lowers LDL very strongly. Two names to remember • Scavenger receptors on macrophages take up oxidised LDL and are NOT switched off by cholesterol. • That is exactly why macrophages become foam cells. 12 How a cell takes up LDL Free cholesterol inside the cell then does three things • Switches OFF HMG-CoA reductase - the cell stops making its own cholesterol. • Switches OFF new LDL receptor synthesis - the cell stops importing more. • Switches ON ACAT - spare cholesterol is stored as cholesteryl ester. Clinical correlation - Familial hypercholesterolaemia Type IIa: the LDL receptor is faulty or missing What goes wrong • Autosomal dominant defect of the LDL receptor gene. • LDL cannot be cleared from plasma. • Liver also keeps making cholesterol because its own cells sense a shortage. • Other causes of the same picture: defective apo B-100, or gain-of-function PCSK9. What you see • Heterozygous: LDL roughly 2 times nor

mal; heart disease in the 30s to 50s. • Homozygous: LDL 4 to 6 times normal; heart attack possible in childhood. • Tendon xanthomas, especially Achilles tendon. • Xanthelasma on the eyelids. • Corneal arcus in a young patient. + Management • High-intensity statin is first line. • Add ezetimibe to block gut absorption. • Add a PCSK9 inhibitor if LDL is still high. • Homozygous cases may need LDL apheresis or lomitapide. • Screen the family - it is dominant, so first-degree relatives have a 50% chance. Bedside rule • Corneal arcus or tendon xanthoma in a patient under 45 years means familial hypercholesterolaemia until proved otherwise. 13 Route 3 - Reverse cholesterol transport (HDL) The only way the body removes cholesterol from peripheral tissues 1 Nascent HDL is born Liver and intestine release a flat, disc-shaped particle made of phospholipid and apo A-I. It carries almost no cholesterol yet. 2 Cholesterol is pulled out of cells The ABCA1 transporter on peripheral cells (including macrophages) hands free cholesterol to apo A-I. 3 LCAT traps it inside Apo A-I switches on LCAT, which converts free cholesterol into cholesteryl ester. chunks: CHOLESTEROL METABOLISM Dr Sabeen Hashmat Qazi 28-9-26 LEARNING OBJECTIVES At the end of this lecture, students should be able to: • Discuss the cholesterol structure with its functions. • Describe the mechanism of cholesterol synthesis and its degradation. • Discuss the regulation of cholesterol metabolism. • Explain the formation of Bile salts and vitamin D. 2 INTRODUCTION • Cholesterol is a yellow crystalline solid. • Soluble in chloroform and other fat solvents. • In a 70 kg individual, a total of 140 grams of cholesterol is present. 3 Brain and nerves 30 Muscles 30 Adipose tissues 30 Skin 20 Blood 10 Liver and spleen 10 Bone marrow 5 Alimentary canal 3 Adrenal glands 2 Cholesterol distribution in various organs (140 grams) Cholesterol is an important constituent of cell membrane. It is important for the synthesis of steroid hormones, bile salts and Vitamin D. Abnormality in cholesterol metabolism may lead to Cerebrovascular accidents (CVA) and heart diseases. INTRODUCTION SOURCES OF CHOLESTEROL EXOGENOUS: Dietary 0.3 g / day Butter, cream, egg yolk, meat From the hydrolysis of cholesteryl esters. ENDOGENOUS: • Synthesized in body from acetyl CoA (1 g / day) STEROIDS • Contain s

teroid nucleus (CYCLOPENTANOPERHYDROPHENANTHRENE). • Phenanthrene nucleus (Rings A, B,C) and cyclopentane ring D. STRUCTURE OF CHOLESTEROL • It possesses “cyclopentano- perhydro-phenanthrene nucleus”. • An –OH group at C3. • An unsaturated double bond between C5 and C6. • Two –CH3 groups at C10 and C13. • An eight-carbon side chain attached to C17. • Cholesterol has OH group which is hydrophilic in nature. • The hydrocarbon tail is hydrophobic. • Cholesterol is therefore termed as Amphipathic molecule OCCURANCE: • Major component of cell membrane and lipoproteins. • Largest amounts in brain and nervous tissue. FORMS: Free Ester form (esterified at position 3 OH group with FA) Hormones formed from cholesterol • Steroids further form the sex hormones Biomedical importance of Cholesterol • Raised levels in blood lead to Atherosclerosis. • Important component of cell membrane. • Poor conductor of electricity so it insulates nerve fibers. • Bile acids and Bile salts are derived from cholesterol .important for lipid digestion. • Steroid hormones are synthesized from it. • 7-dehydrocholesterol is a precursor of Vitamin D. BIOSYNTHESIS OF CHOLESTEROL SITES OF SYNTHESIS Major sites are live

r, adrenal cortex, testes, ovaries & intestine. Liver synthesizes 80% of cholesterol. All nucleated cells can synthesize cholesterol, including arterial wall. LOCATION The enzymes involved in the synthesis of cholesterol are partly located in endoplasmic reticulum & partly in cytoplasm. 12 REQUIREMENTS FOR CHOLESTEROL BIOSYNTHESIS • Acetyl CoA provides all carbon atoms. • Reducing equivalents are supplied by NADPH. (From HMP Shunt) • ATP provides energy. • For production of one molecule of cholesterol, 18 moles of acetyl CoA, 36 moles of ATP and 16 moles of NADPH are required. 13 Synthesis of HMG Co A (β- hydroxy β- methyl glutaryl Co A). Formation of Mevalonate. Production of isoprenoid units. Synthesis of squalene. Conversion of squalene to cholesterol. Five stages BIOSYNTHESIS OF CHOLESTEROL 1 2 3 4 5 Thiolase Condensation of 2 molecules of Acetyl CoA HMG Co A synthase is present in mitochondria for Ketogenesis. Cytoplasmic HMG CoA synthase is used for Cholesterol synthesis Irreversible and rate limiting enzyme Statin drugs used to inhibit this enzyme to lower cholesterol levels Mevalonate 5 phosphate Mevalonate 5 diphosphate Mevalonate 3 phosphate-5 diphosphate (6 C) Isopenteny

l Pyrophosphate (5C) CO2 removed Isopentenyl diphosphate Isopentenyl diphosphate Farnesyl diphosphate (15 C) 30 Carbon compound) 20 STEPS INVOLVED IN BIOSYNTHESIS OF CHOLESTEROL HMG CoAreductase israte-limiting enzyme. Regulation at transcription level: Long-term regulation involves regulation of transcription of gene for HMG CoA reductase. If Sufficient cholesterol is present in the cell, transcription of the gene for HMG CoA reductase is suppressed & cellular synthesis of cholesterol is decreased. If cholesterol in diet is low, synthesis is increased. LONG TERM REGULATION OF CHOLESTEROL SYNTHESIS LONG TERM REGULATION OF CHOLESTEROL • Cholesterol regulates the expression of HMG Co A reductase gene and LDL receptor gene. • A Sterol regulatory element (SRE) is present in DNA. • SRE binding with Sterol regulatory element binding protein (SREBP) is essential for transcription of these genes. • When cholesterol levels are sufficient SREBP remains inactive. • The SREBP cleavage activator protein (SCAP) is intracellular cholesterol sensor. • When cholesterol is less, SCAP (Cleavage protein) escorts SREBP to Golgi bodies. • Two Golgi proteases cleave SREBP to a protein which binds to

SRE and activates transcription of HMG Co A Reductase gene. LONG TERM REGULATION OF CHOLESTEROL Insulin and thyroxine increases the activity of HMG CoAreductase. Cortisol , glucagon and cAMP decrease the activity of HMG CoAreductase. HMG CoA reductase activity is inhibited by bile acids. Fasting also reduces the activity of HMG CoA reductase. HORMONAL REGULATION Average diet contains about 300 mg of cholesterol per day. Body synthesizes about 700 mg/day. About 500 mg of cholesterol is excreted through bile. Some of this partly reabsorbed from intestine. Remaining is converted to bile acids, which are excreted in the bile as bile salts. EXCRETION OF CHOLESTEROL Structure of the bile acids • The bile acids contain 24 carbons, with two or three hydroxyl groups and a side chain that terminates in a carboxyl group. • The bile acids are amphipathic. Therefore, the molecules have both a polar and a nonpolar face, and can act as emulsifying agents in the intestine, helping prepare dietary triacylglycerol and other complex lipids for degradation by pancreatic digestive enzymes. 31 Synthesis of bile acids Bile acids are synthesized in the liver by a multistep, multiorganelle pathway

in which hydroxyl groups are inserted at specific positions on the steroid structure, the double bond of the cholesterol B ring is reduced, and the hydrocarbon chain is shortened by three carbons, introducing a carboxyl group at the end of the chain. The most common resulting compounds, cholic acid (a triol) and chenodeoxycholic acid (a diol, are called “primary” bile acids). 32 Primary bile acids are formed from cholesterol cholesterol cholic acid chenodeoxycholic acid 7--hydroxylase hydroxylation of C7 addition of OH group 7--hydroxycholesterol Secondary bile acids Primary bile acids Bile salts- glycine or taurine conjugated to bile acids in liver 5% lost in feces 34 Synthesis of bile salts Before the bile acids leave the liver, they are conjugated to a molecule of either glycine or taurine (an end product of cysteine metabolism). These new structures are called bile salts: • Glycocholic and glyco-chenodeoxycholic acids. • Taurocholic and tauro-chenodeoxycholic acids. • Bile salts are more effective detergents than bile acids because of their enhanced amphipathic nature. Bile salts provide the only significant mechanism for cholesterol excretion, both as a metabolic product of

cholesterol and as a solubilizer of cholesterol in bile. 35 Bile salt deficiency: Cholelithiasis The movement of cholesterol from the liver into the bile must be accompanied by the simultaneous secretion of phospholipid and bile salts. If this dual process is disrupted and more cholesterol enters the bile than can be solubilized by the bile salts and lecithin present, the cholesterol may precipitate in the gallbladder, initiating the occurrence of cholesterol gallstone disease—Cholelithiasis. Causes of cholelithiasis • Obstruction of the biliary tract, interrupting the enterohepatic circulation. • Severe hepatic dysfunction, leading to decreased synthesis of bile salts, or other abnormalities in bile production. • Cholelithiasis also may result from increased biliary cholesterol excretion. Synthesis of Vitamin D 7-Dehydrocholesterol,an intermediate in the synthesis of cholesterol, is converted to cholecalciferol (vitamin D3) by ultraviolet rays in the skin. 40 SUMMARY Rate limiting enzyme: HMG CoA Reductase

Her laboratory investigations revealed: Fasting glucose: 437 mg/dL (normal value: 70–100 mg/dL), pH : 7.09 (normal value: 7.35–7.45), pCO2 : 23 mmHg (normal value: 38–42 mmHg), Serum bicarbonate: 8.0 mEq/L (normal value: 22–26 mEq/L), Serum ketone: 3.8 mmol/L (normal value: 0.6–1.5 mmol/L). • Fatty acids are released by adipose tissue and converted into acetyl units by the liver, which then exports them as ketone bodies. • Ketone bodies are water-soluble, transportable form of acetyl units. • They do not require carrier proteins. INTRODUCTION Ketone bodies are synthesized in the liver under conditions such as: 1. Prolonged fasting

or starvation, 2. Consumption of low-carbohydrate diets (ketogenic diets), 3. Uncontrolled type 1 diabetes (diabetic ketoacidosis), and 4. Chronic alcoholism. INTRODUCTION SYNTHESIS (KETOGENESIS) • Occurs exclusively in the Liver mitochondria. • Acetyl co A is used as a substrate or a precursor molecule. • Both enzymes (HMG CoA Synthase and HMG Co A Lyase) must be present in mitochondria for ketogenesis to take place. STEP 1 Two molecules of acetyl CoA react with each other in the presence of thiolase enzyme to form acetoacetyl CoA. STEP 2 Condensation of Acetoacetyl CoA with Acetyl CoA to form HMG CoA (3 or β hydroxyl- 3 or β methyl glutaryl CoA) catalyzed by HMG CoA synthetase STEP 3 3-Hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl CoA is then cleaved to Acetyl CoA and Acetoacetate in the presence of HMG Co A lyase . Acetoacetate produces β- hydroxybutyrate in a reaction catalyzed by the enzyme β- hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase in the presence of NADH. FORMATION OF β-HYDROXYBUTYRATE • Both acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate can be transported across the mitochondrial membrane and the plasma membrane of the liver cells. • Next they enter blood stream to be used as a fuel by other cells of the body. FORM

ATION OF ACETONE In the blood stream, small amounts of acetoacetate are spontaneously (non- enzymatically) decarboxyated to acetone. Acetone Breath • The fruity odor of acetone may be detected in the breath of a person who has a high level of acetoacetate in the blood. • “Acetone-breath” has been used as a crude method of diagnosing individuals with untreated Type I diabetes mellitus. Utilization of ketone bodies (Ketolysis) • Ketone bodies serve as a fuel for extra hepatic tissues. • The ketone bodies are water soluble and are transported across the inner mitochondrial membrane as well as across the blood-brain barrier and cell membranes. • They can be used as a fuel source by a variety of tissues including the CNS. KETOLYSIS (USE OF KETONES BY PERIPHERAL TISSUE) 3-Hydroxybutyrate (oxidized) + NAD → Acetoacetate + NADH + H⁺ Enzyme = 3-Hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase Acetoacetate + CoA (from Succinyl CoA by (Thiophorase) → Acetoacetyl CoA Acetoacetyl CoA → 2 Acetyl CoA Occurs in mitochondria of heart, kidney, brain KETOLYSIS (USE OF KETONES BY PERIPHERAL TISSUE) • Liver continuously makes low levels of Ketone bodies. • Increased secretion during fasting / Diabetes Mellitus (Type 1 un

controlled) → provides energy to peripheral tissues. • Liver cannot use Ketone bodies as fuel because it lacks Thiophorase. • RBC can not utilize Ketone Bodies as they lack mitochondria Biological significance of ketone bodies Brain ❑ Requires 60-70% of total body glucose for normal functioning. ❑ No Glucose → Brain cannot use fatty acids as they cannot cross the blood-brain barrier. ❑Decreased Glucose → ketone bodies for fuel in brain (adapts utilization of acetoacetate during starvation and diabetes). ❑ Prolonged starvation → 75% of needs of the brain are met by ketone bodies. Individuals eating diets extremely high in fat and low in carbohydrate (KETOGENIC DIET), starving, or suffering from a severe lack of insulin (Type I diabetes mellitus) increase the synthesis and utilization of ketone bodies KETOACIDOSIS • Normal ketone bodies level in blood is <1 mg/dl above that ketonemia will develops. • When Ketogenesis ˃ Ketolysis → Ketonemia ( 90 mg/dl ) → Ketoacidosis → Fruity odor in breath (Acetone) → Ketonuria (5000 mg/ day) • Diabetic ketoacidosis (Type 1- uncontrolled) / Starvation →Ketoacidosis → Ketonuria (+ Glycosuria) → Dehydration Causes of Ketosis • Uncontrolled diabetes m

ellitus • (Kussmaul’s breathing) • Starvation • Chronic alcoholism • Heavy exercise • Low carbohydrate diet- For weight loss Chronic Alcoholism The second most common cause of ketoacidosis is binge drinking for a prolonged period of time without consuming calories and carbohydrates. This is known as alcoholic ketoacidosis and results in dangerously high levels of plasma ketones and blood sugar as well. KETOACIDOSIS Metabolic acidosis: Ketone bodies (being an organic acid) when increased in plasma, liberate H+ ion which are buffered by bicarbonate system. But if the production is high as compare to buffering capacity , it will decrease pH and caused metabolic acidosis. Ketonuria Medical condition in which ketone bodies appear in urine (acetoacetate and β- hydroxybutyrate). Acetone breath Acetone is only volatile ketone body that can expired through lungs. List the most common cardiac anomalies. • Cardiovascular system consists of the heart and blood vessels. • All of these structures are mesodermal in origin with signifi

cant contributions made by neural crest cells to the development of the heart • Heart is the first fully developed and functional organ in embryogenesis. • The heart tissue, consisting of myocardial, endocardial and epicardial cells, is predominantly derived from the mesodermal layer. • Ectoderm-derived cardiac neural crest cells are involved in the development of the cardiac cushions of the outflow tract • BMP (Bone Morphogenetic Protein) is a group of signaling molecules belonging to the TGF-β superfamily. During embryonic development, BMPs regulate cell differentiation, proliferation, migration, and organ formation. • The primordium of the intraembryonic coelom is formed by the coalescence of spaces within the lateral plate mesoderm during the 3rd week of development, dividing it into somatic and splanchnic layers and ultimately giving rise to the pericardial, pleural, and peritoneal cavities. Early development of cardiovascular system • The early formation of the cardiovascular system is correlated with the urgent need for blood vessels to bring oxygen and nourishment to the embryo from the maternal circulation through the placenta. • Blood islands are clusters of mesodermal ce

lls that develop in the yolk sac during the 3rd week and give rise to primitive blood cells and endothelial cells of the early blood vessels. Blood Islands • Site: Extraembryonic mesoderm of the yolk sac. • Time: Approximately day 17–18. • Process: Vasculogenesis. • Main derivatives: Primitive blood cells and endothelial cells. • Blood islands contribute to the formation of the 1. Early vascular system 2. Development of the cardiovascular system. Cardiac development begins in the 3rd week with the migration of epiblast cells, into the splanchnic layer of lateral plate mesoderm to form a horseshoe shaped region called the primary heart field or cardiogenic area, rostral to the developing forebrain. • Cardiogenic area is a specialized region of the splanchnic mesoderm of the lateral plate mesoderm in the early embryo that gives rise to the primitive heart tube. • Multipotential cardiac progenitor cells from several sources contribute to the formation of the heart. • Components • The cardiogenic region contains: 1. Primary heart field (PHF) 2. Secondary heart field (SHF) • Once cells establish the PHF, they are induced by the underlying pharyngeal endoderm to form cardiac myoblasts an

d blood islands that will form blood cells and vessels by the process of vasculogenesis . With time, the islands unite and form a horseshoe-shaped endothelial-lined tube surrounded by myoblasts. This region is known as the cardiogenic region; the intraembryonic (primitive body) cavity over it later develops into the pericardial cavity • As folding of the head region occurs, the heart and pericardial cavity come to lie ventral to the foregut and caudal to the oropharyngeal membrane Formation of the heart tube • Initially two endocardial heart tubes are formed in the cardiogenic area , which later fuse in craniocaudal sequence to form a sing endocardial heart tube. • The heart is the first functional organ to develop. • It develops from splanchnic mesoderm in the wall of the yolk sac (cardiogenic area), cranial to the developing mouth & nervous system and ventral to the developing pericardial sac. • The heart primordium is first evident at 18 days • As the head fold completed, the developing heart tubes lie in the ventral aspect of the embryo dorsal to the developing pericardial sac. • After lateral folding of the embryo the 2 heart tubes fuse together to form a single endocardial he

art tube. • It begins to beat at 22 to 23 days. Blood flow begins during the beginning of the fourth week and can be visualized Fate of the heart tube The heart tube grows faster than the pericardial sac, so it shows 5 alternate dilations separated by constrictions. These are: Sinus Venosus. Truncus Arteriosus. Bulbus Cordis. Common Ventricle. Common Atrium. The endocardial heart tube has 2 ends: 1. Venous end; Sinus Venosus. 2. Arterial end; Truncus arteriosus Circulation through Primordial Heart • Blood enters the sinus venosus from the: 1. Embryo through the common cardinal veins 2. Developing placenta through the umbilical veins 3. Umbilical vesicle through the vitelline veins Veins Associated With Heart Development Each horn of the sinus venosus receives 3 veins: 1.Common cardinal 2.Vitelline 3.Umbilical Cardinal vein from the fetal body. Vitelline from the yolk sac. Umbilical from the placenta. • Heart tube is suspended within the pericardial sac by a dorsal mesocardium, which later degenerates to create the transverse pericardial sinus. • Developmentally, the heart tube consists of 4 layers: 1. Endocardium: innermost lining, analogous to tunica intima of blood vessels 2. Car

diac jelly: forms the cardiac skeleton • Annulus fibrosus: attachments for the cusps of the cardiac valves trigone - 3. Myocardium: layer that forms cardiac muscle, analogous to tunica media of blood vessels 4. Epicardium: outermost covering of the heart; analogous to the tunica adventitia of blood vessels External layer of the embryonic heart tube, the primordial myocardium, is formed from splanchnic mesoderm surrounding the pericardial cavity (cardiac precursors of the anterior, or second, heart field. At this stage, the developing heart is composed of a thin endothelial tube, separated from a thick myocardium by a gelatinous matrix of connective tissue, cardiac jelly. The endothelial tube becomes the internal endothelial lining of the heart, or endocardium, and the primordial myocardium becomes the muscular wall of the heart, or myocardium. The visceral pericardium, or epicardium, is derived from mesothelial cells that arise from the external surface of the sinus venosus and spread over the myocardium. U-shaped heart tube • Bulbus cordis and ventricle grow faster than other regions. • heart bends upon itself, forming U-shaped heart tube, (bulboventricular loop). Loop formation O

r S-Shaped Heart Tube • Heart tube develops it bends, upon itself: the atrium and sinus venosus become dorsal to the truncus arteriosus, bulbus cordis, and ventricle. • By this stage the sinus venosus has developed 2 lateral expansions, called the 2 horns ( right and left horns). Partitioning of Primordial Heart . Partitioning of the AV canal . primordial atrium . ventricle . Outflow tract begins during the middle of the fourth week. Partitioning is essentially completed by the end of the eighth week. • Toward the end of the fourth week, AV endocardial cushions form on the dorsal and ventral walls of the AV canal • The AV endocardial cushions develop from a specialized extracellular matrix (cardiac jelly), as well as neural crest cells. • As these masses of tissue are invaded by mesenchymal cells during the fifth week, the AV endocardial cushions approach each other and fuse, dividing the AV canal into right and left canals. • These canals partially separate the primordial atrium from the primordial ventricle, and the endocardial cushions function as AV valves. • The septal valves are derived from the fused superior and inferior endocardial cushions. • AV cushions contribute to the

formation of the valves and membranous septa of the heart. • Beginning at the end of the fourth week, the primordial atrium is divided into right and left atria by the formation of, and subsequent modification and fusion of, two septa: 1. Septum primum 2. Septum secundum • Septum primum, a thin crescent-shaped membrane, grows toward the fusing endocardial cushions from the roof of the primordial atrium, partially dividing the common atrium into right and left halves. • This foramen serves as a shunt, enabling oxygenated blood to pass from the right to the left atrium. • The foramen becomes progressively smaller and disappears as the mesenchymal cap of the septum primum fuses with the fused AV endocardial cushions to form a primordial AV septum • This foramen serves as a shunt, enabling oxygenated blood to pass from the right to the left atrium. • The foramen becomes progressively smaller and disappears as the mesenchymal cap of the septum primum fuses with the fused AV endocardial cushions to form a primordial AV septum • At birth when the lung circulation begins the pressure in the left atrium increases and exceeds that of the right atrium. • The two septae oppose each other. • I

chunks: Development of the Veins Prof Dr. Imran Ishaque Shaikh Objectives By the end of the session, students should be able to: Describe the embryological origin of the venous system. Identify the three pairs of major embryonic veins: 1. Vitelline veins 2. Umbilical veins 3. Cardinal veins Describe the development and fate of the vitelline veins. Explain the formation of the hepatic sinusoids and hepatic portal vein. Describe the development and fate of the umbilical veins. Explain the formation and function of the ductus venosus. Describe the development of the anterior, posterior, and common cardinal veins. Explain the formation of the superior vena cava. Describe the development of the inferior vena cava and its major segments. Explain the development of the azygos and hemiazygos systems. Describe the development of the brachiocephalic veins. Explain the development of the renal, gonadal, and suprarenal veins. The embryonic venous system develops mainly from three pairs of primitive veins that drain blood from the embryo, yolk sac, and placenta: Development of the Veins In a 4 weeks embryo, three paired veins open into the tubular heart: ▪Vitelline veins, returning deoxygenated blood f

rom the yolk sac ▪Umbilical veins, bringing oxygenated blood from the placenta. ▪Common cardinal veins, returning deoxygenated blood from the body of the embryo Vitelline Veins Pass through the septum transversum and drain into the sinus venosus In relation to the liver developing within the septum transversum, the vitelline veins are divided into: ▪Pre-hapatic part: forms anastomosis around the duodenum which later on gives rise to the portal vein ▪Hepatic part: interrupted by the liver cords, forms an extensive vascular network called the hepatic sinusoides ▪Post-hepatic part: ▪Left vein disappears ▪Right vein forms the: ▪Hepatic veins & ▪Hepatic segment of inferior vena cava Umbilical Veins Bring oxygenated blood from the placenta Initially run on each side of the developing liver and drain into the sinus venosus As the liver grows, the umbilical veins loose their connection with heart and open into the liver The right vein disappears by the end of the embryonic period. The left vein persists A wide channel, the ductus venosus, appears through the substance of liver to connect the left umbilical vein with the inferior vena cava After birth: ❖ The left umbilical vein obliterate t

o form the ligamentum teres of the liver ❖ The ductus venosus obliterate to form the ligamentum venosum Are responsible to drain the body of the embryo ▪The cranial part of the embryo is drained by paired anterior cardinal veins ▪The caudal part of the embryo is drained by paired posterior cardinal veins ▪The anterior & posterior cardinal veins join to form common cardinal veins, which drain into the sinus venosus Anterior Cardinal Veins Become connected by an oblique anastomosis which shunts blood from left to right This anastomosing channel becomes the left brachiocephalic vein Left anterior cardinal vein ▪Cranial part: becomes the left internal jugular vein ▪Caudal part: degenerates Right anterior cardinal vein ▪Cranial part: (cranial to the 7th intersegmental vein) becomes the right internal jugular vein ▪Middle part: gives rise to the right brachiocephalic vein ▪Caudal part of right anterior cardinal vein and the right common cardinal vein form the superior vena cava Posterior Cardinal Veins Drain the caudal part of the body of embryo including the developing mesonephroi and largely disappear with this transitory kidneys. Caudally the two veins get connected by an anastomosing

channel that directs the blood from the left to the right vein Gradually the posterior cardinal veins are replaced by two new veins: subcardinal & supracardinal The adult derivatives of the posterior cardinal veins are the: ▪Root of the azygos vein & ▪Common iliac veins Subcardinal Veins Appear before the supracardinal veins Become connected: ▪To each other by the subcardinal anastomosis ▪With the posterior cardinal veins through the mesonephros ▪With supracarinal veins through subsupracardinal anastomosis The adult derivatives of the subcardinal veins are the: ▪Stem of the left renal vein ▪Suprarenal veins ▪Gonadal veins ▪Prerenal segment of IVC Supracardinal Veins Last pair of veins to develop Appear lateral to the subcardinal veins Become connected at both ends, to the posterior cardinal veins Get disrupted in the region of the kidney Cranial to the kidney: ▪An anastomosis develops between the two veins shunting blood from the left to the right vein ▪Anterior connection of the left vein with the posterior cardinal vein disappears ▪Gives rise to azygos and hemiazygos veins Caudal to the kidney: ▪Left vein degenerates ▪Right vein forms postrenal segment of IVC Development of Supe

rior Vena Cava SVC is derived from the: ▪Caudal part of the right anterior cardinal vein & ▪Right common cardinal vein Development of Azygos Veins Azygos vein is derived from the: ▪Cranial part of the right supracardinal vein & ▪Terminal part of the right posterior cardinal vein Hemiazygos vein is derived from the cranial part of the left supra- cardinal vein Development of Inferior Vena Cava The IVC develops during a series of changes in the primordial veins Composed of: ⚫Hepatic segment derived from the right vitelline vein ⚫Prerenal segment derived from the right subcardinal vein ⚫Renal segment derived from the subcardinal- supracardinal anastomosis ⚫Postrenal segment derived from the right supr- acardinal vein Anomalies of the Venous System Persistent left SVC (double SVC): is the most common defect Left SVC Absence of IVC Double IVC Double Arch of Aorta With Double Superior Vena Cava Fetal Circulation The main features of the fetal circulation are: Nonfunctioning lungs Course of the blood from the placenta to the heart Three shunts permitting the blood to bypass the liver and lungs: ▪Foramen ovale ▪Ductus venosus ▪Ductus arteriosus The oxygenated blood from the placenta reache

s the fetus by umbilical vein Most of the blood bypasses the liver through the ductus venosus, although little blood enters the liver In the inferior vena cava, the oxygenated blood mixes with the deoxygenated blood arriving from the fetus IVC opens into the right atrium. In the right atrium, the caval blood is guided into the left atrium through the foramen ovale. However, little blood remains in the right atrium, which mixes with the blood arriving through the superior vena cava. In the left atrium also, the oxygenated blood mixes with deoxygenated blood arriving from the lungs. Blood enters the left ventricle and then into the ascending aorta. Thus the heart and the brain receive better oxygenated blood. The blood from the right atrium enters into the right ventricle, and from there into the pulmonary artery. Most of the blood from the pulmonary artery enters into the aorta through the ductus arteriosus. From the aorta, the blood is distributed to body tissues and flows through the umbilical arteries into the placenta. The blood circulating in the fetal arterial system is not fully oxygenated There is mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood in the: I. Liver sinusoids II. Inf

erior vena cava III. Right atrium IV. Left atrium V. Descending aorta. I II V IV III What happens at birth? Oh… let me take a deep breath… and then everything will be OK At birth, dramatic changes occur in the circulatory pattern. The changes are initiated by baby’s first breath. ▪Fetal lungs begin to function ▪Placental circulation ceases ▪The three shunts that short-circuited the blood during the fetal life cease to function 1. The infant’s lungs begin to function: ▪ The lungs inflate, which tends to draw blood from the right ventricle. ▪ Oxygenated blood from the lungs passes through pulmonary veins to left atrium. The increased pressure in the left atrium results in closure of the foramen ovale. effectively separating the two atria. ▪ This also increases blood flow to the lungs as blood entering the right atrium can no longer bypass the right ventricle, which pumps it into the pulmonary artery and on to the lungs. Neonatal Circulation 2. The placental circulation ceases. ▪Umbilical vessels are no longer needed. They become obliterated ▪Occlusion of the placental circulation causes fall of blood pressure in the inferior vena cava and right atrium 3. The shunts stop to function:

▪Within a day or two of birth, the ductus arteriosus closes off, preventing blood from the aorta from entering the pulmonary artery ▪The ductus venosus closes off so that all blood entering the liver passes through the hepatic sinusoids. Adult Derivatives of Fetal Vascular Structures Ductus venosus becomes the ligamentum venosum, attached to the inferior vena cava. Ductus arteriousus becomes ligamentum arteriousum Foramen ovale closes shortly after birth, fuses completely in first year and becomes fossa ovalis The intra-abdominal portions of the umbilical arteries become the medial umbilical ligaments The intra-abdominal portion of the umbilical vein becomes the ligamentum teres. (the umbilical vein remains patent for a long time and may be used for exchange transfusions during early infancy. The lumen of the umbilical vein usually does not disappear completely; hence, the ligamentum teres can be cannulated in adults for the injection of contrast medium or chemotherapeutic drugs). Persistence of Fetal Circulation Patent ductus arteriosus and patent foramen ovale each characterize about 8% of congenital heart defects. degenerates • LEFT: • Proximal part: persists as the proximal part of the left pulmonary artery • Distal part: forms ductus arteriosus, a shunt between pulmonary artery and dorsal aorta Changes in the original aortic arch system • Obliteration of: 1. ary venous return. 4. Coronary sinus ASD: Rare. 5. Results from deficiency of the wall between the coronary sinus and left atrium. Patent Ductus Arteriosus • Before birth, the aorta and the pulmonary artery are normally connected by a blood vessel called the ductus arteriosus, which is an essential part of the fetal circulation. • After birth, the vessel is supposed to close within a few days. chunks: ABNORMALITIES OF VASCULAR SYSTEM DR TAHIR HUSSAIN MBBS, DLO, (FCPS), M.Phil, CHPE DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 2 OBJECTIVES Describe the anomalies of arterial system Describe the anomalies of venous system DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 3 INTRODUCTION The vascular system develops very early because the rapidly growing embryo requires an efficient system for delivery of oxygen and nutrients. Vascular abnormalities may result from: • Failure of normal vascular remodeling • Persistence of embryonic vessels that normally disappear • Abnormal regression of vessels that should persist • Abnormal fusion of vascular channels • Abnormal development of aortic arches • Abnormal septation or positioning of the great vessels DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 4 MAJOR GROUPS OF VASCULAR ABNORMALITIES A. Arterial abnormalities • Patent ductus arteriosus • Coarctation of aorta • Abnormal origin of right subclavian artery • Double aortic arch • Right aortic arch • Interrupted aortic arch DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 5 MAJOR GROUPS OF VASCULAR ABNORMALITIES B. Venous abnormalities • Double inferior vena cava • Absence of inferior vena cava • Left superior vena cava • Double superior vena cava DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 6 PATENT DUCTUS ARTERIOSUS Definition: Persis

tence after birth of the ductus arteriosus, which connects the pulmonary trunk or left pulmonary artery to the descending aorta. Embryological basis: The ductus arteriosus develops from the distal part of the left sixth aortic arch. Normally, it closes functionally shortly after birth and later becomes the ligamentum arteriosum. Pathophysiology: After pulmonary vascular resistance falls, blood usually flows from the aorta into the pulmonary artery, producing a left-to-right shunt. DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 7 PATENT DUCTUS ARTERIOSUS DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 8 CLINICAL FEATURES OF PDA • Continuous, machinery-like murmur • Bounding peripheral pulses • Wide pulse pressure • Increased pulmonary blood flow • Heart failure in significant cases Complication: Long-standing, untreated large PDA can cause pulmonary hypertension. DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 9 COARCTATION OF THE AORTA Definition • Coarctation of the aorta is a congenital narrowing of the aorta. • It most commonly occurs near the junction of: Aortic arch and descending thoracic aorta particularly around the region of the ductus arteriosus. Embryological basis • The abnormality is related to abnormal development of the aortic arch/ductus arteriosus region.

DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 10 COARCTATION OF THE AORTA DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 11 CLINICAL FEATURES OF COARCTATION OF THE AORTA High blood pressure in the upper limbs Weak or delayed femoral pulses Lower blood pressure in the lower limbs Cold lower extremities in significant obstruction Rib notching in older patients due to enlarged collateral intercostal arteries DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 12 ABERRANT RIGHT SUBCLAVIAN ARTERY Definition • The right subclavian artery arises abnormally from the distal part of the aortic arch. Normally: Right subclavian artery → brachiocephalic trunk • In this anomaly: Right subclavian artery arises directly from the aortic arch • It may pass behind the esophagus. DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 13 ABERRANT RIGHT SUBCLAVIAN ARTERY DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 14 ABERRANT RIGHT SUBCLAVIAN ARTERY Clinical manifestation Compression of the esophagus may cause: Dysphagia lusoria DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 15 INTERRUPTED AORTIC ARCH Definition • Complete discontinuity between parts of the aortic arch. • This produces severe obstruction to blood flow from the heart to the lower body. Embryological basis • Abnormal development or regression of portions of the embryonic aortic arch system. DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 17 CLINICAL FEA

TURES OF INTERRUPTED AORTIC ARCH • Severe neonatal illness • Poor systemic perfusion • Weak or absent lower-limb pulses • Cyanosis • Heart failure • The ductus arteriosus may be essential for maintaining blood flow to the descending aorta. DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 18 DOUBLE AORTIC ARCH Definition • Formation of two aortic arches, producing a vascular ring around the: Trachea Esophagus • Embryological basis: Persistence of the right dorsal aorta along with the normal left-sided pathway. • Normally, portions of the right dorsal aorta regress. • Failure of appropriate regression produces the double arch. DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 20 DOUBLE AORTIC ARCH Clinical consequences Compression of: •Trachea → respiratory difficulty •Esophagus → difficulty swallowing DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 21 DOUBLE AORTIC ARCH Clinical features Stridor Respiratory distress Dysphagia Recurrent respiratory infections DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 22 RIGHT AORTIC ARCH Normally: Aortic arch develops predominantly on the left side • In a right aortic arch, the arch passes to the right of the trachea. Embryological basis • Abnormal regression/persistence of the embryonic aortic arch system, particularly involving the dorsal aortae. • It may occur alone

or with other congenital heart defects. DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 23 RIGHT AORTIC ARCH Clinical significance • Usually asymptomatic, but may sometimes form a vascular ring and compress: Trachea Esophagus DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 24 MAJOR GROUPS OF VASCULAR ABNORMALITIES B. Venous abnormalities • Double inferior vena cava • Absence of inferior vena cava • Left superior vena cava • Double superior vena cava DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 25 DOUBLE INFERIOR VENA CAVA Definition: It is a congenital venous anomaly in which two inferior vena cava channels are present, usually one on each side of the abdominal aorta. Embryological basis • Normally, the left supracardinal vein largely regresses, while the right supracardinal vein contributes to the infrarenal IVC. • Persistence of the left supracardinal vein results in a second, left-sided IVC. DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 26 DOUBLE IVS AND ABSENT IVC DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 27 DOUBLE INFERIOR VENA CAVA Anatomical arrangement • The right IVC follows the usual course and drains into the right atrium. • The left IVC commonly joins the left renal vein, which crosses anterior to the aorta to join the right IVC. Clinical significance • Usually asymptomatic and discovered incidentally on CT or

MRI. • Important during retroperitoneal surgery, renal surgery, and IVC filter placement. • May be mistaken for enlarged lymph nodes or other retroperitoneal structures. DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 28 ABSENCE OF INFERIOR VENA CAVA Definition: Absence of the IVC is a rare congenital venous anomaly in which a segment or, rarely, nearly the entire IVC fails to develop normally. The clinical pattern depends on which segment is absent. Embryological basis • Abnormal development or regression of the embryonic cardinal veins may prevent normal formation of the IVC. • The common associated pattern is interruption of the hepatic segment with continuation of venous return through the azygos or hemiazygos system. DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 29 ABSENCE OF INFERIOR VENA CAVA Anatomical consequences • Blood from the lower body is redirected through collateral veins. • With azygos continuation, the azygos vein enlarges and carries blood to the superior vena cava. • Hepatic veins commonly drain directly into the right atrium when the hepatic segment of the IVC is interrupted. DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 30 ABSENCE OF INFERIOR VENA CAVA Clinical significance • May be asymptomatic and detected incidentally. • Can predispose younge

r patients to deep venous thrombosis of the lower limbs. • May cause lower-limb venous insufficiency or collateral vein enlargement. • Important to identify before venous catheterization, abdominal surgery, or IVC filter placement. DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 31 PERSISTENT LEFT SUPERIOR VENA CAVA Normal development • The left anterior cardinal vein normally largely disappears. • The remaining portion contributes to the: Coronary sinus • The right anterior cardinal vein contributes to the: Right superior vena cava • Failure of regression of the left anterior cardinal venous system results in a: Persistent left superior vena cava • It commonly drains into the coronary sinus DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 33 PERSISTENT LEFT SUPERIOR VENA CAVA Clinical significance • Most patients are asymptomatic. • It may be discovered incidentally during: Echocardiography Central venous catheterization Cardiac surgery DR TAHIR HUSSAIN 34 DOUBLE SUPERIOR VENA CAVA A patient may have: • Right SVC • Left SVC • The left SVC usually drains into the: Coronary sinus → Right atrium • This is usually clinically insignificant

Basic concept of the Quran: Although the term Quran is the most frequently used in the Book to refer to itself, Allah describes it with several alternate names such as al-Furqān (the Criterion), al-Dhikr (the Reminder), and al-Kitāb (the Book). Many characteristics of the Quran are also mentioned within such as “glad tiding” (bushrā); “knowledge” (ʿilm); “trustworthy handhold” (al-ʿurwah al- wuthqā); “the Truth” (ḥaqq); ‘the rope of Allah” (ḥabl Allāh); and “a clear statement for mankind” (bayān li-l-nās). Reflecting on these Quranic names increases our faith in the revelation, deepens our understanding of its message, and strengthens our connection with our Creator. Prior to exploring the different approaches of ʿUloom Ul Quran, a brief discussion of the scholarly definition of the Quran itself will help guide our understanding of its genres and their disciplinary designations. Multi-disciplinary engagements with the Quran resulted in multi-dimensional definitions of the sacred text, with each definition highlighting a unique approach to the Book of Allah. Some linguists held that the word Quran is a proper noun. Others held that the

word is a verbal noun derived from the root- verb qaraʾa which means ‘read’ or ‘compile’ (jamaʿa). Although Quranic verses frequently use the word Quran to denote ‘recitation,’ different derivations of qaraʾa also signify meanings of understanding, reflection, learning, worship, and afollowing. Jamaʿa implies the compilation of the Book’s chapters and verses. The technical definition of the Quran aims to describe the words of Allah preserved by oral transmission and written codices. Being concerned with the canonicity and the authenticity of the text, most disciplines (including Quranic studies, law, theology and linguistics) demarcate the boundaries of Allah’s final message by focusing on a common set of textual characteristics including inimitability (iʿjāz), mass transmission (tawātur), and conformity with the ʿUthmānic orthography (rasm). Accordingly, a common interdisciplinary definition of the Quran is: The speech of Allah revealed upon His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. Its recitation is used in acts of worship and its smallest chapter is miraculous in nature. HOLY BOOKS  There are four Holy books  The main and most important subject of the holy book is human being.  The main source

from whome the mankind judge between right and wrong is the Holy Book  The Zaboor is the oldest holy book  The Torait holy book is called the oldest testament.  The Injeel (bible) holy book is the New Testament.  The name of religious book of Muslims is the Quran.  All the religious books were revealed in the month of Ramzan.  Injeel (bible) was revealed on the Prophet Jesus.  The quran was revealed the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ.  Torait was revealed on the prophet Moses.  Zuboor was revealed on the prophet david.  114 number of Surah in the Holy book  The Surah means city of refuge.  Number of Makki Surah’s is 86.  Numbers of Madani Surah’s is 28.  Numbers of Rukus is 540.  The short Shurah of the holy Quran is Al Kausar.  Number of the Holy Quran stages is 7.  Numbers of bows (prostrations)of the holy Quran.14  Surah-Al-Tauba does not start with Bismillah  In Surah Namal Bismillah has occurred twice.  The number of Quranic verses is 6666.  The number of Mukatat words is 29.  Hazarat Zaid Bin Haris (R.A) companion of the Prophet ﷺ been mentioned in the holy Quran.  Hazarat Khalid Bin saeed (R.A)was the first writer of “Wahi”  Dr.khalifa abdul hakeem was the first

muslim to interpret Quran in English in 1905.  Shah Abdul Qadir interpreted the Quran in Urdu  Quran-e-Majeed the last code of heavenly guidance was sent down by Allah upon Muhammad ﷺ in course of 23year.  Surahs revealed before Hijrah are termed Makki and those after Hijrah are termed Madni. They do not mean that the ayat were explicitly revealed in Makkah or Madinah. o In Makki Surahs Allah talks about Tawheed and correcting faith of people while in Madni Surahs, Allah talks about commands and one’s relations with his family other people etc. o There are 86 Makki surahs and 28 Madani Surahs. This show that correcting faith and beliefs is more important than directly ordering someone. o In Makki Surahs, generally the form of address used is ياايّهاالناس (O People) while in Madani Surahs it is ياايّهاالذين آمنوا (O Believers). This is because Allah had to correct the beliefs of all men but he was ordering only those who had believed ( ياايّهاالذين آمنوا) in Madani surahs. 2. History of Quran The very first revelation of the Holy Qur’an took place Ramadhan in the year 610 AD. At this time the Holy Prophet (saw) had reached the age of 40. For many years it had become his practice

to visit a small cave in mount Hira, situated around 3 miles from the city of Makkah. The Holy Prophet (saw) would retreat to this cave in solitude and meditate there for many days. He would take supplies of food and water and engage in long prayers. As the years progressed these periods of solitude became more pronounced extending his stay from days into weeks. During the month of Ramadhan Holy Prophet (saw) would keep fasts and spend the entire month in this spiritual state of solitude. The journey of the Quran, in its original form to the present day is a characteristic that none of the previous sacred books have. The companions of Prophet Muhammad, who were great people, played an important role in the compilation of the Quran, leaving an interesting story behind. Compilation of the Quran During the 23 years of Muhammad's time as a prophet, the verses of the Quran were memorized as they were revealed, and about 42 scribes wrote the verses on different materials such as paper, cloth, bone fragments and leather. During the time of Caliph Abu Bakr, when 700 people who knew the Quran by heart (qari), were killed in the Battle of Yamama, Umar ibn al-Khattab became concerned and app

ealed to Abu Bakr in order to compile the Quran into a book. Abu Bakr formed a delegation under the leadership of Zaid ibn Thabit, one of the leading scribes. This delegation of 12 people, including famous figures such as Usman ibn Affan, Ali ibn Abi Talib, Talha ibn Ubaydullah, Abdullah ibn Masood, Ubayy ibn Kab, Khalid ibn al-Walid and Hudhaifah, came together and collected all the materials on which verses from the Quran were written. In addition, the verses memorized by the companions were heard as well. Each of them was asked to show two witnesses for the verse they read. Mushaf Thus, all the verses of the Quran that describe the creation of the universe and people, judgment day, exemplary stories of the people who lived before and the beliefs, worship, morals and legal bases that believers should obey were collected together into a single-volume book. Each of the verses was taught by the archangel Gabriel and declared by Prophet Muhammad. The verse is the name given to each sentence of the Quran and the surah is the name given to each part of the holy book. There are 6,236/6666 verses, 114 surahs. Saeed ibn al-Aas, who was renowned for the beauty of his handwriting, wrote the

m down on gazelle skin. The writing used was the Arabic script of the time, which was already old and used commonly at that time in Hejaz. The copy of the Quran was recited to the companions at a general meeting. There was no objection. So, a book called "mushaf" emerged, which means written verses. A total of 33,000 companions agreed that every letter of the Quran was in the right place. Then this mushaf was sent to Umar ibn al-Khattab. After his death, this book passed on to Hazrat Hafsah, the daughter of Umar and a wife of Prophet Muhammad. Dialect (Language) of Quraysh A difference was observed in the recitation of the Quran in the Armenia battles between Muslims from Damascus and Iraq during the period of the third caliph, Usman. Hudhaifah, one of the companions, went before the caliph on his way back from an expedition and asked him to prevent this. On the 25th year of the hijra (647), Usman gathered a delegation attended by Abdullah ibn al-Zubair, Saeed ibn al-Aas and Abd al-Rahman ibn Harith under the leadership of Zaid ibn Thabit. All of them, except for Zaid, were from Quraysh. Usman said that the dialect (Language) of Quraysh should be preferred if they were to fall into

conflict with Zaid bin Sabit regarding the dialect(Language), since Muhammad was from the Quraysh tribe. The Quran had been revealed in seven dialects (Language) of the Arabic language of the time. The first Muslims who were literate could easily read the writing of their own language, but somewhat differently, since at the time the Arabic script did not have diacritical marks to differentiate letters or vowel symbols. For example, those from the Tameem tribe pronounced the letter "sin" as "te" and read the word "nas" as "nat." It was diverse and convenient, and did not change the meaning. The delegation brought the original mushaf from Hafsah. In this mushaf, the surahs were not separated from each other. The surahs were sorted according to the order of their descent in Ali's manuscript and according to their lengths in the manuscript of Abdullah ibn Masood. Now the verses were written in the Quraysh dialect. The surahs were arranged in rows, separated from each other regarding their length and alignment with each other. The order of the surahs was not based on the order the archangel Gabriel gave them to Prophet Muhammad, but on the consensus of the companions. Seven copies From

Islamic Concept of Society: • In Islam, society is not merely a group of people — it is an organized community bound by the principles of Allah's guidance. • The Islamic society is built on Tawheed (Oneness of Allah), brotherhood, justice, and mutual cooperation. • Every member of Islamic society has rights AND responsibilities toward others. • Islam gives a complete social code: duties to Allah, to oneself, to family, to neighbors, and to the whole of mankind. Islam is not only a religion of worship — it is a complete system that governs every aspect of social life. No Arab has superiority over a non-Arab, nor does a non-Arab have superiority over an Arab, nor does a red man have superiority over a black man, nor does a black man over a red man — except through piety (Taqwa). • This declaration came at the Farewell Hajj — it is Islam's eternal charter of human equality. • Status in Islam is determined by piety (Taqwa) alone — not by birth, wealth, race, or nationality. Equality before Allah is Islam's foundational principle of social justice. Rights of Humans in Islam Islam guarantees the following fundamental rights to every human being: • ①Living Freely — Every person has the right to life and freedom. No one can be enslaved unjustly. • ②Economic Rights — Every

person has the right to earn and own property lawfully. • ③Education — Seeking knowledge is obligatory upon every Muslim, male and female. • ④Right of Free Thinking — Islam grants freedom of thought, within the boundaries of Shariah. • ⑤Political Rights — Muslims have the right to participate in governance through Shura (consultation). • ⑥Justice — Every person has the right to equal treatment before the law. • ⑦Marriage — Every adult Muslim has the right to marry lawfully. "There is no compulsion in religion." (Surah Al-Baqarah 2:256) — Islam is built on freedom and choice. his Hadith from the Farewell Sermon is Islam's declaration of the sanctity of human life, property and honor. • Killing an innocent person is among the gravest sins in Islam. (Surah Al-Alaq 96:1) Education is not a privilege in Islam — it is a right AND a religious obligation for every Muslim. Women's Rights in Islam ①Women's Education: • Islam grants women the full right to seek education. The Prophet ﷺsaid: 'Seeking knowledge is an obligation upon every Muslim.' (Ibn Majah 224) ②Economic Rights: • Women have the right to own property, conduct trade, and inherit wealth independently. Their wealth belongs to them

alone. ③Social Rights: • Women have the right to choose their spouse, to divorce (through Khul'), to participate in society, and to express their opinions. ④Duties of Men toward Women: • The husband must provide maintenance (Nafaqah), kind treatment, and fulfill the rights of his wife. • 'The best of you are those who are the best to their wives.' Maintaining family ties earns Allah's mercy. Cutting them earns Allah's displeasure. Rights of Neighbors in Islam Three Types of Neighbors: • ①The neighbor who is also a relative — has THREE rights: neighbor's right, relative's right, and Muslim's right. • ②The neighbor who is a stranger — has TWO rights: neighbor's right and the general right of humanity. • ③The casual or temporary neighbor — has ONE right: general human dignity. And if you disclose what is in your hearts or conceal it Allah shall make you account for it, then He shall forgive whom He wills and punish whom He wills. And Allah is powerful over everything. ؤ ّ ونِ و ِ ِل ء نِ ِِّّ بِّ ّ ِّ و ّ و بّ ّ وَ رُسُلّهّۦ لَِ نُفَرلّ قُِ بَيأنَِ أَحَد ِ ملّن رُّسُلّهّۦ ِۚ وَ قَالُوا ِ سَمّعأنَا وَ أَطَعأنَا ِۖ غُفأرَ انَكَِ رَبَنَا وَ إّلَيأكَِ ٱلأِ مَصّ يرُِ ٥٨٢ The Messenger has believed in what has been revealed to him from his Lord, and the believers as well. All have believed in Allah, and His angels and His Books, and His Messengers. "We make no division between any of His Messengers," and they have said: "We have listened and obeyed Our لَا يُكَل ِّفُا ٱّللَ ُا نَفْسًا إِّلَا وُسْعَهَا اۚ لَهَا مَا كَسَبَتْا وَعَلَيْهَا امَا ٱكْتَسَبَتْا اۗ رَبَنَا لَا تُؤَاخِّ ذْنَا ا إِّن نَسِّينَا ا أَا أَوْا خْطَأْنَا اۚ رَبَنَا

وَلَا تَحْمِّا لْا عَلَيْنَا ا إِّصْرً ًۭ ا كَمَا حَمَلْتَهُۥ عَلَى ٱلَذِّينَا مِّن قَبْلِّنَا ۚۚاAllah does not obligate anyone beyond his capacity. For him is what he has earned, and on him what he has incurred. "Our Lord, do not hold us accountable, if we forget or make a mistake and, Our Lord, do not place on us a burden such as You have placed on those before us. رَبَنَا وَلَا تُحَم ِّلْنَا مَا لَا طَاقَةَا لَنَا بِّهِّۦ اۖ وَ ٱعْفُا عَنَا وَ ٱغْفِّرْا لَنَا وَ ٱرْحَمْنَا ا اۚ أَنتَا مَوْ لَىٰنَا فَٱنصُرْنَا لَى عَا ٱلْقَوْ مِّا ٱلْكَـٰفِّرِّ ينَا ٦٨٢ And our Lord, do not make us bear that for which we have no strength. And pardon us. And grant us forgiveness. And have mercy on us. You are our Lord. Help us, then, against the disbelieving people. جزاکما ہللااخيرااکثيرااوااجرااجزيال HABIB-UN-NABI Associaet Professor Govt. College of Education FB Area, Karachi

subject: Islamiat
chunks: َوَ عِبَادُ ٱلرَّحْمَـٰنِ ٱلَّذِينَ يَمْشُونَ ع لَى ٱْلْ َرْ ضِ هَوْ ن ًۭا وَ إِذَا خَ اطَبَهُمُ ٱلْجَـٰهِلُونَ قَالُوا۟ سَلَـٰم ًۭ ا ٣٦ And the slaves of the Rahman are those who walk on the earth humbly and when the ignorant people speak to them, they reply peacefully, ًۭ وَ ٱلَّذِينَ يَبِيتُونَ لِرَب ِهِمْ سُجَّد ا وَ قِيَـٰم ًۭ ا ٤٦ and those who pass the night prostrating and standing before their Lord, َّوَ ٱلَّذِينَ يَقُولُونَ رَبَّنَا ٱصْرِ فْ عَن ا عَذَابَ جَهَنَّمَ ۖ إِنَّ عَذَ ابَهَا كَانَ غَرَ ام ا ٥٦ and those who say, "Our Lord, avert from us the punishment of Jahannam; indeed, its punishment is a persisting affliction. إِنَّهَا سَآءَتْ مُسْتَقَر ًۭ ا وَ مُقَام ًۭ ا ٦٦ Indeed, evil it is as an abode and a place to dwell in ۟وَ ٱلَّذِينَ إِذَآ أَنفَقُوا۟ لَمْ يُسْرِ فُوا وَ لَمْ يَقْتُرُوا۟ وَ كَانَ بَيْنَ ذَٰلِكَ قَوَ ام ًۭ ا ٧٦ - and those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant nor miserly, and it (i.e. their spending) is moderate in between (the two extremes) َوَ ٱلَّذِينَ َلَ يَدْعُونَ مَعَ ٱَّللَّ ِ إِلَـٰه ا ء اخَرَ وَ َلَ يَقْتُلُونَ ٱلنَّفْ سَ ٱلَّتِى حَرَّمَ ٱَّللَّ ُ إَِلَّ بِٱلْحَق ِ وَ َلَ يَزْ نُونَ ۚ وَ مَ ن يَفْعَلْ ذَٰلِكَ يَلْقَ أَثَام ًۭ ا ٨٦

- and those who do not invoke any other god along with Allah, and do not kill a person whom Allah has given sanctity, except rightfully, nor do they fornicate; and whoever does it, shall face the recompense of his sin, َيُضَـٰعَفْ لَهُ ٱلْعَذَابُ يَوْ مَ ٱلْقِيَـٰم ةِ وَ يَخْلُدْ فِيهِۦ مُهَان ا ٩٦ ]the punishment will be doubled for him and he will remain there disdained, forever, َإَِلَّ مَن تَابَ وَ ءَامَنَ وَ عَمِلَ عَمًَل ًۭ ص ـٰلِح ًۭ ا فَأُو۟ لَـٰٓئِكَ يُبَ د ِلُ ٱَّللَّ ُ سَي ِـَٔاتِهِمْ حَسَنَـٰت ٍۢ ۗ وَ كَانَ ٱَّللَّ ُ غَفُور ًۭ ا رَّحِ يم ًۭ ا ٠٧ except the one who repents and believes and does good deeds, then Allah will change the bad deeds of such people into good ones, and Allah is Most- Forgiving, Very-Merciful. ُوَ مَن تَابَ وَ عَمِلَ صَـٰلِح ًۭ ا فَإِنَّهُۥ يَت وبُ إِلَى ٱَّللَّ ِ مَتَاب ًۭا ١٧ And whoever repents and does righteous deeds turns to Allah truly ُّوَ ٱلَّذِينَ َلَ يَشْهَدُونَ ٱلزُّ ورَ وَ إِذَا مَر وا۟ بِٱللَّ ْوِ مَرُّ وا۟ كِرَ ام ًۭ ا ٢٧ - and those who do not witness falsehood, and when they pass by the absurd things, Pass by with dignity ِ وَ ٱلَّذِينَ إِذَا ذُك ِرُوا۟ بِـَٔايَـٰتِ رَب هِمْ لَمْ يَخِ رُّ وا۟ عَلَيْهَا صُ م ًۭ ا وَ عُمْيَان ًۭا ٣

٧ ]and those who, when they are reminded of the verses of their Lord, do not fall at them as deaf and blind ones َوَ ٱلَّذِينَ يَقُولُونَ رَبَّنَا هَبْ لَنَا مِنْ أ زْ وَٰ جِ نَا وَ ذُر ِ يَّـٰتِنَا قُرَّ ةَ أَعْيُن ٍۢ وَ ٱجْعَلْنَا لِلْمُتَّقِينَ إِمَام ا ٤٧ - and those who say, "Our Lord, Give us, from our spouses and our children, coolness of eyes and make us heads of the God-fearing. َأُو۟ لَـٰٓئِكَ يُجْزَوْ نَ ٱلُْْرْ فَةَ بِمَا ص بَرُوا۟ وَ يُلَقَّوْ نَ فِيهَا تَ حِ يَّة ًۭ وَ سَلَـٰم ا ٥٧ Such people will be rewarded with the high place - because they observed patience - and will be received therein with prayers of their eternal life and peace, َخَـٰلِدِينَ فِيهَا ۚ حَسُنَتْ مُسْتَقَر ًۭ ا و مُقَام ًۭ ا ٦٧ living in it (the Paradise) forever. It is best as an abode and as a place to dwell in. َقُلْ مَا يَعْبَؤُا۟ بِكُمْ رَب ِى لَوْ َلَ دُع آؤُكُمْ ۖ فَقَدْ كَذَّبْتُمْ فَ سَوْ فَ يَكُونُ لِزَ ام ٍۢ ا ٧٧ Say (0 Prophet), "My Lord will never care about you, if you will not invoke Him. Now since you belied (the truth), the punishment will be inseparable from you. جزاکم ہللا خیرا کثیرا و اجرا جزیال HABIB-UN-NABI Associaet Professor Govt. College of Education FB Area, Karachi

subject: Islamiat
chunks: َقَدْ أَفْلَحَ ٱلْمُؤْمِنُون ١Success is really attained by the believers َٱلَّذِينَ هُمْ فِى صََلَ تِهِمْ خَـٰشِعُون ٢ who are concentrative in their Salah (prayers) َوَ ٱلَّذِينَ هُمْ عَنِ ٱللَّغْوِ مُعْرِ ضُون ٣ and who keep themselves away from vain things َوَ ٱلَّذِينَ هُمْ لِلزَّكَوٰ ةِ فَـٰعِلُون , ٤and who are performers of Zakah, َوَ ٱلَّذِينَ هُمْ لِفُرُوجِ هِمْ حَـٰفِظُون ٥and who guard their private parts َإَِّلَّ عَلَىٰٰٓ أَزْ وَٰ جِ هِمْ أَوْ مَا مَلَكَتْ أ يْمَـٰنُهُمْ فَإِنَّهُمْ غَيْرُ مَ لُومِينَ ٦ except from their wives or from those (slave- girls) owned by their right hands, because they are not liable to blame. ٰٰٓفَمَنِ ٱبْتَغَىٰ وَ رَآٰءَ ذَٰلِكَ فَأُو۟ لَـ ئِكَ هُمُ ٱلْعَادُونَ ٧ However, those who seek (sexual pleasure) beyond that are the transgressors ْوَ ٱلَّذِينَ هُمْ ِلِ َمَـٰنَـٰتِهِمْ وَ عَهْدِهِم رَٰ عُونَ ٨ -and (success is attained) by those who honestly look after their trusts and covenant, ِوَ ٱلَّذِينَ هُمْ عَلَىٰ صَلَوَٰ تِهِمْ يُحَاف ظُونَ ٩ and who consistently observe their prayers. َأُو۟ لَـٰٰٓئِكَ هُمُ ٱلْوَٰ رِ ثُون ٠١Those are the inheritors َٱلَّذِينَ يَرِ ثُونَ ٱلْفِرْ دَوْ سَ هُمْ فِيه ا خَـٰلِدُونَ ١١ who will inherit Firdaus (the

chunks: ISLAMIC STUDIES TOPIC/ CHAPTER 3 SEERAT E NABAVI ﷺ LECTURE 1ST Life Of Prophet Muhammad ﷺBefore Prophethood His Noble Birth. • The Messenger of Allah ﷺ, was from the noblest tribe of the Quraish, Bani Hashim. He was born on the 9th or 12th of Rabi al-Awwal, Monday, April 20, 571. • He was born in Shaab Abi Talib in the morning of Sadiq Razaat (Feeding/Fostering). • The Prophet ﷺinitially nursed from his mother, Amina bint Wahib. Later, he was also nourished by Mrs. Thawbia (sobia) and then Mrs. Halima Saadia, both of whom were blessed to provide him with their milk. Boyhood. • Halima Saadia says that the Holy Prophet ﷺwas different from other children and the Holy Prophet ﷺnever did anything wrong. In the books of Hadith and Sear and in Nahj al- Balaghah, it is narrated from Hazrat Ameerul Momineen Ali bin Abi Talib that Allah appointed a high angel who always kept the Holy Prophet ﷺon good manners and morals. Journey of Madina Munawwara with mother to visit grave of father. • When the Holy Prophet ﷺreached the age of six years, his mother(Amna rz) took him to Medina to visit the grave of his respected father Abdullah, and the Holy Prophet ﷺ stayed there for a month with his belove

d mother. Death of mother (at the age of 6). • After a month, when she returned to Makkah, she died on the way at Maqam Abuwa Miss. Umm Amin took the Prophet ﷺto Makkah. In this way, the Holy Prophet ﷺwas separated from both his mother and father at the age of 6. Life with grandfather. • After the death of his mother, the Prophet ﷺwas given a place in his love by Abdul Muttalib, the grandfather of the Prophet ﷺ and he trained him. He always kept the Holy Prophet ﷺwith him and preferred the Holy Prophet ﷺover his children. But God Almighty approved something else. The Prophet ﷺlost this love too at the age of 8. Life with uncle (at the age of 8). • "When the Holy Prophet ﷺ' s grandfather, respected Abdul Muttalib, was on his deathbed, he handed over the Prophet's ﷺcare to his son, respected Abu Talib, and advised him, 'Look after him in such a way that he does not suffer any sorrow or pain after my passing, nor become dependent on others.'" Event of shaq e sadar (splitting the chest and wasning the heart) • Shaq Sadr was done four times, that is, Sina Mubarak was chalked.In the early years of Umar Mubarak, Hazrat Halimah Sadia, may Allah be pleased with her, • At the age of ten, • I

n the Cave of Hira on the occasion of the beginning of revelation • And the Night of Ascension. Trade journey and meeting with the monk baheera • The Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) was 9 years old when he went on his first trade journey with his uncle Abu Talib. They traveled from makkah to Syria, a distance of about 1,000 miles. They traveled to Syria and along the way, they met a monk named Bahira. Bahira was a Christian monk who was well-versed in the scriptures. He recognized the Prophet Muhammad as a special child and told Abu Talib to protect him from harm. Bahira also predicted that the Prophet Muhammad would one day become a great prophet. Titles of Al-Ameen and Al-Sadiq • The Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) was known by two titles: Al-Ameen and Al-Sadiq. Al-Ameen means "the Trustworthy" and Al-Sadiq means "the Truthful." These titles were given to him because he was known for his honesty, trustworthiness, and truthfulness. He was always true to his word and he was always honest in his dealings with others. • The title of Al-Ameen was given to the Prophet Muhammad when he was just a young boy. The people of makkah used to trust him with their valuables and they knew that he would never betray t

heir trust. The title of Al-Sadiq was given to him later in life, after he had proven his trustworthiness and truthfulness on many occasions. Adolescence • The youth of our beloved and esteemed Prophet ﷺholds great significance, and two particular incidents bear witness to the truth of his prophethood. • One is the incident of "Halful-Fudul" (Alliance of Virtue) and the other is the rebuilding of the Kaaba. Reconciliation and making compromise.(Renovation of KABA and event of TAHKEEM) The Ka'bah, the House of Allah, has served the purpose for which it was built by Abraham and his son Ismael thousands of years ago, At the time of Muhammad ﷺwas thirty-five years old. His wisdom benefited many people. One such time was when Quraysh decided to rebuild the Ka‟bah. Each tribe brought stones and they built the Ka'bah up until they reached the place where the black stone was to be set. They then began to argue about who should have the honor of carrying the black stone and lifting it to its place in one of the corners of the Ka'bah. Normal way of life.(Marriage, business) Business Among Quraysh was a respected and wealthy woman named Khadijah. She was involved in trade and on hearing of Mo

hammed‟s reputation, sent for him and asked him to take her goods and trade with them in Syria. Muhammad (ﷺ) agreed and left for Syria with one of Khadijah's caravans. With him went her slave, Maysarah, and they spent a great deal of time talking together. Maysarah soon came to admire Muhammad (ﷺ). He thought he was quite different from all the other men of Quraysh. Marriage with Khadijah bint-e-Khwailid rz By the time Muhammad (ﷺ) was twenty-five , Khadijah was a widow in her forties and as well as being rich and highly respected she was also very beautiful. Many men wanted to marry her but none of them suited her. When she met Muhammad (ﷺ), however, she thought he was very special. She sent a friend to ask Muhammad (ﷺ) why he was not married. Muhammad (ﷺ) said that it was because he had no money, to which the friend replied: 'Supposing a rich, beautiful and noble lady agreed to marry you?' Muhammad (ﷺ) wanted to know who that could be. The friend told him it was Khadijah. Muhammad (ﷺ) was very happy, because he greatly respected Khadijah. He went with his uncles, Abu Talib and Hamzah, to Khadijah's uncle, and asked his permission to marry her. The uncle gave his permission and so

on after, Muhammad (ﷺ) and Khadijah were married. Their marriage was a joyful one and Muhammad (ﷺ) and Khadijah were well suited. Their life together, however, was not without some sadness. They were blessed with six children, two sons and four daughters. Sadly their first born, a son called Qasim, died shortly before his second birthday, and their last child, also a son, only lived for a short time. Happily, their four daughters-Zaynab, Ruqayyah, Umm Kulthum, and Fatimah-all survived. LECTURE 2ND Life Of Prophet Muhammad ﷺafter Prophet hood in MAKKAH Announcement of Prophet hood.(at the age of 40=1 N) • Muhammad ﷺbelieved that there was only one Allah, Creator of the sun, the moon, the earth, the sky, and of all living things, and that all people should worship only Him. Muhammad ﷺwould often leave the crowded city and go to the cave in Mount Hira'. He liked to be alone there, away from all thoughts of the world and daily life, eating and drinking little. In his fortieth year, Muhammad ﷺleft Makkah to spend Ramadan, the traditional month of retreat, in the cave. In the second half of Ramadan, Allah began to reveal His message for mankind through Muhammad ﷺ. This first Revelation o

ccurred as follows. The Angel Gabriel came to Muhammad ﷺin the cave and commanded him to 'Read'. • Muhammad ﷺwas stopped by a voice from heaven which said; '0 Muhammad ﷺyou are the Messenger of Allah, and I am Gabriel.' He looked up at the sky and wherever he turned he saw the Angel Gabriel. Meeting with Warqa Bin Nofil • After 1st Wahi Muhammad ﷺreturned home to Khadijah. When his wife saw him she became very worried as he began to shiver, as though in a fever. He asked her to wrap him in blankets, which she did. After a while he recovered sufficiently to tell her what had happened at Hira'. Khadijah believed all that he told her and with great respect said: 'Be happy, 0 son of my uncle and be confident. Truly I swear by Allah who has my soul in His hands, that you will be our people's Prophet.' Muhammad ﷺ, the Messenger of Allah, was eased by her faith in him, but after all that had happened he was exhausted and felt fast asleep. • After that Khadijah and Prophet ﷺwent to see her cousin, Waraqah Ibn Nawfal, to ask him what he thought about all that had happened. Waraqah was a very wise man who had read many books and had become a Christian after studying the Bible. He told Khadij

ah that Muhammad ﷺhad been chosen by Allah to be His Messenger. Just as the Angel Gabriel had come to Moses before and had ordered him to guide his people, so, too, would Muhammad ﷺ be the Prophet of his people. But Waraqah warned that all the people would not listen to the Prophet and some would mistreat his followers. He must, however, be patient because he had a great message for all the world. From that day on, the Angel Gabriel came often to the Prophet ﷺand the verses he taught him, the message from Allah to man, were later written down, and are known to us as the Holy Qur'an. Time gap between 1st and 2nd revelation (fatrat ul wahi) • The time gap between the first and second revelation is known as Fatrat ul Wahi. It is a period of time when the Prophet Muhammad did not receive any revelations from Allah. • There are a number of reasons why the Prophet Muhammad did not receive any revelations during this time. Some scholars believe that it was a period of preparation for the Prophet Muhammad, during which he was learning and growing spiritually.
